{{draft}} {{Expand Japanese|シタテルヒメ}}{{Infobox deity | type = [[Shinto]] | father = [[Ōkuninushi]] | mother = {{ill|Takiribime|ja|タキリビメ|simple|User:Immanuelle/Takiribime|en:draft}} |cult_centre={{ill|Shitori Shrine (Tottori)|lt=Shitori Shrine|en}},
{{ill|Kifune Shrine|simple|User:Immanuelle/Kifune Shrine|en}}|name=Shitateruhime|siblings=[[Ajisukitakahikone]]|spouse={{ill|Ame no Wakahiko|en}}|image=File:Shitori-jinja, haiden.jpg|caption={{ill|Shitori Shrine (Tottori)|lt=Shitori Shrine|en}} where she is worshipped}}{{complex}} {{User:Immanuelle/Promising Draft}} {{ill|Shitateruhime|lt=Shitateruhime-no-Mikoto|ja|シタテルヒメ|simple|User:Immanuelle/Shitateruhime|en:draft|8=fr}} is a daughter of {{ill|Takiribime|ja|タキリビメ|simple|User:Immanuelle/Takiribime|en:draft|8=fr}}, one of the three sisters worshipped at [[Munakata Taisha|Munakata Taisha]] The origins of {{ill|Shitori Shrine (Tottori)|lt=Shitori Shrine|en|4=fr|5=Shitori-jinja|6=ja|7=倭文神社_(湯梨浜町)|8=simple|9=User:Immanuelle/Shitori Shrine (Tottori)}} are unknown. Although there is no documentary evidence, it is believed that it began as the family shrine for the {{Nihongo|Shitori clan|倭文氏}} of [[Kofun period|Kofun period]] craftsmen who weavers, who regarded {{ill|Takehazuchi|lt=Takehazuchi-no-Mikoto|ja|天羽槌雄神|simple|User:Immanuelle/Takehazuchi|en:draft|8=fr}} as their ancestor. However, the shrine's legends are all centered around {{ill|Shitateruhime|lt=Shitateruhime-no-Mikoto|ja|シタテルヒメ|simple|User:Immanuelle/Shitateruhime|en:draft|8=fr}}, whom the shrine legend claims arrived in this location from [[Izumo Taisha|Izumo]] by boat. She established her residence on the mountain behind this shrine, and after her death, she was buried in a ''[[kofun|kofun]]'' constructed in the shrine's precincts.{{cite book |last1=Yoshiki |first1=Emi |title=Zenkoku 'Ichinomiya' tettei gaido |date=2007 |publisher=PHP Institute |isbn=978-4569669304 |language=Japanese}} == Marriage == In many versions of the myth {{ill|Ame no Hohi|en}} did not send a word for three years after going down to earth, all the gods gathered up, and {{ill|Ame no Wakahiko|en}} was one who was chosen to rule the earth. In many versions {{ill|Ame no Wakahiko|en}} was given a bow.{{Cite web|title=Encyclopedia of Shinto - Home: Kami in Classic Texts: Ame no Wakahiko|url=http://eos.kokugakuin.ac.jp/modules/xwords/entry.php?entryID=46|access-date=2020-09-29|website=eos.kokugakuin.ac.jp}}{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=xdfgjV2kw6oC&q=Ame+no+Wakahiko&pg=PA6|title=Japanese Mythology A to Z|last=Roberts|first=Jeremy|date=2009|publisher=Infobase Publishing|isbn=978-1-4381-2802-3|language=en}} In some versions, however, Ame no Wakahiko is the son of Ame no Hohi and Ame no Wakahiko was sent to earth to look for him.{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=xdfgjV2kw6oC&dq=Ame+no+Wakahiko&pg=PA6|title=Japanese Mythology a to Z|publisher=Infobase|year=2009|isbn=9781438128023}} She married {{ill|Ame no Wakahiko|en}}, when he came from heaven to discuss the "{{ill|Kuni-yuzuri|en}}". === Death === Eight years later, the gods had not yet heard a response so they sent a bird named Nakime down to earth to check in on him. Following the advice of a wise woman, Ame no Wakahiko used his bow to shoot the bird.{{Cite book|title=Handbook of Japanese mythology|last=Ashkenazi|first=Michael|date=2008|publisher=Oxford University Press|isbn=978-0-19-533262-9|series=Handbooks of world mythology|location=Oxford|pages=114}} The bird was killed but the arrow flew all the way to heaven. {{ill|Takamimusubi|en}} saw the arrow and threw it back at the earth where it hit Ame no Wakahiko while he was laying in bed, killing him.{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=uAj_PQ8o40sC&q=Takamimusubi|title=The East|date=1992|publisher=East Publications, Incorporated|language=en}} Other versions state that {{ill|Amaterasu|en}} was the one who shot the arrow back at him.{{cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=FlZxh5OaZxoC&pg=PA38|title=Impurity and Death: A Japanese Perspective|last=Abe|first=C.|publisher=Universal Publishers|year=2003|isbn=978-1-58112-195-7|page=38|access-date=2020-09-29}} This myth is the origin of a Japanese saying about the returning arrow. It is likely also be a mythicisation of attempts made by the {{ill|Yamato Kingship|en}} to impose its authority over neighbouring states. === Funeral === After Ame no Wakahiko's death, his parents built a hut (喪屋 moya) for their son. {{ill|Ajisukitakahikone|en}} went down to pay his respect. However, due to Ajisukitakahikone looking similar to Ame no Wakahiko he was mistaken to be Ame no Wakahiko brought back to life. Ajisukitakahikone was offended by this and destroyed the hut and kicked it. The hut landed in the land of Mino and became a mountain called Moyama.{{Cite book|title=Nihongi: Chronicles of Japan from the Earliest Times to A.D. 697, Volume 1|chapter=Book II|chapter-url=https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/Nihongi:_Chronicles_of_Japan_from_the_Earliest_Times_to_A.D._697/Book_II}} When {{ill|Ame no Wakahiko|en}} passed away, Shitateruhime's sorrowful voice was heard in the Plain of High Heaven. During his funeral, Amewakahiko's father, Amatsukunitama, and other family members confused Shitateruhime's step-brother, [[Ajisukitakahikone]], for the deceased Amewakahiko. [[Ajisukitakahikone]] left in rage. In response, Shitateruhime sang a song of a type called hinaburi, or "rustic song" to honor her deceased husband.{{Cite web|title=Encyclopedia of Shinto詳細|url=https://d-museum.kokugakuin.ac.jp/eos/detail/?id=9155|access-date=2024-03-24|website=國學院大學デジタルミュージアム|language=ja}} == See Also == * {{ill|Munakata clan|ja|宗像氏|simple|User:Immanuelle/Munakata_clan|ja|宗像氏|fr|Clan Munakata}} ==References== {{reflist|draft}} == Further reading == * Jugon, Jean-Claude. {{draft}} {{Expand Japanese|シタテルヒメ}}{{Infobox deity | type = [[Shinto]] | father = [[Ōkuninushi]] | mother = {{ill|Takiribime|ja|タキリビメ|simple|User:Immanuelle/Takiribime|en:draft}} |cult_centre={{ill|Shitori Shrine (Tottori)|lt=Shitori Shrine|en}},
{{ill|Kifune Shrine|simple|User:Immanuelle/Kifune Shrine|en}}|name=Shitateruhime|siblings=[[Ajisukitakahikone]]|spouse={{ill|Ame no Wakahiko|en|10=en:draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ame-No-Wakahiko}}|image=File:Shitori-jinja, haiden.jpg|caption={{ill|Shitori Shrine (Tottori)|lt=Shitori Shrine|en}} where she is worshipped}}{{complex}} {{User:Immanuelle/Promising Draft}} {{ill|Shitateruhime|lt=Shitateruhime-no-Mikoto|ja|シタテルヒメ|simple|User:Immanuelle/Shitateruhime|en:draft|8=fr}} is a daughter of {{ill|Takiribime|ja|タキリビメ|simple|User:Immanuelle/Takiribime|en:draft|8=fr}}, one of the three sisters worshipped at [[Munakata Taisha|Munakata Taisha]] The origins of {{ill|Shitori Shrine (Tottori)|lt=Shitori Shrine|en|4=fr|5=Shitori-jinja|6=ja|7=倭文神社_(湯梨浜町)|8=simple|9=User:Immanuelle/Shitori Shrine (Tottori)}} are unknown. Although there is no documentary evidence, it is believed that it began as the family shrine for the {{Nihongo|Shitori clan|倭文氏}} of [[Kofun period|Kofun period]] craftsmen who weavers, who regarded {{ill|Takehazuchi|lt=Takehazuchi-no-Mikoto|ja|天羽槌雄神|simple|User:Immanuelle/Takehazuchi|en:draft|8=fr}} as their ancestor. However, the shrine's legends are all centered around {{ill|Shitateruhime|lt=Shitateruhime-no-Mikoto|ja|シタテルヒメ|simple|User:Immanuelle/Shitateruhime|en:draft|8=fr}}, whom the shrine legend claims arrived in this location from [[Izumo Taisha|Izumo]] by boat. She established her residence on the mountain behind this shrine, and after her death, she was buried in a ''[[kofun|kofun]]'' constructed in the shrine's precincts.{{cite book |last1=Yoshiki |first1=Emi |title=Zenkoku 'Ichinomiya' tettei gaido |date=2007 |publisher=PHP Institute |isbn=978-4569669304 |language=Japanese}} == Marriage == In many versions of the myth {{ill|Ame no Hohi|en}} did not send a word for three years after going down to earth, all the gods gathered up, and {{ill|Ame no Wakahiko|en|10=en:draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ame-No-Wakahiko}} was one who was chosen to rule the earth. In many versions {{ill|Ame no Wakahiko|en|10=en:draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ame-No-Wakahiko}} was given a bow.{{Cite web|title=Encyclopedia of Shinto - Home: Kami in Classic Texts: Ame no Wakahiko|url=http://eos.kokugakuin.ac.jp/modules/xwords/entry.php?entryID=46|access-date=2020-09-29|website=eos.kokugakuin.ac.jp}}{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=xdfgjV2kw6oC&q=Ame+no+Wakahiko&pg=PA6|title=Japanese Mythology A to Z|last=Roberts|first=Jeremy|date=2009|publisher=Infobase Publishing|isbn=978-1-4381-2802-3|language=en}} In some versions, however, Ame no Wakahiko is the son of Ame no Hohi and Ame no Wakahiko was sent to earth to look for him.{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=xdfgjV2kw6oC&dq=Ame+no+Wakahiko&pg=PA6|title=Japanese Mythology a to Z|publisher=Infobase|year=2009|isbn=9781438128023}} She married {{ill|Ame no Wakahiko|en|10=en:draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ame-No-Wakahiko}}, when he came from heaven to discuss the "{{ill|Kuni-yuzuri|en}}". === Death === Eight years later, the gods had not yet heard a response so they sent a bird named Nakime down to earth to check in on him. Following the advice of a wise woman, Ame no Wakahiko used his bow to shoot the bird.{{Cite book|title=Handbook of Japanese mythology|last=Ashkenazi|first=Michael|date=2008|publisher=Oxford University Press|isbn=978-0-19-533262-9|series=Handbooks of world mythology|location=Oxford|pages=114}} The bird was killed but the arrow flew all the way to heaven. {{ill|Takamimusubi|en}} saw the arrow and threw it back at the earth where it hit Ame no Wakahiko while he was laying in bed, killing him.{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=uAj_PQ8o40sC&q=Takamimusubi|title=The East|date=1992|publisher=East Publications, Incorporated|language=en}} Other versions state that {{ill|Amaterasu|en}} was the one who shot the arrow back at him.{{cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=FlZxh5OaZxoC&pg=PA38|title=Impurity and Death: A Japanese Perspective|last=Abe|first=C.|publisher=Universal Publishers|year=2003|isbn=978-1-58112-195-7|page=38|access-date=2020-09-29}} This myth is the origin of a Japanese saying about the returning arrow. It is likely also be a mythicisation of attempts made by the {{ill|Yamato Kingship|en}} to impose its authority over neighbouring states. === Funeral === After Ame no Wakahiko's death, his parents built a hut (喪屋 moya) for their son. {{ill|Ajisukitakahikone|en}} went down to pay his respect. However, due to Ajisukitakahikone looking similar to Ame no Wakahiko he was mistaken to be Ame no Wakahiko brought back to life. Ajisukitakahikone was offended by this and destroyed the hut and kicked it. The hut landed in the land of Mino and became a mountain called Moyama.{{Cite book|title=Nihongi: Chronicles of Japan from the Earliest Times to A.D. 697, Volume 1|chapter=Book II|chapter-url=https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/Nihongi:_Chronicles_of_Japan_from_the_Earliest_Times_to_A.D._697/Book_II}} When {{ill|Ame no Wakahiko|en|10=en:draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ame-No-Wakahiko}} passed away, Shitateruhime's sorrowful voice was heard in the Plain of High Heaven. During his funeral, Amewakahiko's father, Amatsukunitama, and other family members confused Shitateruhime's step-brother, [[Ajisukitakahikone]], for the deceased Amewakahiko. [[Ajisukitakahikone]] left in rage. In response, Shitateruhime sang a song of a type called hinaburi, or "rustic song" to honor her deceased husband.{{Cite web|title=Encyclopedia of Shinto詳細|url=https://d-museum.kokugakuin.ac.jp/eos/detail/?id=9155|access-date=2024-03-24|website=國學院大學デジタルミュージアム|language=ja}} == See Also == * {{ill|Munakata clan|ja|宗像氏|simple|User:Immanuelle/Munakata_clan|ja|宗像氏|fr|Clan Munakata}} ==References== {{reflist|draft}} == Further reading == * Jugon, Jean-Claude. "[https://www.france-japon.net/documents/La%20romance%20du%20sentiment%20et%20de%20la%20pensee.pdf?x36399 La romance du sentiment et de la pensée dans les légendes de Tanabata (Japon) et d’Éros-Psyché (Grèce), une interprétation transculturelle: «Oni» soit qui mal y pense!]". In: 論叢現代語・現代文化　2015 Vol.14　pp. 1-92. (in French) * Nüffer, Laura. “Humans and Non-Humans: Animal Bridegrooms and Brides in Japanese Otogizōshi.” In: ''A Cultural History of Fairy Tales in the Age of the Marvelous''. Edited by Suzanne Magnanini. London: Bloomsbury Academic Press, 2021. pp. 95-118. * ITO, Yuko. "[https://tsuru.repo.nii.ac.jp/?action=pages_view_main&active_action=repository_view_main_item_detail&item_id=201&item_no=1&page_id=4&block_id=34 Origins and development of the two versions of "Ame no Wakahiko Soshi": a comparative study]". In: 都留文科大学研究紀要 [The Tsuru University Review], Mar/2007, volume 65, pp. 258–241. https://ci.nii.ac.jp/naid/110007055993/en/; {{ISSN|0286-3774}}. DOI: info:doi/10.34356/00000195 (in Japanese) * Yasufuku, Junko. "[http://ir.lib.osaka-kyoiku.ac.jp/dspace/handle/123456789/6149 The Tale of Ame no Wakahiko and the Psychic Development of the Feminine]". In: ''Memoirs of Osaka Kyoiku University. IV, Education, pshychology, special education and physical culture'', Osaka Kyoiku University, Feb/1995, volume 43, no. 2, pp. 251–258. {{ISSN|0389-3472}}. In many versions {{ill|Ame no Wakahiko|en|10=en:draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ame-No-Wakahiko}} was given a bow.{{Cite web|title=Encyclopedia of Shinto - Home: Kami in Classic Texts: Ame no Wakahiko|url=http://eos.kokugakuin.ac.jp/modules/xwords/entry.php?entryID=46|access-date=2020-09-29|website=eos.kokugakuin.ac.jp}}{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=xdfgjV2kw6oC&q=Ame+no+Wakahiko&pg=PA6|title=Japanese Mythology A to Z|last=Roberts|first=Jeremy|date=2009|publisher=Infobase Publishing|isbn=978-1-4381-2802-3|language=en}} In some versions, however, Ame no Wakahiko is the son of Ame no Hohi and Ame no Wakahiko was sent to earth to look for him.{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=xdfgjV2kw6oC&dq=Ame+no+Wakahiko&pg=PA6|title=Japanese Mythology a to Z|publisher=Infobase|year=2009|isbn=9781438128023}} She married {{ill|Ame no Wakahiko|en|10=en:draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ame-No-Wakahiko}}, when he came from heaven to discuss the "{{ill|Kuni-yuzuri|en}}". === Death === Eight years later, the gods had not yet heard a response so they sent a bird named Nakime down to earth to check in on him. Following the advice of a wise woman, Ame no Wakahiko used his bow to shoot the bird.{{Cite book|title=Handbook of Japanese mythology|last=Ashkenazi|first=Michael|date=2008|publisher=Oxford University Press|isbn=978-0-19-533262-9|series=Handbooks of world mythology|location=Oxford|pages=114}} The bird was killed but the arrow flew all the way to heaven. {{ill|Takamimusubi|en}} saw the arrow and threw it back at the earth where it hit Ame no Wakahiko while he was laying in bed, killing him.{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=uAj_PQ8o40sC&q=Takamimusubi|title=The East|date=1992|publisher=East Publications, Incorporated|language=en}} Other versions state that {{ill|Amaterasu|en}} was the one who shot the arrow back at him.{{cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=FlZxh5OaZxoC&pg=PA38|title=Impurity and Death: A Japanese Perspective|last=Abe|first=C.|publisher=Universal Publishers|year=2003|isbn=978-1-58112-195-7|page=38|access-date=2020-09-29}} This myth is the origin of a Japanese saying about the returning arrow. It is likely also be a mythicisation of attempts made by the {{ill|Yamato Kingship|en}} to impose its authority over neighbouring states. === Funeral === After Ame no Wakahiko's death, his parents built a hut (喪屋 moya) for their son. {{ill|Ajisukitakahikone|en}} went down to pay his respect. However, due to Ajisukitakahikone looking similar to Ame no Wakahiko he was mistaken to be Ame no Wakahiko brought back to life. Ajisukitakahikone was offended by this and destroyed the hut and kicked it. The hut landed in the land of Mino and became a mountain called Moyama.{{Cite book|title=Nihongi: Chronicles of Japan from the Earliest Times to A.D. 697, Volume 1|chapter=Book II|chapter-url=https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/Nihongi:_Chronicles_of_Japan_from_the_Earliest_Times_to_A.D._697/Book_II}} When {{ill|Ame no Wakahiko|en|10=en:draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ame-No-Wakahiko}} passed away, Shitateruhime's sorrowful voice was heard in the Plain of High Heaven. During his funeral, Amewakahiko's father, Amatsukunitama, and other family members confused Shitateruhime's step-brother, [[Ajisukitakahikone]], for the deceased Amewakahiko. [[Ajisukitakahikone]] left in rage. In response, Shitateruhime sang a song of a type called hinaburi, or "rustic song" to honor her deceased husband.{{Cite web|title=Encyclopedia of Shinto詳細|url=https://d-museum.kokugakuin.ac.jp/eos/detail/?id=9155|access-date=2024-03-24|website=國學院大學デジタルミュージアム|language=ja}} == See Also == * {{ill|Munakata clan|ja|宗像氏|simple|User:Immanuelle/Munakata_clan|ja|宗像氏|fr|Clan Munakata}} ==References== {{reflist|draft}} == Further reading == * Jugon, Jean-Claude. {{draft}} {{Expand Japanese|シタテルヒメ}}{{Infobox deity | type = [[Shinto]] | father = [[Ōkuninushi]] | mother = {{ill|Takiribime|ja|タキリビメ|simple|User:Immanuelle/Takiribime|en:draft}} |cult_centre={{ill|Shitori Shrine (Tottori)|lt=Shitori Shrine|en}},
{{ill|Kifune Shrine|simple|User:Immanuelle/Kifune Shrine|en}}|name=Shitateruhime|siblings=[[Ajisukitakahikone]]|spouse={{ill|Ame no Wakahiko|en|10=en:draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ame-No-Wakahiko}}|image=File:Shitori-jinja, haiden.jpg|caption={{ill|Shitori Shrine (Tottori)|lt=Shitori Shrine|en}} where she is worshipped}}{{complex}} {{User:Immanuelle/Promising Draft}} {{ill|Shitateruhime|lt=Shitateruhime-no-Mikoto|ja|シタテルヒメ|simple|User:Immanuelle/Shitateruhime|en:draft|8=fr}} is a daughter of {{ill|Takiribime|ja|タキリビメ|simple|User:Immanuelle/Takiribime|en:draft|8=fr}}, one of the three sisters worshipped at [[Munakata Taisha|Munakata Taisha]] The origins of {{ill|Shitori Shrine (Tottori)|lt=Shitori Shrine|en|4=fr|5=Shitori-jinja|6=ja|7=倭文神社_(湯梨浜町)|8=simple|9=User:Immanuelle/Shitori Shrine (Tottori)}} are unknown. Although there is no documentary evidence, it is believed that it began as the family shrine for the {{Nihongo|Shitori clan|倭文氏}} of [[Kofun period|Kofun period]] craftsmen who weavers, who regarded {{ill|Takehazuchi|lt=Takehazuchi-no-Mikoto|ja|天羽槌雄神|simple|User:Immanuelle/Takehazuchi|en:draft|8=fr}} as their ancestor. However, the shrine's legends are all centered around {{ill|Shitateruhime|lt=Shitateruhime-no-Mikoto|ja|シタテルヒメ|simple|User:Immanuelle/Shitateruhime|en:draft|8=fr}}, whom the shrine legend claims arrived in this location from [[Izumo Taisha|Izumo]] by boat. She established her residence on the mountain behind this shrine, and after her death, she was buried in a ''[[kofun|kofun]]'' constructed in the shrine's precincts.{{cite book |last1=Yoshiki |first1=Emi |title=Zenkoku 'Ichinomiya' tettei gaido |date=2007 |publisher=PHP Institute |isbn=978-4569669304 |language=Japanese}} == Marriage == In many versions of the myth {{ill|Ame no Hohi|en}} did not send a word for three years after going down to earth, all the gods gathered up, and {{ill|Ame no Wakahiko|en|10=en:draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ame-No-Wakahiko}} was one who was chosen to rule the earth. In many versions {{ill|Ame no Wakahiko|en|10=en:draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ame-No-Wakahiko}} was given a bow.{{Cite web|title=Encyclopedia of Shinto - Home: Kami in Classic Texts: Ame no Wakahiko|url=http://eos.kokugakuin.ac.jp/modules/xwords/entry.php?entryID=46|access-date=2020-09-29|website=eos.kokugakuin.ac.jp}}{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=xdfgjV2kw6oC&q=Ame+no+Wakahiko&pg=PA6|title=Japanese Mythology A to Z|last=Roberts|first=Jeremy|date=2009|publisher=Infobase Publishing|isbn=978-1-4381-2802-3|language=en}} In some versions, however, Ame no Wakahiko is the son of Ame no Hohi and Ame no Wakahiko was sent to earth to look for him.{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=xdfgjV2kw6oC&dq=Ame+no+Wakahiko&pg=PA6|title=Japanese Mythology a to Z|publisher=Infobase|year=2009|isbn=9781438128023}} She married {{ill|Ame no Wakahiko|en|10=en:draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ame-No-Wakahiko}}, when he came from heaven to discuss the "{{ill|Kuni-yuzuri|en}}". === Death === Eight years later, the gods had not yet heard a response so they sent a bird named Nakime down to earth to check in on him. Following the advice of a wise woman, Ame no Wakahiko used his bow to shoot the bird.{{Cite book|title=Handbook of Japanese mythology|last=Ashkenazi|first=Michael|date=2008|publisher=Oxford University Press|isbn=978-0-19-533262-9|series=Handbooks of world mythology|location=Oxford|pages=114}} The bird was killed but the arrow flew all the way to heaven. {{ill|Takamimusubi|en}} saw the arrow and threw it back at the earth where it hit Ame no Wakahiko while he was laying in bed, killing him.{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=uAj_PQ8o40sC&q=Takamimusubi|title=The East|date=1992|publisher=East Publications, Incorporated|language=en}} Other versions state that {{ill|Amaterasu|en}} was the one who shot the arrow back at him.{{cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=FlZxh5OaZxoC&pg=PA38|title=Impurity and Death: A Japanese Perspective|last=Abe|first=C.|publisher=Universal Publishers|year=2003|isbn=978-1-58112-195-7|page=38|access-date=2020-09-29}} This myth is the origin of a Japanese saying about the returning arrow. It is likely also be a mythicisation of attempts made by the {{ill|Yamato Kingship|en}} to impose its authority over neighbouring states. === Funeral === After Ame no Wakahiko's death, his parents built a hut (喪屋 moya) for their son. {{ill|Ajisukitakahikone|en}} went down to pay his respect. However, due to Ajisukitakahikone looking similar to Ame no Wakahiko he was mistaken to be Ame no Wakahiko brought back to life. Ajisukitakahikone was offended by this and destroyed the hut and kicked it. The hut landed in the land of Mino and became a mountain called Moyama.{{Cite book|title=Nihongi: Chronicles of Japan from the Earliest Times to A.D. 697, Volume 1|chapter=Book II|chapter-url=https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/Nihongi:_Chronicles_of_Japan_from_the_Earliest_Times_to_A.D._697/Book_II}} When {{ill|Ame no Wakahiko|en|10=en:draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ame-No-Wakahiko}} passed away, Shitateruhime's sorrowful voice was heard in the Plain of High Heaven. During his funeral, Amewakahiko's father, Amatsukunitama, and other family members confused Shitateruhime's step-brother, [[Ajisukitakahikone]], for the deceased Amewakahiko. [[Ajisukitakahikone]] left in rage. In response, Shitateruhime sang a song of a type called hinaburi, or "rustic song" to honor her deceased husband.{{Cite web|title=Encyclopedia of Shinto詳細|url=https://d-museum.kokugakuin.ac.jp/eos/detail/?id=9155|access-date=2024-03-24|website=國學院大學デジタルミュージアム|language=ja}} == See Also == * {{ill|Munakata clan|ja|宗像氏|simple|User:Immanuelle/Munakata_clan|ja|宗像氏|fr|Clan Munakata}} ==References== {{reflist|draft}} == Further reading == * Jugon, Jean-Claude. {{基礎情報 日本の神 | 名 = 下光比売命 | 世代名 = | 先代 = | 次代 = | 神祇 = [[国津神]] | 全名 = 下光比売命（シタテルヒメノミコト） | 別名 = 下照比売、高比売命、下照姫命、高姫命、稚国玉、等 | 別称 = | 神階 = | 神格 = [[雷神]] | 陵所 = | 父 = [[大国主神]] | 母 = [[多紀理毘売命]] | 親 = | 兄弟姉妹 = 同母：[[阿遅鉏高日子根神]]
異母：[[事代主神]]、[[建沼河男命]]、[[建御名方神]]、[[木俣神]] 等 | 配偶者 = [[天若日子]] | 子 = | 宮 = | 神社 = [[売布神社]]、[[比売許曽神社]]等 }} '''シタテルヒメ'''（下光比売、下照比売、下照姫、下照媛）は、[[日本神話]]に登場する[[神道]]の[[神 (神道)|女神]]である。 == 概要 == 『[[古事記]]』では本名を'''高比売命'''（たかひめのみこと）、亦の名を'''下光比売命'''・'''下照比売命'''（したてるひめのみこと）、『[[日本書紀]]』では'''下照姫'''・'''下照媛'''、亦の名は'''高姫'''、'''稚国玉'''（わかくにたま）、『[[先代旧事本紀]]』地神本紀では'''下照姫命'''と記述される。 『古事記』および『日本書紀』正伝によれば、[[葦原中国平定]]のために[[高天原]]から遣わされた[[天若日子]]が、[[大国主神]]に取り入ってあわよくば[[葦原中国]]を自分のものにしようと目論み、その娘である高比売命と結婚した。天若日子が高天原からの返し矢に当たって死んだとき、高比売命の泣く声が天（『古事記』では[[高天原]]）まで届き、その声を聞いた天若日子の父の[[天津国玉神]]や天若日子の妻子らは葦原中国に降臨し、天若日子の喪屋を建て[[殯]]を行った。そこに[[阿遅鉏高日子根神]]が訪れたが、その姿が天若日子にそっくりであったため、天津国玉神や妻子らは天若日子が生き返ったと喜んだ。阿遅鉏高日子根神は穢わしい死人と間違えられたことに怒り、喪屋を[[神度剣|大量]]で斬り倒し、蹴り飛ばして去って行った。高比売命は、阿遅鉏高日子根神の名を明かす歌を詠んだ。この歌は「[[夷振]]（ひなぶり）」と呼ばれる（夷振を詠んだという記述は『日本書紀』正伝にはない）。『日本書紀』の第一の一書では、天稚彦の妻の名は記されておらず、夷振を詠んだ者の名としてのみ下照媛の名が登場し、味耜高彦根神の妹であるとしている。 別名の高比売命と音が似ていることから、『[[出雲国風土記]]』[[神門郡]]の多伎郷条に登場する所造天下大神（大国主神）の[[御子神|御子]]である[[アダカヤヌシタキキヒメ]]（阿陀加夜努志多伎吉比売命）と同一神とする説があり、さらに「カヤ」から『[[延喜式]]』巻八に掲載されている[[祝詞]]「[[出雲国造神賀詞]]」に登場する[[カヤナルミ]]（賀夜奈流美命）とも同一神とする説もある{{Sfn|鈴木|1940|pp=557-558}}{{Sfn|次田|2008|p=534}}。 == 系譜 == [[画像:Ohokuninushi family tree.png|right|thumb|250px|大国主の系図（『古事記』による）。青は男神、赤は女神、黄は性別不詳]] 『古事記』では[[大国主神]]（『日本書紀』では顕国玉）と[[多紀理毘売命]]の娘で、[[アヂスキタカヒコネ|阿遅鉏高日子根神]]の妹としており、『先代旧事本紀』地神本紀でも『古事記』同様に大己貴神と田心姫命の娘で、味耜高彦根神の同母妹とする。 == 祀る神社 == *[http://himenojinjya.or.jp 比賣神社]（富山県南砺市高宮）：主祭神　下照比賣命 *玉津岡神社（京都府綴喜郡井手町）：主祭神　下照比賣命 *大穴持御子玉江神社（[[乙見社]]とも。[[出雲大社#荒垣外摂末社]]）：主祭神　下照比賣命 *[[比売許曽神社]]（難波　[[大阪市]][[東成区]]東小橋）『古事記』では[[アメノヒボコ]]（天之日矛）、『日本書紀』では[[ツヌガアラシト]]（都怒我阿羅斯等）が逃げた妻（[[阿加流比売神]]）を追って[[渡来人|渡来]]し、逃げた阿加流比売神が身をひそめたという記述がある。『延喜式神名帳』では阿加流比売命の赤留比売神社は[[住吉郡]]にあるとする。：主祭神　下照比賣命（江戸時代までは[[牛頭天王]]） {{基礎情報 日本の神 | 名 = 下光比売命 | 世代名 = | 先代 = | 次代 = | 神祇 = <!-- 天神、地祇、天津神、国津神など -->[[国津神]] | 全名 = 下光比売命（シタテルヒメノミコト） | 別名 = 下照比売、高比売命、下照姫命、高姫命、稚国玉、等 | 別称 = | 神階 = | 神格 = <!-- 太陽、月、山、海など司るもの -->[[雷神]] | 陵所 = | 父 = [[大国主神]] | 母 = [[多紀理毘売命]] | 親 = <!-- まぐあいによって生まれない場合 --> | 兄弟姉妹 = {{Plainlist| * 同母：[[阿遅鉏高日子根神]] * 異母：[[事代主神]]、[[建沼河男命]]、[[建御名方神]]、[[木俣神]] 等 }} | 配偶者 = [[天若日子]] | 子 = | 宮 = | 神社 = {{Plainlist| * [[売布神社]] * [[比売許曽神社]] 等 }} | 記紀等 = 古事記、日本書紀 }} '''シタテルヒメ'''（下光比売、下照比売、下照姫、下照媛）は、[[日本神話]]に登場する[[神道]]の[[神 (神道)|女神]]である。 == 概要 == 『[[古事記]]』では本名を'''高比売命'''（たかひめのみこと）、亦の名を'''下光比売命'''・'''下照比売命'''（したてるひめのみこと）、『[[日本書紀]]』では'''下照姫'''・'''下照媛'''、亦の名は'''高姫'''、'''稚国玉'''（わかくにたま）、『[[先代旧事本紀]]』地神本紀では'''下照姫命'''と記述される。
『古事記』および『日本書紀』正伝によれば、[[葦原中国平定]]のために[[高天原]]から遣わされた[[天若日子]]が、[[大国主神]]に取り入ってあわよくば[[葦原中国]]を自分のものにしようと目論み、その娘である高比売命と結婚した。天若日子が高天原からの返し矢に当たって死んだとき、高比売命の泣く声が天（『古事記』では[[高天原]]）まで届き、その声を聞いた天若日子の父の[[天津国玉神]]や天若日子の妻子らは葦原中国に降臨し、天若日子の喪屋を建て[[殯]]を行った。そこに[[阿遅鉏高日子根神]]が訪れたが、その姿が天若日子にそっくりであったため、天津国玉神や妻子らは天若日子が生き返ったと喜んだ。阿遅鉏高日子根神は穢わしい死人と間違えられたことに怒り、喪屋を[[神度剣|大量]]で斬り倒し、蹴り飛ばして去って行った。高比売命は、阿遅鉏高日子根神の名を明かす歌を詠んだ。この歌は「[[夷振]]（ひなぶり）」と呼ばれる（夷振を詠んだという記述は『日本書紀』正伝にはない）。『日本書紀』の第一の一書では、天稚彦の妻の名は記されておらず、夷振を詠んだ者の名としてのみ下照媛の名が登場し、味耜高彦根神の妹であるとしている。
別名の高比売命と音が似ていることから、『[[出雲国風土記]]』[[神門郡]]の多伎郷条に登場する所造天下大神（大国主神）の[[御子神|御子]]である[[アダカヤヌシタキキヒメ]]（阿陀加夜努志多伎吉比売命）と同一神とする説があり、さらに「カヤ」から『[[延喜式]]』巻八に掲載されている[[祝詞]]「[[出雲国造神賀詞]]」に登場する[[カヤナルミ]]（賀夜奈流美命）とも同一神とする説もある{{Sfn|鈴木|1940|pp=557-558}}{{Sfn|次田|2008|p=534}}。 == 系譜 == [[画像:Ohokuninushi family tree.png|right|thumb|250px|大国主の系図（『古事記』による）。青は男神、赤は女神、黄は性別不詳]] 『古事記』では[[大国主神]]（『日本書紀』では顕国玉）と[[多紀理毘売命]]の娘で、[[アヂスキタカヒコネ|阿遅鉏高日子根神]]の妹としており、『先代旧事本紀』地神本紀でも『古事記』同様に大己貴神と田心姫命の娘で、味耜高彦根神の同母妹とする。 == 祀る神社 == * 比賣神社（[[富山県]][[南砺市]]高宮） - 主祭神 * 玉津岡神社（[[京都府]][[綴喜郡]][[井手町]]） - 主祭神 * [[比売許曽神社]]（[[大阪府]][[大阪市]][[東成区]]）<ref group="注">『古事記』では[[アメノヒボコ]]（天之日矛）、『日本書紀』では[[ツヌガアラシト]]（都怒我阿羅斯等）が逃げた妻（[[阿加流比売神]]）を追って[[渡来人|渡来]]し、逃げた阿加流比売神が身をひそめたという記述がある。『延喜式神名帳』では阿加流比売命の赤留比売神社は[[住吉郡]]にあるとする。</ref> - 主祭神（江戸時代までは[[牛頭天王]]） : 『[[延喜式神名帳]]』では下照比売社が比売許曽神社であると記す。なお、比売碁曾社の主祭神は明治以降は[[牛頭天王]]から下照比売命に代わっている。 * 売豆紀神社（島根県[[松江市]]雑賀町） - 主祭神 * 内神社（島根県松江市大垣町） - 主祭神 : 高野宮とも呼ばれる。 * [[出雲大社#施設|大穴持御子玉江神社]]（[[島根県]][[出雲市]][[大社町]]） - 祭神 : [[出雲大社]]の境外社。乙見社とも呼ばれる。 * [[売布神社 (宝塚市)|売布神社]]（[[兵庫県]][[宝塚市]][[売布山手町]]） - 主祭神 * [[倭文神社 (湯梨浜町)|倭文神社]]（[[鳥取県]][[東伯郡]][[湯梨浜町]]） - 配祀 : 現在は[[天羽槌雄神|建葉槌命]]が主祭神となっているが、社伝にはシタテルヒメに関するものが多く、大正時代まではシタテルヒメが主祭神であると考えられていた。倭文神社内の塚がシタテルヒメの墓であると考えられていたが、発掘により経塚であると判明した。 == 脚注 == {{脚注ヘルプ}} === 注釈 === <references group="注" /> === 出典 === <references /> == 参考文献 == * {{Cite book|和書 |title=延喜式祝詞講義 |date=1940年4月20日、初出1851年 |publisher=鈴木重胤先生學德顯揚會 |author=[[鈴木重胤]] |editor=樹下快淳 |ncid=BA79958552 |volume=3 |ref={{SfnRef|鈴木|1940}} |edition=普及版}} * {{Cite book|和書 |title=新版 祝詞新講 |date=2008年5月、初版1927年 |publisher=戎光祥出版 |ref={{SfnRef|次田|2008}} |author=[[次田潤]] |isbn=978-4-900901-85-8}} == 関連項目 == * [[日本の神の一覧]] {{神道 横}} {{shinto-stub}} {{DEFAULTSORT:したてるひめ}} [[Category:日本の神]] [[Category:国津神]] [[Category:女神]]

別名の高比売命と音が似ていることから、『[[出雲国風土記]]』[[神門郡]]の多伎郷条に登場する所造天下大神（大国主神）の[[御子神|御子]]である[[アダカヤヌシタキキヒメ]]（阿陀加夜努志多伎吉比売命）と同一神とする説があり、さらに「カヤ」から『[[延喜式]]』巻八に掲載されている[[祝詞]]「[[出雲国造神賀詞]]」に登場する[[カヤナルミ]]（賀夜奈流美命）とも同一神とする説もある{{Sfn|鈴木|1940|pp=557-558}}{{Sfn|次田|2008|p=534}}。 == 系譜 == [[画像:Ohokuninushi family tree.png|right|thumb|250px|大国主の系図（『古事記』による）。青は男神、赤は女神、黄は性別不詳]] 『古事記』では[[大国主神]]（『日本書紀』では顕国玉）と[[多紀理毘売命]]の娘で、[[アヂスキタカヒコネ|阿遅鉏高日子根神]]の妹としており、『先代旧事本紀』地神本紀でも『古事記』同様に大己貴神と田心姫命の娘で、味耜高彦根神の同母妹とする。 == 祀る神社 == * 比賣神社（[[富山県]][[南砺市]]高宮） - 主祭神 * 玉津岡神社（[[京都府]][[綴喜郡]][[井手町]]井出東垣内） - 主祭神 * [[比売許曽神社]]（[[大阪府]][[大阪市]][[東成区]]東小橋）<ref group="注">『古事記』では[[アメノヒボコ]]（天之日矛）、『日本書紀』では[[ツヌガアラシト]]（都怒我阿羅斯等）が逃げた妻（[[阿加流比売神]]）を追って[[渡来人|渡来]]し、逃げた阿加流比売神が身をひそめたという記述がある。『延喜式神名帳』では阿加流比売命の赤留比売神社は[[住吉郡]]にあるとする。</ref> - 主祭神（江戸時代までは[[牛頭天王]]） : 『[[延喜式神名帳]]』では下照比売社が比売許曽神社であると記す。なお、比売碁曾社の主祭神は明治以降は[[牛頭天王]]から下照比売命に代わっている。 * 売豆紀神社（島根県[[松江市]]雑賀町） - 主祭神 * 内神社（島根県松江市大垣町） - 主祭神 : 高野宮とも呼ばれる。 * [[出雲大社#施設|大穴持御子玉江神社]]（[[島根県]][[出雲市]][[大社町]]杵築東） - 祭神 : [[出雲大社]]の境外社。乙見社とも呼ばれる。 * [[売布神社 (宝塚市)|売布神社]]（[[兵庫県]][[宝塚市]][[売布山手町]]） - 主祭神 * [[倭文神社 (湯梨浜町)|倭文神社]]（[[鳥取県]][[東伯郡]][[湯梨浜町]]宮内） - 配祀 : 現在は[[天羽槌雄神|建葉槌命]]が主祭神となっているが、社伝にはシタテルヒメに関するものが多く、大正時代まではシタテルヒメが主祭神であると考えられていた。倭文神社内の塚がシタテルヒメの墓であると考えられていたが、発掘により経塚であると判明した。 == 脚注 == {{脚注ヘルプ}} === 注釈 === <references group="注" /> === 出典 === <references /> == 参考文献 == * {{Cite book|和書 |title=延喜式祝詞講義 |date=1940年4月20日、初出1851年 |publisher=鈴木重胤先生學德顯揚會 |author=[[鈴木重胤]] |editor=樹下快淳 |ncid=BA79958552 |volume=3 |ref={{SfnRef|鈴木|1940}} |edition=普及版}} * {{Cite book|和書 |title=新版 祝詞新講 |date=2008年5月、初版1927年 |publisher=戎光祥出版 |ref={{SfnRef|次田|2008}} |author=[[次田潤]] |isbn=978-4-900901-85-8}} == 関連項目 == * [[日本の神の一覧]] {{神道 横}} {{shinto-stub}} {{DEFAULTSORT:したてるひめ}} [[Category:日本の神]] [[Category:国津神]] [[Category:女神]]

別名の高比売命と音が似ていることから、『[[出雲国風土記]]』[[神門郡]]の多伎郷条に登場する所造天下大神（大国主神）の[[御子神|御子]]である[[アダカヤヌシタキキヒメ]]（阿陀加夜努志多伎吉比売命）と同一神とする説があり、さらに「カヤ」から『[[延喜式]]』巻八に掲載されている[[祝詞]]「[[出雲国造神賀詞]]」に登場する[[カヤナルミ]]（賀夜奈流美命）とも同一神とする説もある{{Sfn|鈴木|1940|pp=557-558}}{{Sfn|次田|2008|p=534}}。 == 系譜 == [[画像:Ohokuninushi family tree.png|right|thumb|250px|大国主の系図（『古事記』による）。青は男神、赤は女神、黄は性別不詳]] 『古事記』では[[大国主神]]（『日本書紀』では顕国玉）と[[多紀理毘売命]]の娘で、[[アヂスキタカヒコネ|阿遅鉏高日子根神]]の妹としており、『先代旧事本紀』地神本紀でも『古事記』同様に大己貴神と田心姫命の娘で、味耜高彦根神の同母妹とする。 == 祀る神社 == * 比賣神社（[[富山県]][[南砺市]]高宮） - 主祭神 * 玉津岡神社（[[京都府]][[綴喜郡]][[井手町]]井出東垣内） - 主祭神 * [[比売許曽神社]]（[[大阪府]][[大阪市]][[東成区]]東小橋）<ref group="注">『古事記』では[[アメノヒボコ]]（天之日矛）、『日本書紀』では[[ツヌガアラシト]]（都怒我阿羅斯等）が逃げた妻（[[阿加流比売神]]）を追って[[渡来人|渡来]]し、逃げた阿加流比売神が身をひそめたという記述がある。『延喜式神名帳』では阿加流比売命の赤留比売神社は[[住吉郡]]にあるとする。</ref> - 主祭神（江戸時代までは[[牛頭天王]]） : 『[[延喜式神名帳]]』では下照比売社が比売許曽神社であると記す。なお、比売碁曾社の主祭神は明治以降は[[牛頭天王]]から下照比売命に代わっている。 * 売豆紀神社（島根県[[松江市]]雑賀町） - 主祭神 * 内神社（島根県松江市大垣町） - 主祭神 : 高野宮とも呼ばれる。 * [[出雲大社#施設|大穴持御子玉江神社]]（[[島根県]][[出雲市]][[大社町]]杵築東） - 祭神 : [[出雲大社]]の境外社。乙見社とも呼ばれる。 * [[売布神社 (宝塚市)|売布神社]]（[[兵庫県]][[宝塚市]][[売布山手町]]） - 主祭神 * [[倭文神社 (湯梨浜町)|倭文神社]]（[[鳥取県]][[東伯郡]][[湯梨浜町]]宮内） - 配祀 : 現在は[[天羽槌雄神|建葉槌命]]が主祭神となっているが、社伝にはシタテルヒメに関するものが多く、大正時代まではシタテルヒメが主祭神であると考えられていた。倭文神社内の塚がシタテルヒメの墓であると考えられていたが、発掘により経塚であると判明した。 == 脚注 == {{脚注ヘルプ}} === 注釈 === <references group="注" /> === 出典 === <references /> == 参考文献 == * {{Cite book|和書 |title=延喜式祝詞講義 |date=1940年4月20日、初出1851年 |publisher=鈴木重胤先生學德顯揚會 |author=[[鈴木重胤]] |editor=樹下快淳 |ncid=BA79958552 |volume=3 |ref={{SfnRef|鈴木|1940}} |edition=普及版}} * {{Cite book|和書 |title=新版 祝詞新講 |date=2008年5月、初版1927年 |publisher=戎光祥出版 |ref={{SfnRef|次田|2008}} |author=[[次田潤]] |isbn=978-4-900901-85-8}} == 関連項目 == * [[日本の神の一覧]] {{神道 横}} {{日本神話}} {{shinto-stub}} {{DEFAULTSORT:したてるひめ}} [[Category:日本の神]] [[Category:国津神]] [[Category:女神]]

別名の高比売命と音が似ていることから、『[[出雲国風土記]]』[[神門郡]]の多伎郷条に登場する所造天下大神（大国主神）の[[御子神|御子]]である[[アダカヤヌシタキキヒメ]]（阿陀加夜努志多伎吉比売命）と同一神とする説があり、さらに「カヤ」から『[[延喜式]]』巻八に掲載されている[[祝詞]]「[[出雲国造神賀詞]]」に登場する[[カヤナルミ]]（賀夜奈流美命）とも同一神とする説もある{{Sfn|鈴木|1940|pp=557-558}}{{Sfn|次田|2008|p=534}}。 == 系譜 == [[画像:Ohokuninushi family tree.png|right|thumb|250px|大国主の系図（『古事記』による）。青は男神、赤は女神、黄は性別不詳]] 『古事記』では[[大国主神]]（『日本書紀』では顕国玉）と[[多紀理毘売命]]の娘で、[[アヂスキタカヒコネ|阿遅鉏高日子根神]]の妹としており、『先代旧事本紀』地神本紀でも『古事記』同様に大己貴神と田心姫命の娘で、味耜高彦根神の同母妹とする。 == 祀る神社 == * 比賣神社（[[富山県]][[南砺市]]高宮） - 主祭神 * 玉津岡神社（[[京都府]][[綴喜郡]][[井手町]]井出東垣内） - 主祭神 * [[比売許曽神社]]（[[大阪府]][[大阪市]][[東成区]]東小橋）<ref group="注">『古事記』では[[アメノヒボコ]]（天之日矛）、『日本書紀』では[[ツヌガアラシト]]（都怒我阿羅斯等）が逃げた妻（[[阿加流比売神]]）を追って[[渡来人|渡来]]し、逃げた阿加流比売神が身をひそめたという記述がある。『延喜式神名帳』では阿加流比売命の赤留比売神社は[[住吉郡]]にあるとする。</ref> - 主祭神（江戸時代までは[[牛頭天王]]） ** 『[[延喜式神名帳]]』では下照比売社が比売許曽神社であると記す。なお、比売碁曾社の主祭神は明治以降は[[牛頭天王]]から下照比売命に代わっている。 * 売豆紀神社（島根県[[松江市]]雑賀町） - 主祭神 * 内神社（島根県松江市大垣町） - 主祭神 ** 高野宮とも呼ばれる。 * [[出雲大社#施設|大穴持御子玉江神社]]（[[島根県]][[出雲市]][[大社町]]杵築東） - 祭神 ** [[出雲大社]]の境外社。乙見社とも呼ばれる。 * [[売布神社 (宝塚市)|売布神社]]（[[兵庫県]][[宝塚市]][[売布山手町]]） - 主祭神 * [[倭文神社 (湯梨浜町)|倭文神社]]（[[鳥取県]][[東伯郡]][[湯梨浜町]]宮内） - 配祀 ** 現在は[[天羽槌雄神|建葉槌命]]が主祭神となっているが、社伝にはシタテルヒメに関するものが多く、大正時代まではシタテルヒメが主祭神であると考えられていた。倭文神社内の塚がシタテルヒメの墓であると考えられていたが、発掘により経塚であると判明した。

別名の高比売命と音が似ていることから、『[[出雲国風土記]]』[[神門郡]]の多伎郷条に登場する所造天下大神（大国主神）の[[御子神|御子]]である[[アダカヤヌシタキキヒメ]]（阿陀加夜努志多伎吉比売命）と同一神とする説があり、さらに「カヤ」から『[[延喜式]]』巻八に掲載されている[[祝詞]]「[[出雲国造神賀詞]]」に登場する[[カヤナルミ]]（賀夜奈流美命）とも同一神とする説もある{{Sfn|鈴木|1940|pp=557-558}}{{Sfn|次田|2008|p=534}}。 == 系譜 == [[画像:Ohokuninushi family tree.png|right|thumb|250px|大国主の系図（『古事記』による）。青は男神、赤は女神、黄は性別不詳]] 『古事記』では[[大国主神]]（『日本書紀』では顕国玉）と[[多紀理毘売命]]の娘で、[[アヂスキタカヒコネ|阿遅鉏高日子根神]]の妹としており、『先代旧事本紀』地神本紀でも『古事記』同様に大己貴神と田心姫命の娘で、味耜高彦根神の同母妹とする。 == 祀る神社 == * 比賣神社（[[富山県]][[南砺市]]高宮） - 主祭神 * 玉津岡神社（[[京都府]][[綴喜郡]][[井手町]]井出東垣内） - 主祭神 * [[比売許曽神社]]（[[大阪府]][[大阪市]][[東成区]]東小橋）<ref group="注">『古事記』では[[アメノヒボコ]]（天之日矛）、『日本書紀』では[[ツヌガアラシト]]（都怒我阿羅斯等）が逃げた妻（[[阿加流比売神]]）を追って[[渡来人|渡来]]し、逃げた阿加流比売神が身をひそめたという記述がある。『延喜式神名帳』では阿加流比売命の赤留比売神社は[[住吉郡]]にあるとする。</ref> - 主祭神（江戸時代までは[[牛頭天王]]） ** 『[[延喜式神名帳]]』では下照比売社が比売許曽神社であると記す。なお、比売碁曾社の主祭神は明治以降は[[牛頭天王]]から下照比売命に代わっている。 * 売豆紀神社（島根県[[松江市]]雑賀町） - 主祭神 * 内神社（島根県松江市大垣町） - 主祭神 ** 高野宮とも呼ばれる。 * [[出雲大社#施設|大穴持御子玉江神社]]（[[島根県]][[出雲市]][[大社町]]杵築東） - 祭神 ** [[出雲大社]]の境外社。乙見社とも呼ばれる。 * [[売布神社 (宝塚市)|売布神社]]（[[兵庫県]][[宝塚市]][[売布山手町]]） - 主祭神 * [[倭文神社 (湯梨浜町)|倭文神社]]（[[鳥取県]][[東伯郡]][[湯梨浜町]]宮内） - 配祀 ** 現在は[[天羽槌雄神|建葉槌命]]が主祭神となっているが、社伝にはシタテルヒメに関するものが多く、大正時代まではシタテルヒメが主祭神であると考えられていた。倭文神社内の塚がシタテルヒメの墓であると考えられていたが、発掘により経塚であると判明した。

{{draft}} {{Expand Japanese|シタテルヒメ}}{{Infobox deity | type = [[Shinto]] | father = [[Ōkuninushi]] | mother = {{ill|Tagorihime|ja|タキリビメ|simple|User:Immanuelle/Takiribime|en:draft}} |cult_centre={{ill|Shitori Shrine (Tottori)|lt=Shitori Shrine|en}},
{{ill|Kifune Shrine|simple|User:Immanuelle/Kifune Shrine|en}}|name=Shitateruhime|siblings=[[Ajisukitakahikone]]|spouse={{ill|Ame no Wakahiko|en|10=en:draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ame-No-Wakahiko}}|image=File:Shitori-jinja, haiden.jpg|caption={{ill|Shitori Shrine (Tottori)|lt=Shitori Shrine|en}} where she is worshipped}}{{complex}} {{User:Immanuelle/Promising Draft}} {{ill|Shitateruhime|lt=Shitateruhime-no-Mikoto|ja|シタテルヒメ|simple|User:Immanuelle/Shitateruhime|en:draft|8=fr}} is a daughter of {{ill|Tagorihime|ja|タキリビメ|simple|User:Immanuelle/Takiribime|en:draft|8=fr}}, one of the three sisters worshipped at [[Munakata Taisha|Munakata Taisha]] The origins of {{ill|Shitori Shrine (Tottori)|lt=Shitori Shrine|en|4=fr|5=Shitori-jinja|6=ja|7=倭文神社_(湯梨浜町)|8=simple|9=User:Immanuelle/Shitori Shrine (Tottori)}} are unknown. Although there is no documentary evidence, it is believed that it began as the family shrine for the {{Nihongo|Shitori clan|倭文氏}} of [[Kofun period|Kofun period]] craftsmen who weavers, who regarded {{ill|Takehazuchi|lt=Takehazuchi-no-Mikoto|ja|天羽槌雄神|simple|User:Immanuelle/Takehazuchi|en:draft|8=fr}} as their ancestor. However, the shrine's legends are all centered around {{ill|Shitateruhime|lt=Shitateruhime-no-Mikoto|ja|シタテルヒメ|simple|User:Immanuelle/Shitateruhime|en:draft|8=fr}}, whom the shrine legend claims arrived in this location from [[Izumo Taisha|Izumo]] by boat. She established her residence on the mountain behind this shrine, and after her death, she was buried in a ''[[kofun|kofun]]'' constructed in the shrine's precincts.{{cite book |last1=Yoshiki |first1=Emi |title=Zenkoku 'Ichinomiya' tettei gaido |date=2007 |publisher=PHP Institute |isbn=978-4569669304 |language=Japanese}} == Marriage == In many versions of the myth {{ill|Ame no Hohi|en}} did not send a word for three years after going down to earth, all the gods gathered up, and {{ill|Ame no Wakahiko|en|10=en:draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ame-No-Wakahiko}} was one who was chosen to rule the earth. In many versions {{ill|Ame no Wakahiko|en|10=en:draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ame-No-Wakahiko}} was given a bow.{{Cite web|title=Encyclopedia of Shinto - Home: Kami in Classic Texts: Ame no Wakahiko|url=http://eos.kokugakuin.ac.jp/modules/xwords/entry.php?entryID=46|access-date=2020-09-29|website=eos.kokugakuin.ac.jp}}{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=xdfgjV2kw6oC&q=Ame+no+Wakahiko&pg=PA6|title=Japanese Mythology A to Z|last=Roberts|first=Jeremy|date=2009|publisher=Infobase Publishing|isbn=978-1-4381-2802-3|language=en}} In some versions, however, Ame no Wakahiko is the son of Ame no Hohi and Ame no Wakahiko was sent to earth to look for him.{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=xdfgjV2kw6oC&dq=Ame+no+Wakahiko&pg=PA6|title=Japanese Mythology a to Z|publisher=Infobase|year=2009|isbn=9781438128023}} She married {{ill|Ame no Wakahiko|en|10=en:draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ame-No-Wakahiko}}, when he came from heaven to discuss the "{{ill|Kuni-yuzuri|en}}". === Death === Eight years later, the gods had not yet heard a response so they sent a bird named Nakime down to earth to check in on him. Following the advice of a wise woman, Ame no Wakahiko used his bow to shoot the bird.{{Cite book|title=Handbook of Japanese mythology|last=Ashkenazi|first=Michael|date=2008|publisher=Oxford University Press|isbn=978-0-19-533262-9|series=Handbooks of world mythology|location=Oxford|pages=114}} The bird was killed but the arrow flew all the way to heaven. {{ill|Takamimusubi|en}} saw the arrow and threw it back at the earth where it hit Ame no Wakahiko while he was laying in bed, killing him.{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=uAj_PQ8o40sC&q=Takamimusubi|title=The East|date=1992|publisher=East Publications, Incorporated|language=en}} Other versions state that {{ill|Amaterasu|en}} was the one who shot the arrow back at him.{{cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=FlZxh5OaZxoC&pg=PA38|title=Impurity and Death: A Japanese Perspective|last=Abe|first=C.|publisher=Universal Publishers|year=2003|isbn=978-1-58112-195-7|page=38|access-date=2020-09-29}} This myth is the origin of a Japanese saying about the returning arrow. It is likely also be a mythicisation of attempts made by the {{ill|Yamato Kingship|en}} to impose its authority over neighbouring states. === Funeral === After Ame no Wakahiko's death, his parents built a hut (喪屋 moya) for their son. {{ill|Ajisukitakahikone|en}} went down to pay his respect. However, due to Ajisukitakahikone looking similar to Ame no Wakahiko he was mistaken to be Ame no Wakahiko brought back to life. Ajisukitakahikone was offended by this and destroyed the hut and kicked it. The hut landed in the land of Mino and became a mountain called Moyama.{{Cite book|title=Nihongi: Chronicles of Japan from the Earliest Times to A.D. 697, Volume 1|chapter=Book II|chapter-url=https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/Nihongi:_Chronicles_of_Japan_from_the_Earliest_Times_to_A.D._697/Book_II}} When {{ill|Ame no Wakahiko|en|10=en:draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ame-No-Wakahiko}} passed away, Shitateruhime's sorrowful voice was heard in the Plain of High Heaven. During his funeral, Amewakahiko's father, Amatsukunitama, and other family members confused Shitateruhime's step-brother, [[Ajisukitakahikone]], for the deceased Amewakahiko. [[Ajisukitakahikone]] left in rage. In response, Shitateruhime sang a song of a type called hinaburi, or "rustic song" to honor her deceased husband.{{Cite web|title=Encyclopedia of Shinto詳細|url=https://d-museum.kokugakuin.ac.jp/eos/detail/?id=9155|access-date=2024-03-24|website=國學院大學デジタルミュージアム|language=ja}} == See Also == * {{ill|Munakata clan|ja|宗像氏|simple|User:Immanuelle/Munakata_clan|ja|宗像氏|fr|Clan Munakata}} ==References== {{reflist|draft}} == Further reading == * Jugon, Jean-Claude. {{draft}} {{Expand Japanese|シタテルヒメ}}{{Infobox deity | type = [[Shinto]] | father = [[Ōkuninushi]] | mother = {{ill|Tagorihime|ja|タキリビメ|simple|User:Immanuelle/Takiribime|en:draft}} |cult_centre={{ill|Shitori Shrine (Tottori)|lt=Shitori Shrine|en}},
{{ill|Kifune Shrine|simple|User:Immanuelle/Kifune Shrine|en}}|name=Shitateruhime|siblings=[[Ajisukitakahikone]]|spouse={{ill|Ame no Wakahiko|en|10=en:draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ame-No-Wakahiko}}|image=File:Shitori-jinja, haiden.jpg|caption={{ill|Shitori Shrine (Tottori)|lt=Shitori Shrine|en}} where she is worshipped}}{{complex}} {{User:Immanuelle/Promising Draft}} {{ill|Shitateruhime|lt=Shitateruhime-no-Mikoto|ja|シタテルヒメ|simple|User:Immanuelle/Shitateruhime|en:draft|8=fr}} is a daughter of {{ill|Tagorihime|ja|タキリビメ|simple|User:Immanuelle/Takiribime|en:draft|8=fr}}, one of the three sisters worshipped at [[Munakata Taisha|Munakata Taisha]] The origins of {{ill|Shitori Shrine (Tottori)|lt=Shitori Shrine|en|4=fr|5=Shitori-jinja|6=ja|7=倭文神社_(湯梨浜町)|8=simple|9=User:Immanuelle/Shitori Shrine (Tottori)}} are unknown. Although there is no documentary evidence, it is believed that it began as the family shrine for the {{Nihongo|Shitori clan|倭文氏}} of [[Kofun period|Kofun period]] craftsmen who weavers, who regarded {{ill|Takehazuchi|lt=Takehazuchi-no-Mikoto|ja|天羽槌雄神|simple|User:Immanuelle/Takehazuchi|en:draft|8=fr}} as their ancestor. However, the shrine's legends are all centered around {{ill|Shitateruhime|lt=Shitateruhime-no-Mikoto|ja|シタテルヒメ|simple|User:Immanuelle/Shitateruhime|en:draft|8=fr}}, whom the shrine legend claims arrived in this location from [[Izumo Taisha|Izumo]] by boat. She established her residence on the mountain behind this shrine, and after her death, she was buried in a ''[[kofun|kofun]]'' constructed in the shrine's precincts.{{cite book |last1=Yoshiki |first1=Emi |title=Zenkoku 'Ichinomiya' tettei gaido |date=2007 |publisher=PHP Institute |isbn=978-4569669304 |language=Japanese}} == Marriage == In many versions of the myth {{ill|Ame no Hohi|en}} did not send a word for three years after going down to earth, all the gods gathered up, and {{ill|Ame no Wakahiko|en|10=en:draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ame-No-Wakahiko}} was one who was chosen to rule the earth. In many versions {{ill|Ame no Wakahiko|en|10=en:draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ame-No-Wakahiko}} was given a bow.{{Cite web|title=Encyclopedia of Shinto - Home: Kami in Classic Texts: Ame no Wakahiko|url=http://eos.kokugakuin.ac.jp/modules/xwords/entry.php?entryID=46|access-date=2020-09-29|website=eos.kokugakuin.ac.jp}}{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=xdfgjV2kw6oC&q=Ame+no+Wakahiko&pg=PA6|title=Japanese Mythology A to Z|last=Roberts|first=Jeremy|date=2009|publisher=Infobase Publishing|isbn=978-1-4381-2802-3|language=en}} In some versions, however, Ame no Wakahiko is the son of Ame no Hohi and Ame no Wakahiko was sent to earth to look for him.{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=xdfgjV2kw6oC&dq=Ame+no+Wakahiko&pg=PA6|title=Japanese Mythology a to Z|publisher=Infobase|year=2009|isbn=9781438128023}} She married {{ill|Ame no Wakahiko|en|10=en:draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ame-No-Wakahiko}}, when he came from heaven to discuss the "{{ill|Kuni-yuzuri|en}}". === Death === Eight years later, the gods had not yet heard a response so they sent a bird named Nakime down to earth to check in on him. Following the advice of a wise woman, Ame no Wakahiko used his bow to shoot the bird.{{Cite book|title=Handbook of Japanese mythology|last=Ashkenazi|first=Michael|date=2008|publisher=Oxford University Press|isbn=978-0-19-533262-9|series=Handbooks of world mythology|location=Oxford|pages=114}} The bird was killed but the arrow flew all the way to heaven. {{ill|Takamimusubi|en}} saw the arrow and threw it back at the earth where it hit Ame no Wakahiko while he was laying in bed, killing him.{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=uAj_PQ8o40sC&q=Takamimusubi|title=The East|date=1992|publisher=East Publications, Incorporated|language=en}} Other versions state that {{ill|Amaterasu|en}} was the one who shot the arrow back at him.{{cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=FlZxh5OaZxoC&pg=PA38|title=Impurity and Death: A Japanese Perspective|last=Abe|first=C.|publisher=Universal Publishers|year=2003|isbn=978-1-58112-195-7|page=38|access-date=2020-09-29}} This myth is the origin of a Japanese saying about the returning arrow. It is likely also be a mythicisation of attempts made by the {{ill|Yamato Kingship|en}} to impose its authority over neighbouring states. === Funeral === After Ame no Wakahiko's death, his parents built a hut (喪屋 moya) for their son. {{ill|Ajisukitakahikone|en}} went down to pay his respect. However, due to Ajisukitakahikone looking similar to Ame no Wakahiko he was mistaken to be Ame no Wakahiko brought back to life. Ajisukitakahikone was offended by this and destroyed the hut and kicked it. The hut landed in the land of Mino and became a mountain called Moyama.{{Cite book|title=Nihongi: Chronicles of Japan from the Earliest Times to A.D. 697, Volume 1|chapter=Book II|chapter-url=https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/Nihongi:_Chronicles_of_Japan_from_the_Earliest_Times_to_A.D._697/Book_II}} When {{ill|Ame no Wakahiko|en|10=en:draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ame-No-Wakahiko}} passed away, Shitateruhime's sorrowful voice was heard in the Plain of High Heaven. During his funeral, Amewakahiko's father, Amatsukunitama, and other family members confused Shitateruhime's step-brother, [[Ajisukitakahikone]], for the deceased Amewakahiko. [[Ajisukitakahikone]] left in rage. In response, Shitateruhime sang a song of a type called hinaburi, or "rustic song" to honor her deceased husband.{{Cite web|title=Encyclopedia of Shinto詳細|url=https://d-museum.kokugakuin.ac.jp/eos/detail/?id=9155|access-date=2024-03-24|website=國學院大學デジタルミュージアム|language=ja}} == See Also == * {{ill|Munakata clan|ja|宗像氏|simple|User:Immanuelle/Munakata_clan|ja|宗像氏|fr|Clan Munakata}} ==References== {{reflist|draft}} == Further reading == * Jugon, Jean-Claude. "[https://www.france-japon.net/documents/La%20romance%20du%20sentiment%20et%20de%20la%20pensee.pdf?x36399 La romance du sentiment et de la pensée dans les légendes de Tanabata (Japon) et d’Éros-Psyché (Grèce), une interprétation transculturelle: «Oni» soit qui mal y pense!]". In: 論叢現代語・現代文化　2015 Vol.14　pp. 1-92. (in French) * Nüffer, Laura. “Humans and Non-Humans: Animal Bridegrooms and Brides in Japanese Otogizōshi.” In: ''A Cultural History of Fairy Tales in the Age of the Marvelous''. Edited by Suzanne Magnanini. London: Bloomsbury Academic Press, 2021. pp. 95-118. * ITO, Yuko. "[https://tsuru.repo.nii.ac.jp/?action=pages_view_main&active_action=repository_view_main_item_detail&item_id=201&item_no=1&page_id=4&block_id=34 Origins and development of the two versions of "Ame no Wakahiko Soshi": a comparative study]". In: 都留文科大学研究紀要 [The Tsuru University Review], Mar/2007, volume 65, pp. 258–241. https://ci.nii.ac.jp/naid/110007055993/en/; {{ISSN|0286-3774}}. DOI: info:doi/10.34356/00000195 (in Japanese) * Yasufuku, Junko. "[http://ir.lib.osaka-kyoiku.ac.jp/dspace/handle/123456789/6149 The Tale of Ame no Wakahiko and the Psychic Development of the Feminine]". In: ''Memoirs of Osaka Kyoiku University. IV, Education, pshychology, special education and physical culture'', Osaka Kyoiku University, Feb/1995, volume 43, no. 2, pp. 251–258. {{ISSN|0389-3472}}. In many versions {{ill|Ame no Wakahiko|en|10=en:draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ame-No-Wakahiko}} was given a bow.{{Cite web|title=Encyclopedia of Shinto - Home: Kami in Classic Texts: Ame no Wakahiko|url=http://eos.kokugakuin.ac.jp/modules/xwords/entry.php?entryID=46|access-date=2020-09-29|website=eos.kokugakuin.ac.jp}}{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=xdfgjV2kw6oC&q=Ame+no+Wakahiko&pg=PA6|title=Japanese Mythology A to Z|last=Roberts|first=Jeremy|date=2009|publisher=Infobase Publishing|isbn=978-1-4381-2802-3|language=en}} In some versions, however, Ame no Wakahiko is the son of Ame no Hohi and Ame no Wakahiko was sent to earth to look for him.{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=xdfgjV2kw6oC&dq=Ame+no+Wakahiko&pg=PA6|title=Japanese Mythology a to Z|publisher=Infobase|year=2009|isbn=9781438128023}} She married {{ill|Ame no Wakahiko|en|10=en:draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ame-No-Wakahiko}}, when he came from heaven to discuss the "{{ill|Kuni-yuzuri|en}}". === Death === Eight years later, the gods had not yet heard a response so they sent a bird named Nakime down to earth to check in on him. Following the advice of a wise woman, Ame no Wakahiko used his bow to shoot the bird.{{Cite book|title=Handbook of Japanese mythology|last=Ashkenazi|first=Michael|date=2008|publisher=Oxford University Press|isbn=978-0-19-533262-9|series=Handbooks of world mythology|location=Oxford|pages=114}} The bird was killed but the arrow flew all the way to heaven. {{ill|Takamimusubi|en}} saw the arrow and threw it back at the earth where it hit Ame no Wakahiko while he was laying in bed, killing him.{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=uAj_PQ8o40sC&q=Takamimusubi|title=The East|date=1992|publisher=East Publications, Incorporated|language=en}} Other versions state that {{ill|Amaterasu|en}} was the one who shot the arrow back at him.{{cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=FlZxh5OaZxoC&pg=PA38|title=Impurity and Death: A Japanese Perspective|last=Abe|first=C.|publisher=Universal Publishers|year=2003|isbn=978-1-58112-195-7|page=38|access-date=2020-09-29}} This myth is the origin of a Japanese saying about the returning arrow. It is likely also be a mythicisation of attempts made by the {{ill|Yamato Kingship|en}} to impose its authority over neighbouring states. === Funeral === After Ame no Wakahiko's death, his parents built a hut (喪屋 moya) for their son. {{ill|Ajisukitakahikone|en}} went down to pay his respect. However, due to Ajisukitakahikone looking similar to Ame no Wakahiko he was mistaken to be Ame no Wakahiko brought back to life. Ajisukitakahikone was offended by this and destroyed the hut and kicked it. The hut landed in the land of Mino and became a mountain called Moyama.{{Cite book|title=Nihongi: Chronicles of Japan from the Earliest Times to A.D. 697, Volume 1|chapter=Book II|chapter-url=https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/Nihongi:_Chronicles_of_Japan_from_the_Earliest_Times_to_A.D._697/Book_II}} When {{ill|Ame no Wakahiko|en|10=en:draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ame-No-Wakahiko}} passed away, Shitateruhime's sorrowful voice was heard in the Plain of High Heaven. During his funeral, Amewakahiko's father, Amatsukunitama, and other family members confused Shitateruhime's step-brother, [[Ajisukitakahikone]], for the deceased Amewakahiko. [[Ajisukitakahikone]] left in rage. In response, Shitateruhime sang a song of a type called hinaburi, or "rustic song" to honor her deceased husband.{{Cite web|title=Encyclopedia of Shinto詳細|url=https://d-museum.kokugakuin.ac.jp/eos/detail/?id=9155|access-date=2024-03-24|website=國學院大學デジタルミュージアム|language=ja}} == See Also == * {{ill|Munakata clan|ja|宗像氏|simple|User:Immanuelle/Munakata_clan|ja|宗像氏|fr|Clan Munakata}} ==References== {{reflist|draft}} == Further reading == * Jugon, Jean-Claude. {{draft}} {{Expand Japanese|シタテルヒメ}}{{Infobox deity | type = [[Shinto]] | father = [[Ōkuninushi]] | mother = {{ill|Tagorihime|ja|タキリビメ|simple|User:Immanuelle/Takiribime|en:draft}} |cult_centre={{ill|Shitori Shrine (Tottori)|lt=Shitori Shrine|en}},
{{ill|Kifune Shrine|simple|User:Immanuelle/Kifune Shrine|en}}|name=Shitateruhime|siblings=[[Ajisukitakahikone]]|spouse={{ill|Ame no Wakahiko|en|10=en:draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ame-No-Wakahiko}}|image=File:Shitori-jinja, haiden.jpg|caption={{ill|Shitori Shrine (Tottori)|lt=Shitori Shrine|en}} where she is worshipped}}{{complex}} {{User:Immanuelle/Promising Draft}} {{ill|Shitateruhime|lt=Shitateruhime-no-Mikoto|ja|シタテルヒメ|simple|User:Immanuelle/Shitateruhime|en:draft|8=fr}} is a daughter of {{ill|Tagorihime|ja|タキリビメ|simple|User:Immanuelle/Takiribime|en:draft|8=fr}}, one of the three sisters worshipped at [[Munakata Taisha|Munakata Taisha]] The origins of {{ill|Shitori Shrine (Tottori)|lt=Shitori Shrine|en|4=fr|5=Shitori-jinja|6=ja|7=倭文神社_(湯梨浜町)|8=simple|9=User:Immanuelle/Shitori Shrine (Tottori)}} are unknown. Although there is no documentary evidence, it is believed that it began as the family shrine for the {{Nihongo|Shitori clan|倭文氏}} of [[Kofun period|Kofun period]] craftsmen who weavers, who regarded {{ill|Takehazuchi|lt=Takehazuchi-no-Mikoto|ja|天羽槌雄神|simple|User:Immanuelle/Takehazuchi|en:draft|8=fr}} as their ancestor. However, the shrine's legends are all centered around {{ill|Shitateruhime|lt=Shitateruhime-no-Mikoto|ja|シタテルヒメ|simple|User:Immanuelle/Shitateruhime|en:draft|8=fr}}, whom the shrine legend claims arrived in this location from [[Izumo Taisha|Izumo]] by boat. She established her residence on the mountain behind this shrine, and after her death, she was buried in a ''[[kofun|kofun]]'' constructed in the shrine's precincts.{{cite book |last1=Yoshiki |first1=Emi |title=Zenkoku 'Ichinomiya' tettei gaido |date=2007 |publisher=PHP Institute |isbn=978-4569669304 |language=Japanese}} == Marriage == In many versions of the myth {{ill|Ame no Hohi|en}} did not send a word for three years after going down to earth, all the gods gathered up, and {{ill|Ame no Wakahiko|en|10=en:draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ame-No-Wakahiko}} was one who was chosen to rule the earth. In many versions {{ill|Ame no Wakahiko|en|10=en:draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ame-No-Wakahiko}} was given a bow.{{Cite web|title=Encyclopedia of Shinto - Home: Kami in Classic Texts: Ame no Wakahiko|url=http://eos.kokugakuin.ac.jp/modules/xwords/entry.php?entryID=46|access-date=2020-09-29|website=eos.kokugakuin.ac.jp}}{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=xdfgjV2kw6oC&q=Ame+no+Wakahiko&pg=PA6|title=Japanese Mythology A to Z|last=Roberts|first=Jeremy|date=2009|publisher=Infobase Publishing|isbn=978-1-4381-2802-3|language=en}} In some versions, however, Ame no Wakahiko is the son of Ame no Hohi and Ame no Wakahiko was sent to earth to look for him.{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=xdfgjV2kw6oC&dq=Ame+no+Wakahiko&pg=PA6|title=Japanese Mythology a to Z|publisher=Infobase|year=2009|isbn=9781438128023}} She married {{ill|Ame no Wakahiko|en|10=en:draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ame-No-Wakahiko}}, when he came from heaven to discuss the "{{ill|Kuni-yuzuri|en}}". === Death === Eight years later, the gods had not yet heard a response so they sent a bird named Nakime down to earth to check in on him. Following the advice of a wise woman, Ame no Wakahiko used his bow to shoot the bird.{{Cite book|title=Handbook of Japanese mythology|last=Ashkenazi|first=Michael|date=2008|publisher=Oxford University Press|isbn=978-0-19-533262-9|series=Handbooks of world mythology|location=Oxford|pages=114}} The bird was killed but the arrow flew all the way to heaven. {{ill|Takamimusubi|en}} saw the arrow and threw it back at the earth where it hit Ame no Wakahiko while he was laying in bed, killing him.{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=uAj_PQ8o40sC&q=Takamimusubi|title=The East|date=1992|publisher=East Publications, Incorporated|language=en}} Other versions state that {{ill|Amaterasu|en}} was the one who shot the arrow back at him.{{cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=FlZxh5OaZxoC&pg=PA38|title=Impurity and Death: A Japanese Perspective|last=Abe|first=C.|publisher=Universal Publishers|year=2003|isbn=978-1-58112-195-7|page=38|access-date=2020-09-29}} This myth is the origin of a Japanese saying about the returning arrow. It is likely also be a mythicisation of attempts made by the {{ill|Yamato Kingship|en}} to impose its authority over neighbouring states. === Funeral === After Ame no Wakahiko's death, his parents built a hut (喪屋 moya) for their son. {{ill|Ajisukitakahikone|en}} went down to pay his respect. However, due to Ajisukitakahikone looking similar to Ame no Wakahiko he was mistaken to be Ame no Wakahiko brought back to life. Ajisukitakahikone was offended by this and destroyed the hut and kicked it. The hut landed in the land of Mino and became a mountain called Moyama.{{Cite book|title=Nihongi: Chronicles of Japan from the Earliest Times to A.D. 697, Volume 1|chapter=Book II|chapter-url=https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/Nihongi:_Chronicles_of_Japan_from_the_Earliest_Times_to_A.D._697/Book_II}} When {{ill|Ame no Wakahiko|en|10=en:draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ame-No-Wakahiko}} passed away, Shitateruhime's sorrowful voice was heard in the Plain of High Heaven. During his funeral, Amewakahiko's father, Amatsukunitama, and other family members confused Shitateruhime's step-brother, [[Ajisukitakahikone]], for the deceased Amewakahiko. [[Ajisukitakahikone]] left in rage. In response, Shitateruhime sang a song of a type called hinaburi, or "rustic song" to honor her deceased husband.{{Cite web|title=Encyclopedia of Shinto詳細|url=https://d-museum.kokugakuin.ac.jp/eos/detail/?id=9155|access-date=2024-03-24|website=國學院大學デジタルミュージアム|language=ja}} == See Also == * {{ill|Munakata clan|ja|宗像氏|simple|User:Immanuelle/Munakata_clan|ja|宗像氏|fr|Clan Munakata}} ==References== {{reflist|draft}} == Further reading == * Jugon, Jean-Claude. It is likely also be a mythicisation of attempts made by the {{ill|Yamato Kingship|en}} to impose its authority over neighbouring states. === Funeral === After Ame no Wakahiko's death, his parents built a hut (喪屋 moya) for their son. {{ill|Ajisukitakahikone|en}} went down to pay his respect. However, due to Ajisukitakahikone looking similar to Ame no Wakahiko he was mistaken to be Ame no Wakahiko brought back to life. Ajisukitakahikone was offended by this and destroyed the hut and kicked it. The hut landed in the land of Mino and became a mountain called Moyama.{{Cite book|title=Nihongi: Chronicles of Japan from the Earliest Times to A.D. 697, Volume 1|chapter=Book II|chapter-url=https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/Nihongi:_Chronicles_of_Japan_from_the_Earliest_Times_to_A.D._697/Book_II}} When {{ill|Ame no Wakahiko|en|10=en:draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ame-No-Wakahiko}} passed away, Shitateruhime's sorrowful voice was heard in the Plain of High Heaven. During his funeral, Amewakahiko's father, Amatsukunitama, and other family members confused Shitateruhime's step-brother, [[Ajisukitakahikone]], for the deceased Amewakahiko. [[Ajisukitakahikone]] left in rage. In response, Shitateruhime sang a song of a type called hinaburi, or "rustic song" to honor her deceased husband.{{Cite web|title=Encyclopedia of Shinto詳細|url=https://d-museum.kokugakuin.ac.jp/eos/detail/?id=9155|access-date=2024-03-24|website=國學院大學デジタルミュージアム|language=ja}} == See Also == * {{ill|Munakata clan|ja|宗像氏|simple|User:Immanuelle/Munakata_clan|ja|宗像氏|fr|Clan Munakata}} ==References== {{reflist|draft}} == Further reading == * Jugon, Jean-Claude. {{ill|Kifune Shrine|simple|User:Immanuelle/Kifune Shrine|en}}|name=Shitateruhime|siblings=[[Ajisukitakahikone]]|spouse={{ill|Ame no Wakahiko|en|10=en:draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ame-No-Wakahiko}}|image=File:Shitori-jinja, haiden.jpg|caption={{ill|Shitori Shrine (Tottori)|lt=Shitori Shrine|en}} where she is worshipped}}{{complex}} {{User:Immanuelle/Promising Draft}} {{ill|Shitateruhime|lt=Shitateruhime-no-Mikoto|ja|シタテルヒメ|simple|User:Immanuelle/Shitateruhime|en:draft|8=fr}} is a daughter of {{ill|Tagorihime|ja|タキリビメ|simple|User:Immanuelle/Takiribime|en:draft|8=fr}}, one of the three sisters worshipped at [[Munakata Taisha|Munakata Taisha]] The origins of {{ill|Shitori Shrine (Tottori)|lt=Shitori Shrine|en|4=fr|5=Shitori-jinja|6=ja|7=倭文神社_(湯梨浜町)|8=simple|9=User:Immanuelle/Shitori Shrine (Tottori)}} are unknown. Although there is no documentary evidence, it is believed that it began as the family shrine for the {{Nihongo|Shitori clan|倭文氏}} of [[Kofun period|Kofun period]] craftsmen who weavers, who regarded {{ill|Takehazuchi|lt=Takehazuchi-no-Mikoto|ja|天羽槌雄神|simple|User:Immanuelle/Takehazuchi|en:draft|8=fr}} as their ancestor. However, the shrine's legends are all centered around {{ill|Shitateruhime|lt=Shitateruhime-no-Mikoto|ja|シタテルヒメ|simple|User:Immanuelle/Shitateruhime|en:draft|8=fr}}, whom the shrine legend claims arrived in this location from [[Izumo Taisha|Izumo]] by boat. She established her residence on the mountain behind this shrine, and after her death, she was buried in a ''[[kofun|kofun]]'' constructed in the shrine's precincts.{{cite book |last1=Yoshiki |first1=Emi |title=Zenkoku 'Ichinomiya' tettei gaido |date=2007 |publisher=PHP Institute |isbn=978-4569669304 |language=Japanese}} ==overview== [[category:new pages]] {{Infobox Japanese deity | Name = Shitateruhime (下光比売命) | Generation = | Predecessor = | Successor = | DeityType = {{ill|Kunitsukami|ja|国津神}} | FullName = Shitateruhime-no-Mikoto (下光比売命) | OtherNames = Shitateruhime, Shitateruhime-no-Mikoto, Takahime, Takahime-no-Mikoto, Waka-kunitama, and others | AlternateNames = | DivineRank = | DivineRole = {{ill|God of Thunder|ja|雷神}} | BurialPlace = | Father = {{ill|Ōkuninushi|ja|大国主神}} | Mother = {{ill|Takirihime-no-Mikoto|ja|多紀理毘売命}} | Relatives = * {{ill|Ajisukitakahikone|ja|阿遅鉏高日子根神}} * {{ill|Kotoshironushi|ja|事代主神}} * {{ill|Takeminakata|ja|建御名方神}} * {{ill|Kimata-no-Kami|ja|木俣神}} * {{ill|Torinonami-no-Kami|ja|鳥鳴海神}} | Spouse = {{ill|Ame-wakahiko|ja|天若日子}} | Children = | Shrine = {{Plainlist| * {{ill|Mefu Shrine|ja|売布神社}} * {{ill|Himekoso Shrine|ja|比売許曽神社}} }} | Texts = {{ill|Kojiki|ja|古事記}}, {{ill|Nihon Shoki|ja|日本書紀}} }} '''Shitateruhime''' (下光比売命) is a female deity in {{ill|Japanese mythology|ja|日本神話}} associated with {{ill|Shinto|ja|神道}}. She is also known by the names '''Takahime''' (高比売) and '''Waka-kunitama''' (稚国玉). == Overview == In the ''{{ill|Kojiki|ja|古事記}}'', she is referred to as '''Takahime-no-Mikoto''' (高比売命) and also as '''Shitateruhime-no-Mikoto''' (下光比売命). In the ''{{ill|Nihon Shoki|ja|日本書紀}}'', she appears as '''Shitateruhime''' (下照姫) or '''Shitateruhime-no-Mikoto''', and in the ''{{ill|Sendai Kuji Hongi|ja|先代旧事本紀}}'', she is called '''Shitateruhime-no-Mikoto'''. According to the ''Kojiki'' and the ''Nihon Shoki,'' she married {{ill|Ame-wakahiko|ja|天若日子}}, who had been dispatched from {{ill|Takamagahara|ja|高天原}} to subjugate the {{ill|Ashihara no Nakatsukuni|ja|葦原中国}} (the Central Land of Reed Plains). However, Ame-wakahiko secretly plotted to claim the land for himself. When Ame-wakahiko was killed by a divine arrow sent from Takamagahara, Shitateruhime’s grief-stricken cries reached the heavens. Her mourning led to the descent of Ame-wakahiko's family, including his father {{ill|Amatsukunitama-no-Mikoto|ja|天津国玉神}}, to perform his funeral rites. During this event, her brother {{ill|Ajisukitakahikone|ja|阿遅鉏高日子根神}} was mistaken for the deceased Ame-wakahiko due to their resemblance, leading to a conflict. Shitateruhime composed a lament known as the ''Hina-buri'' (夷振), expressing her sorrow. == Genealogy == [[File:Ohokuninushi family tree.png|thumb|250px|right|Genealogy of Ōkuninushi (''Kojiki''). Blue indicates male deities, red indicates female deities, and yellow indicates unspecified gender.]] According to the ''Kojiki,'' Shitateruhime is the daughter of {{ill|Ōkuninushi|ja|大国主神}} and {{ill|Takirihime-no-Mikoto|ja|多紀理毘売命}}, making her the sister of {{ill|Ajisukitakahikone|ja|阿遅鉏高日子根神}}. This genealogy is also supported by the ''Sendai Kuji Hongi.'' == Shrines == Shitateruhime is enshrined at several locations, including: * {{ill|Hime Shrine (Toyama)|ja|比賣神社}} in {{ill|Toyama Prefecture|ja|富山県}}, where she is the main deity. * {{ill|Tamatsuoka Shrine|ja|玉津岡神社}} in {{ill|Kyoto Prefecture|ja|京都府}}, dedicated to her worship. * {{ill|Himekoso Shrine|ja|比売許曽神社}} in {{ill|Osaka Prefecture|ja|大阪府}}. * {{ill|Izumo Taisha|ja|出雲大社}}’s external shrine, known as ''Ōanamochi-no-Miko Tamae Shrine'' (大穴持御子玉江神社). == References == {{Reflist}} == Related Articles == * {{ill|List of Japanese deities|ja|日本の神の一覧}} {{Japanese mythology}} {{Shinto Horizontal}} {{shinto-stub}} [[Category:Japanese deities]] [[Category:Kunitsukami]] [[Category:Goddesses]] [[ja:下光比売命]] == Marriage == In many versions of the myth {{ill|Ame no Hohi|en}} did not send a word for three years after going down to earth, all the gods gathered up, and {{ill|Ame no Wakahiko|en|10=en:draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ame-No-Wakahiko}} was one who was chosen to rule the earth. In many versions {{ill|Ame no Wakahiko|en|10=en:draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ame-No-Wakahiko}} was given a bow.{{Cite web|title=Encyclopedia of Shinto - Home: Kami in Classic Texts: Ame no Wakahiko|url=http://eos.kokugakuin.ac.jp/modules/xwords/entry.php?entryID=46|access-date=2020-09-29|website=eos.kokugakuin.ac.jp}}{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=xdfgjV2kw6oC&q=Ame+no+Wakahiko&pg=PA6|title=Japanese Mythology A to Z|last=Roberts|first=Jeremy|date=2009|publisher=Infobase Publishing|isbn=978-1-4381-2802-3|language=en}} In some versions, however, Ame no Wakahiko is the son of Ame no Hohi and Ame no Wakahiko was sent to earth to look for him.{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=xdfgjV2kw6oC&dq=Ame+no+Wakahiko&pg=PA6|title=Japanese Mythology a to Z|publisher=Infobase|year=2009|isbn=9781438128023}} She married {{ill|Ame no Wakahiko|en|10=en:draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ame-No-Wakahiko}}, when he came from heaven to discuss the "{{ill|Kuni-yuzuri|en}}". === Death === Eight years later, the gods had not yet heard a response so they sent a bird named Nakime down to earth to check in on him. Following the advice of a wise woman, Ame no Wakahiko used his bow to shoot the bird.{{Cite book|title=Handbook of Japanese mythology|last=Ashkenazi|first=Michael|date=2008|publisher=Oxford University Press|isbn=978-0-19-533262-9|series=Handbooks of world mythology|location=Oxford|pages=114}} The bird was killed but the arrow flew all the way to heaven. {{ill|Takamimusubi|en}} saw the arrow and threw it back at the earth where it hit Ame no Wakahiko while he was laying in bed, killing him.{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=uAj_PQ8o40sC&q=Takamimusubi|title=The East|date=1992|publisher=East Publications, Incorporated|language=en}} Other versions state that {{ill|Amaterasu|en}} was the one who shot the arrow back at him.{{cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=FlZxh5OaZxoC&pg=PA38|title=Impurity and Death: A Japanese Perspective|last=Abe|first=C.|publisher=Universal Publishers|year=2003|isbn=978-1-58112-195-7|page=38|access-date=2020-09-29}} This myth is the origin of a Japanese saying about the returning arrow. It is likely also be a mythicisation of attempts made by the {{ill|Yamato Kingship|en}} to impose its authority over neighbouring states. === Funeral === After Ame no Wakahiko's death, his parents built a hut (喪屋 moya) for their son. {{ill|Ajisukitakahikone|en}} went down to pay his respect. However, due to Ajisukitakahikone looking similar to Ame no Wakahiko he was mistaken to be Ame no Wakahiko brought back to life. Ajisukitakahikone was offended by this and destroyed the hut and kicked it. The hut landed in the land of Mino and became a mountain called Moyama.{{Cite book|title=Nihongi: Chronicles of Japan from the Earliest Times to A.D. 697, Volume 1|chapter=Book II|chapter-url=https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/Nihongi:_Chronicles_of_Japan_from_the_Earliest_Times_to_A.D._697/Book_II}} When {{ill|Ame no Wakahiko|en|10=en:draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ame-No-Wakahiko}} passed away, Shitateruhime's sorrowful voice was heard in the Plain of High Heaven. During his funeral, Amewakahiko's father, Amatsukunitama, and other family members confused Shitateruhime's step-brother, [[Ajisukitakahikone]], for the deceased Amewakahiko. [[Ajisukitakahikone]] left in rage. In response, Shitateruhime sang a song of a type called hinaburi, or "rustic song" to honor her deceased husband.{{Cite web|title=Encyclopedia of Shinto詳細|url=https://d-museum.kokugakuin.ac.jp/eos/detail/?id=9155|access-date=2024-03-24|website=國學院大學デジタルミュージアム|language=ja}} == See Also == * {{ill|Munakata clan|ja|宗像氏|simple|User:Immanuelle/Munakata_clan|ja|宗像氏|fr|Clan Munakata}} ==References== {{reflist|draft}} == Further reading == * Jugon, Jean-Claude. {{ill|Kifune Shrine|simple|User:Immanuelle/Kifune Shrine|en}}|name=Shitateruhime|siblings=[[Ajisukitakahikone]]|spouse={{ill|Ame no Wakahiko|en|10=en:draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ame-No-Wakahiko}}|image=File:Shitori-jinja, haiden.jpg|caption={{ill|Shitori Shrine (Tottori)|lt=Shitori Shrine|en}} where she is worshipped}}{{complex}} {{User:Immanuelle/Promising Draft}} {{ill|Shitateruhime|lt=Shitateruhime-no-Mikoto|ja|シタテルヒメ|simple|User:Immanuelle/Shitateruhime|en:draft|8=fr}} is a daughter of {{ill|Tagorihime|ja|タキリビメ|simple|User:Immanuelle/Takiribime|en:draft|8=fr}}, one of the three sisters worshipped at [[Munakata Taisha|Munakata Taisha]] The origins of {{ill|Shitori Shrine (Tottori)|lt=Shitori Shrine|en|4=fr|5=Shitori-jinja|6=ja|7=倭文神社_(湯梨浜町)|8=simple|9=User:Immanuelle/Shitori Shrine (Tottori)}} are unknown. Although there is no documentary evidence, it is believed that it began as the family shrine for the {{Nihongo|Shitori clan|倭文氏}} of [[Kofun period|Kofun period]] craftsmen who weavers, who regarded {{ill|Takehazuchi|lt=Takehazuchi-no-Mikoto|ja|天羽槌雄神|simple|User:Immanuelle/Takehazuchi|en:draft|8=fr}} as their ancestor. However, the shrine's legends are all centered around {{ill|Shitateruhime|lt=Shitateruhime-no-Mikoto|ja|シタテルヒメ|simple|User:Immanuelle/Shitateruhime|en:draft|8=fr}}, whom the shrine legend claims arrived in this location from [[Izumo Taisha|Izumo]] by boat. She established her residence on the mountain behind this shrine, and after her death, she was buried in a ''[[kofun|kofun]]'' constructed in the shrine's precincts.{{cite book |last1=Yoshiki |first1=Emi |title=Zenkoku 'Ichinomiya' tettei gaido |date=2007 |publisher=PHP Institute |isbn=978-4569669304 |language=Japanese}} ==overview== [[Category:Pages with redlinks to fill]] {{Infobox Japanese deity | Name = Shitateruhime (下光比売命) | Generation = | Predecessor = | Successor = | DeityType = {{ill|Kunitsukami|ja|国津神}} | FullName = Shitateruhime-no-Mikoto (下光比売命) | OtherNames = Shitateruhime, Shitateruhime-no-Mikoto, Takahime, Takahime-no-Mikoto, Waka-kunitama, and others | AlternateNames = | DivineRank = | DivineRole = {{ill|God of Thunder|ja|雷神}} | BurialPlace = | Father = {{ill|Ōkuninushi|ja|大国主神}} | Mother = {{ill|Takirihime-no-Mikoto|ja|多紀理毘売命}} | Relatives = * {{ill|Ajisukitakahikone|ja|阿遅鉏高日子根神}} * {{ill|Kotoshironushi|ja|事代主神}} * {{ill|Takeminakata|ja|建御名方神}} * {{ill|Kimata-no-Kami|ja|木俣神}} * {{ill|Torinonami-no-Kami|ja|鳥鳴海神}} | Spouse = {{ill|Ame-wakahiko|ja|天若日子}} | Children = | Shrine = {{Plainlist| * {{ill|Mefu Shrine|ja|売布神社}} * {{ill|Himekoso Shrine|ja|比売許曽神社}} }} | Texts = {{ill|Kojiki|ja|古事記}}, {{ill|Nihon Shoki|ja|日本書紀}} }} '''Shitateruhime''' (下光比売命) is a female deity in {{ill|Japanese mythology|ja|日本神話}} associated with {{ill|Shinto|ja|神道}}. She is also known by the names '''Takahime''' (高比売) and '''Waka-kunitama''' (稚国玉). == Overview == In the ''{{ill|Kojiki|ja|古事記}}'', she is referred to as '''Takahime-no-Mikoto''' (高比売命) and also as '''Shitateruhime-no-Mikoto''' (下光比売命). In the ''{{ill|Nihon Shoki|ja|日本書紀}}'', she appears as '''Shitateruhime''' (下照姫) or '''Shitateruhime-no-Mikoto''', and in the ''{{ill|Sendai Kuji Hongi|ja|先代旧事本紀}}'', she is called '''Shitateruhime-no-Mikoto'''. According to the ''Kojiki'' and the ''Nihon Shoki,'' she married {{ill|Ame-wakahiko|ja|天若日子}}, who had been dispatched from {{ill|Takamagahara|ja|高天原}} to subjugate the {{ill|Ashihara no Nakatsukuni|ja|葦原中国}} (the Central Land of Reed Plains). However, Ame-wakahiko secretly plotted to claim the land for himself. When Ame-wakahiko was killed by a divine arrow sent from Takamagahara, Shitateruhime’s grief-stricken cries reached the heavens. Her mourning led to the descent of Ame-wakahiko's family, including his father {{ill|Amatsukunitama-no-Mikoto|ja|天津国玉神}}, to perform his funeral rites. During this event, her brother {{ill|Ajisukitakahikone|ja|阿遅鉏高日子根神}} was mistaken for the deceased Ame-wakahiko due to their resemblance, leading to a conflict. Shitateruhime composed a lament known as the ''Hina-buri'' (夷振), expressing her sorrow. == Genealogy == [[File:Ohokuninushi family tree.png|thumb|250px|right|Genealogy of Ōkuninushi (''Kojiki''). Blue indicates male deities, red indicates female deities, and yellow indicates unspecified gender.]] According to the ''Kojiki,'' Shitateruhime is the daughter of {{ill|Ōkuninushi|ja|大国主神}} and {{ill|Takirihime-no-Mikoto|ja|多紀理毘売命}}, making her the sister of {{ill|Ajisukitakahikone|ja|阿遅鉏高日子根神}}. This genealogy is also supported by the ''Sendai Kuji Hongi.'' == Shrines == Shitateruhime is enshrined at several locations, including: * {{ill|Hime Shrine (Toyama)|ja|比賣神社}} in {{ill|Toyama Prefecture|ja|富山県}}, where she is the main deity. * {{ill|Tamatsuoka Shrine|ja|玉津岡神社}} in {{ill|Kyoto Prefecture|ja|京都府}}, dedicated to her worship. * {{ill|Himekoso Shrine|ja|比売許曽神社}} in {{ill|Osaka Prefecture|ja|大阪府}}. * {{ill|Izumo Taisha|ja|出雲大社}}’s external shrine, known as ''Ōanamochi-no-Miko Tamae Shrine'' (大穴持御子玉江神社). == References == {{Reflist}} == Related Articles == * {{ill|List of Japanese deities|ja|日本の神の一覧}} {{Japanese mythology}} {{Shinto Horizontal}} {{shinto-stub}} [[Category:Japanese deities]] [[Category:Kunitsukami]] [[Category:Goddesses]] [[ja:下光比売命]] == Marriage == In many versions of the myth {{ill|Ame no Hohi|en}} did not send a word for three years after going down to earth, all the gods gathered up, and {{ill|Ame no Wakahiko|en|10=en:draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ame-No-Wakahiko}} was one who was chosen to rule the earth. The hut landed in the land of Mino and became a mountain called Moyama.{{Cite book|title=Nihongi: Chronicles of Japan from the Earliest Times to A.D. 697, Volume 1|chapter=Book II|chapter-url=https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/Nihongi:_Chronicles_of_Japan_from_the_Earliest_Times_to_A.D._697/Book_II}} When {{ill|Ame no Wakahiko|en|10=en:draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ame-No-Wakahiko}} passed away, Shitateruhime's sorrowful voice was heard in the Plain of High Heaven. In response, Shitateruhime sang a song of a type called hinaburi, or "rustic song" to honor her deceased husband.{{Cite web|title=Encyclopedia of Shinto詳細|url=https://d-museum.kokugakuin.ac.jp/eos/detail/?id=9155|access-date=2024-03-24|website=國學院大學デジタルミュージアム|language=ja}} == See Also == * {{ill|Munakata clan|ja|宗像氏|simple|User:Immanuelle/Munakata_clan|ja|宗像氏|fr|Clan Munakata}} ==References== {{reflist|draft}} == Further reading == * Jugon, Jean-Claude.
