She established her residence on the mountain behind this shrine, and after her death, she was buried in a ''[[kofun|kofun]]'' constructed in the shrine's precincts.{{cite book |last1=Yoshiki |first1=Emi |title=Zenkoku 'Ichinomiya' tettei gaido |date=2007 |publisher=PHP Institute |isbn=978-4569669304 |language=Japanese}} ==overview== [[Category:Pages with redlinks to fill]] {{Infobox Japanese deity | Name = Shitateruhime (下光比売命) | Generation = | Predecessor = | Successor = | DeityType = {{ill|Kunitsukami|ja|国津神}} | FullName = Shitateruhime-no-Mikoto (下光比売命) | OtherNames = Shitateruhime, Shitateruhime-no-Mikoto, Takahime, Takahime-no-Mikoto, Waka-kunitama, and others | AlternateNames = | DivineRank = | DivineRole = {{ill|God of Thunder|ja|雷神}} | BurialPlace = | Father = {{ill|Ōkuninushi|ja|大国主神}} | Mother = {{ill|Takirihime-no-Mikoto|ja|多紀理毘売命}} | Relatives = * {{ill|Ajisukitakahikone|ja|阿遅鉏高日子根神}} * {{ill|Kotoshironushi|ja|事代主神}} * {{ill|Takeminakata|ja|建御名方神}} * {{ill|Kimata-no-Kami|ja|木俣神}} * {{ill|Torinonami-no-Kami|ja|鳥鳴海神}} | Spouse = {{ill|Ame-wakahiko|ja|天若日子}} | Children = | Shrine = {{Plainlist| * {{ill|Mefu Shrine|ja|売布神社}} * {{ill|Himekoso Shrine|ja|比売許曽神社}} }} | Texts = {{ill|Kojiki|ja|古事記}}, {{ill|Nihon Shoki|ja|日本書紀}} }} '''Shitateruhime''' (下光比売命) is a female deity in {{ill|Japanese mythology|ja|日本神話}} associated with {{ill|Shinto|ja|神道}}. She is also known by the names '''Takahime''' (高比売) and '''Waka-kunitama''' (稚国玉). == Overview == In the ''{{ill|Kojiki|ja|古事記}}'', she is referred to as '''Takahime-no-Mikoto''' (高比売命) and also as '''Shitateruhime-no-Mikoto''' (下光比売命). In the ''{{ill|Nihon Shoki|ja|日本書紀}}'', she appears as '''Shitateruhime''' (下照姫) or '''Shitateruhime-no-Mikoto''', and in the ''{{ill|Sendai Kuji Hongi|ja|先代旧事本紀}}'', she is called '''Shitateruhime-no-Mikoto'''. According to the ''Kojiki'' and the ''Nihon Shoki,'' she married {{ill|Ame-wakahiko|ja|天若日子}}, who had been dispatched from {{ill|Takamagahara|ja|高天原}} to subjugate the {{ill|Ashihara no Nakatsukuni|ja|葦原中国}} (the Central Land of Reed Plains). However, Ame-wakahiko secretly plotted to claim the land for himself. When Ame-wakahiko was killed by a divine arrow sent from Takamagahara, Shitateruhime’s grief-stricken cries reached the heavens. Her mourning led to the descent of Ame-wakahiko's family, including his father {{ill|Amatsukunitama-no-Mikoto|ja|天津国玉神}}, to perform his funeral rites. During this event, her brother {{ill|Ajisukitakahikone|ja|阿遅鉏高日子根神}} was mistaken for the deceased Ame-wakahiko due to their resemblance, leading to a conflict. Shitateruhime composed a lament known as the ''Hina-buri'' (夷振), expressing her sorrow. == Genealogy == [[File:Ohokuninushi family tree.png|thumb|250px|right|Genealogy of Ōkuninushi (''Kojiki''). Blue indicates male deities, red indicates female deities, and yellow indicates unspecified gender.]] According to the ''Kojiki,'' Shitateruhime is the daughter of {{ill|Ōkuninushi|ja|大国主神}} and {{ill|Takirihime-no-Mikoto|ja|多紀理毘売命}}, making her the sister of {{ill|Ajisukitakahikone|ja|阿遅鉏高日子根神}}. This genealogy is also supported by the ''Sendai Kuji Hongi.'' == Shrines == Shitateruhime is enshrined at several locations, including: * {{ill|Hime Shrine (Toyama)|ja|比賣神社}} in {{ill|Toyama Prefecture|ja|富山県}}, where she is the main deity. * {{ill|Tamatsuoka Shrine|ja|玉津岡神社}} in {{ill|Kyoto Prefecture|ja|京都府}}, dedicated to her worship. * {{ill|Himekoso Shrine|ja|比売許曽神社}} in {{ill|Osaka Prefecture|ja|大阪府}}. * {{ill|Izumo Taisha|ja|出雲大社}}’s external shrine, known as ''Ōanamochi-no-Miko Tamae Shrine'' (大穴持御子玉江神社). == References == {{Reflist}} == Related Articles == * {{ill|List of Japanese deities|ja|日本の神の一覧}} {{Japanese mythology}} {{Shinto Horizontal}} {{shinto-stub}} [[Category:Japanese deities]] [[Category:Kunitsukami]] [[Category:Goddesses]] [[ja:下光比売命]] == Marriage == In many versions of the myth {{ill|Ame no Hohi|en}} did not send a word for three years after going down to earth, all the gods gathered up, and {{ill|Ame no Wakahiko|en|10=en:draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ame-No-Wakahiko}} was one who was chosen to rule the earth. In many versions {{ill|Ame no Wakahiko|en|10=en:draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ame-No-Wakahiko}} was given a bow.{{Cite web|title=Encyclopedia of Shinto - Home: Kami in Classic Texts: Ame no Wakahiko|url=http://eos.kokugakuin.ac.jp/modules/xwords/entry.php?entryID=46|access-date=2020-09-29|website=eos.kokugakuin.ac.jp}}{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=xdfgjV2kw6oC&q=Ame+no+Wakahiko&pg=PA6|title=Japanese Mythology A to Z|last=Roberts|first=Jeremy|date=2009|publisher=Infobase Publishing|isbn=978-1-4381-2802-3|language=en}} In some versions, however, Ame no Wakahiko is the son of Ame no Hohi and Ame no Wakahiko was sent to earth to look for him.{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=xdfgjV2kw6oC&dq=Ame+no+Wakahiko&pg=PA6|title=Japanese Mythology a to Z|publisher=Infobase|year=2009|isbn=9781438128023}} She married {{ill|Ame no Wakahiko|en|10=en:draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ame-No-Wakahiko}}, when he came from heaven to discuss the "{{ill|Kuni-yuzuri|en}}". === Death === Eight years later, the gods had not yet heard a response so they sent a bird named Nakime down to earth to check in on him. Following the advice of a wise woman, Ame no Wakahiko used his bow to shoot the bird.{{Cite book|title=Handbook of Japanese mythology|last=Ashkenazi|first=Michael|date=2008|publisher=Oxford University Press|isbn=978-0-19-533262-9|series=Handbooks of world mythology|location=Oxford|pages=114}} The bird was killed but the arrow flew all the way to heaven. {{ill|Takamimusubi|en}} saw the arrow and threw it back at the earth where it hit Ame no Wakahiko while he was laying in bed, killing him.{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=uAj_PQ8o40sC&q=Takamimusubi|title=The East|date=1992|publisher=East Publications, Incorporated|language=en}} Other versions state that {{ill|Amaterasu|en}} was the one who shot the arrow back at him.{{cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=FlZxh5OaZxoC&pg=PA38|title=Impurity and Death: A Japanese Perspective|last=Abe|first=C.|publisher=Universal Publishers|year=2003|isbn=978-1-58112-195-7|page=38|access-date=2020-09-29}} This myth is the origin of a Japanese saying about the returning arrow. It is likely also be a mythicisation of attempts made by the {{ill|Yamato Kingship|en}} to impose its authority over neighbouring states. === Funeral === After Ame no Wakahiko's death, his parents built a hut (喪屋 moya) for their son. {{ill|Ajisukitakahikone|en}} went down to pay his respect. However, due to Ajisukitakahikone looking similar to Ame no Wakahiko he was mistaken to be Ame no Wakahiko brought back to life. Ajisukitakahikone was offended by this and destroyed the hut and kicked it. The hut landed in the land of Mino and became a mountain called Moyama.{{Cite book|title=Nihongi: Chronicles of Japan from the Earliest Times to A.D. 697, Volume 1|chapter=Book II|chapter-url=https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/Nihongi:_Chronicles_of_Japan_from_the_Earliest_Times_to_A.D._697/Book_II}} When {{ill|Ame no Wakahiko|en|10=en:draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ame-No-Wakahiko}} passed away, Shitateruhime's sorrowful voice was heard in the Plain of High Heaven. During his funeral, Amewakahiko's father, Amatsukunitama, and other family members confused Shitateruhime's step-brother, [[Ajisukitakahikone]], for the deceased Amewakahiko. [[Ajisukitakahikone]] left in rage. In response, Shitateruhime sang a song of a type called hinaburi, or "rustic song" to honor her deceased husband.{{Cite web|title=Encyclopedia of Shinto詳細|url=https://d-museum.kokugakuin.ac.jp/eos/detail/?id=9155|access-date=2024-03-24|website=國學院大學デジタルミュージアム|language=ja}} == See Also == * {{ill|Munakata clan|ja|宗像氏|simple|User:Immanuelle/Munakata_clan|ja|宗像氏|fr|Clan Munakata}} ==References== {{reflist|draft}} == Further reading == * Jugon, Jean-Claude. {{ill|Kifune Shrine|simple|User:Immanuelle/Kifune Shrine|en}}|name=Shitateruhime|siblings=[[Ajisukitakahikone]]|spouse={{ill|Ame no Wakahiko|ja|10=en:draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ame-No-Wakahiko}}|image=File:Shitori-jinja, haiden.jpg|caption={{ill|Shitori Shrine (Tottori)|lt=Shitori Shrine|en}} where she is worshipped}}{{complex}} {{User:Immanuelle/Promising Draft}} {{ill|Shitateruhime|lt=Shitateruhime-no-Mikoto|ja|シタテルヒメ|simple|User:Immanuelle/Shitateruhime|en:draft|8=fr}} is a daughter of {{ill|Tagorihime|ja|タキリビメ|simple|User:Immanuelle/Takiribime|en:draft|8=fr}}, one of the three sisters worshipped at [[Munakata Taisha|Munakata Taisha]] The origins of {{ill|Shitori Shrine (Tottori)|lt=Shitori Shrine|ja|4=fr|5=Shitori-jinja|6=ja|7=倭文神社_(湯梨浜町)|8=simple|9=User:Immanuelle/Shitori Shrine (Tottori)}} are unknown. Although there is no documentary evidence, it is believed that it began as the family shrine for the {{Nihongo|Shitori clan|倭文氏}} of [[Kofun period|Kofun period]] craftsmen who weavers, who regarded {{ill|Takehazuchi|lt=Takehazuchi-no-Mikoto|ja|天羽槌雄神|simple|User:Immanuelle/Takehazuchi|en:draft|8=fr}} as their ancestor. However, the shrine's legends are all centered around {{ill|Shitateruhime|lt=Shitateruhime-no-Mikoto|ja|シタテルヒメ|simple|User:Immanuelle/Shitateruhime|en:draft|8=fr}}, whom the shrine legend claims arrived in this location from [[Izumo Taisha|Izumo]] by boat. She established her residence on the mountain behind this shrine, and after her death, she was buried in a ''[[kofun|kofun]]'' constructed in the shrine's precincts.{{cite book |last1=Yoshiki |first1=Emi |title=Zenkoku 'Ichinomiya' tettei gaido |date=2007 |publisher=PHP Institute |isbn=978-4569669304 |language=Japanese}} ==overview== [[Category:Pages with redlinks to fill]] [[Category:kkk]]{{DEFAULTSORT:Shitateruhime}}[[category:kk]] {{Infobox Japanese deity | Name = Shitateruhime (下光比売命) | Generation = | Predecessor = | Successor = | DeityType = {{ill|Kunitsukami|ja|国津神}} | FullName = Shitateruhime-no-Mikoto (下光比売命) | OtherNames = Shitateruhime, Shitateruhime-no-Mikoto, Takahime, Takahime-no-Mikoto, Waka-kunitama, and others | AlternateNames = | DivineRank = | DivineRole = {{ill|God of Thunder|ja|雷神}} | BurialPlace = | Father = {{ill|Ōkuninushi|ja|大国主神}} | Mother = {{ill|Takirihime-no-Mikoto|ja|多紀理毘売命}} | Relatives = * {{ill|Ajisukitakahikone|ja|阿遅鉏高日子根神}} * {{ill|Kotoshironushi|ja|事代主神}} * {{ill|Takeminakata|ja|建御名方神}} * {{ill|Kimata-no-Kami|ja|木俣神}} * {{ill|Torinonami-no-Kami|ja|鳥鳴海神}} | Spouse = {{ill|Ame-wakahiko|ja|天若日子}} | Children = | Shrine = {{Plainlist| * {{ill|Mefu Shrine|ja|売布神社}} * {{ill|Himekoso Shrine|ja|比売許曽神社}} }} | Texts = {{ill|Kojiki|ja|古事記}}, {{ill|Nihon Shoki|ja|日本書紀}} }} '''Shitateruhime''' (下光比売命) is a female deity in {{ill|Japanese mythology|ja|日本神話}} associated with {{ill|Shinto|ja|神道}}. She is also known by the names '''Takahime''' (高比売) and '''Waka-kunitama''' (稚国玉). == Overview == In the ''{{ill|Kojiki|ja|古事記}}'', she is referred to as '''Takahime-no-Mikoto''' (高比売命) and also as '''Shitateruhime-no-Mikoto''' (下光比売命). In the ''{{ill|Nihon Shoki|ja|日本書紀}}'', she appears as '''Shitateruhime''' (下照姫) or '''Shitateruhime-no-Mikoto''', and in the ''{{ill|Sendai Kuji Hongi|ja|先代旧事本紀}}'', she is called '''Shitateruhime-no-Mikoto'''. According to the ''Kojiki'' and the ''Nihon Shoki,'' she married {{ill|Ame-wakahiko|ja|天若日子}}, who had been dispatched from {{ill|Takamagahara|ja|高天原}} to subjugate the {{ill|Ashihara no Nakatsukuni|ja|葦原中国}} (the Central Land of Reed Plains). However, Ame-wakahiko secretly plotted to claim the land for himself. When Ame-wakahiko was killed by a divine arrow sent from Takamagahara, Shitateruhime’s grief-stricken cries reached the heavens. Her mourning led to the descent of Ame-wakahiko's family, including his father {{ill|Amatsukunitama-no-Mikoto|ja|天津国玉神}}, to perform his funeral rites. During this event, her brother {{ill|Ajisukitakahikone|ja|阿遅鉏高日子根神}} was mistaken for the deceased Ame-wakahiko due to their resemblance, leading to a conflict. Shitateruhime composed a lament known as the ''Hina-buri'' (夷振), expressing her sorrow. == Genealogy == [[File:Ohokuninushi family tree.png|thumb|250px|right|Genealogy of Ōkuninushi (''Kojiki''). Blue indicates male deities, red indicates female deities, and yellow indicates unspecified gender.]] According to the ''Kojiki,'' Shitateruhime is the daughter of {{ill|Ōkuninushi|ja|大国主神}} and {{ill|Takirihime-no-Mikoto|ja|多紀理毘売命}}, making her the sister of {{ill|Ajisukitakahikone|ja|阿遅鉏高日子根神}}. This genealogy is also supported by the ''Sendai Kuji Hongi.'' == Shrines == Shitateruhime is enshrined at several locations, including: * {{ill|Hime Shrine (Toyama)|ja|比賣神社}} in {{ill|Toyama Prefecture|ja|富山県}}, where she is the main deity. * {{ill|Tamatsuoka Shrine|ja|玉津岡神社}} in {{ill|Kyoto Prefecture|ja|京都府}}, dedicated to her worship. * {{ill|Himekoso Shrine|ja|比売許曽神社}} in {{ill|Osaka Prefecture|ja|大阪府}}. * {{ill|Izumo Taisha|ja|出雲大社}}’s external shrine, known as ''Ōanamochi-no-Miko Tamae Shrine'' (大穴持御子玉江神社). == References == {{Reflist}} == Related Articles == * {{ill|List of Japanese deities|ja|日本の神の一覧}} {{Japanese mythology}} {{Shinto Horizontal}} {{shinto-stub}} [[Category:Japanese deities]] [[Category:Kunitsukami]] [[Category:Goddesses]] [[ja:下光比売命]] == Marriage == In many versions of the myth {{ill|Ame no Hohi|en}} did not send a word for three years after going down to earth, all the gods gathered up, and {{ill|Ame no Wakahiko|ja|10=en:draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ame-No-Wakahiko}} was one who was chosen to rule the earth. In many versions {{ill|Ame no Wakahiko|ja|10=en:draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ame-No-Wakahiko}} was given a bow.{{Cite web|title=Encyclopedia of Shinto - Home: Kami in Classic Texts: Ame no Wakahiko|url=http://eos.kokugakuin.ac.jp/modules/xwords/entry.php?entryID=46|access-date=2020-09-29|website=eos.kokugakuin.ac.jp}}{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=xdfgjV2kw6oC&q=Ame+no+Wakahiko&pg=PA6|title=Japanese Mythology A to Z|last=Roberts|first=Jeremy|date=2009|publisher=Infobase Publishing|isbn=978-1-4381-2802-3|language=en}} In some versions, however, Ame no Wakahiko is the son of Ame no Hohi and Ame no Wakahiko was sent to earth to look for him.{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=xdfgjV2kw6oC&dq=Ame+no+Wakahiko&pg=PA6|title=Japanese Mythology a to Z|publisher=Infobase|year=2009|isbn=9781438128023}} She married {{ill|Ame no Wakahiko|ja|10=en:draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ame-No-Wakahiko}}, when he came from heaven to discuss the "{{ill|Kuni-yuzuri|en}}". === Death === Eight years later, the gods had not yet heard a response so they sent a bird named Nakime down to earth to check in on him. Following the advice of a wise woman, Ame no Wakahiko used his bow to shoot the bird.{{Cite book|title=Handbook of Japanese mythology|last=Ashkenazi|first=Michael|date=2008|publisher=Oxford University Press|isbn=978-0-19-533262-9|series=Handbooks of world mythology|location=Oxford|pages=114}} The bird was killed but the arrow flew all the way to heaven. {{ill|Takamimusubi|en}} saw the arrow and threw it back at the earth where it hit Ame no Wakahiko while he was laying in bed, killing him.{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=uAj_PQ8o40sC&q=Takamimusubi|title=The East|date=1992|publisher=East Publications, Incorporated|language=en}} Other versions state that {{ill|Amaterasu|en}} was the one who shot the arrow back at him.{{cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=FlZxh5OaZxoC&pg=PA38|title=Impurity and Death: A Japanese Perspective|last=Abe|first=C.|publisher=Universal Publishers|year=2003|isbn=978-1-58112-195-7|page=38|access-date=2020-09-29}} This myth is the origin of a Japanese saying about the returning arrow. It is likely also be a mythicisation of attempts made by the {{ill|Yamato Kingship|en}} to impose its authority over neighbouring states. === Funeral === After Ame no Wakahiko's death, his parents built a hut (喪屋 moya) for their son. {{ill|Ajisukitakahikone|en}} went down to pay his respect. However, due to Ajisukitakahikone looking similar to Ame no Wakahiko he was mistaken to be Ame no Wakahiko brought back to life. Ajisukitakahikone was offended by this and destroyed the hut and kicked it. The hut landed in the land of Mino and became a mountain called Moyama.{{Cite book|title=Nihongi: Chronicles of Japan from the Earliest Times to A.D. 697, Volume 1|chapter=Book II|chapter-url=https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/Nihongi:_Chronicles_of_Japan_from_the_Earliest_Times_to_A.D._697/Book_II}} When {{ill|Ame no Wakahiko|ja|10=en:draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ame-No-Wakahiko}} passed away, Shitateruhime's sorrowful voice was heard in the Plain of High Heaven. During his funeral, Amewakahiko's father, Amatsukunitama, and other family members confused Shitateruhime's step-brother, [[Ajisukitakahikone]], for the deceased Amewakahiko. [[Ajisukitakahikone]] left in rage. In response, Shitateruhime sang a song of a type called hinaburi, or "rustic song" to honor her deceased husband.{{Cite web|title=Encyclopedia of Shinto詳細|url=https://d-museum.kokugakuin.ac.jp/eos/detail/?id=9155|access-date=2024-03-24|website=國學院大學デジタルミュージアム|language=ja}} == See Also == * {{ill|Munakata clan|ja|宗像氏|simple|User:Immanuelle/Munakata_clan|ja|宗像氏|fr|Clan Munakata}} ==References== {{reflist|draft}} == Further reading == * Jugon, Jean-Claude. "[https://www.france-japon.net/documents/La%20romance%20du%20sentiment%20et%20de%20la%20pensee.pdf?x36399 La romance du sentiment et de la pensée dans les légendes de Tanabata (Japon) et d’Éros-Psyché (Grèce), une interprétation transculturelle: «Oni» soit qui mal y pense!]". In: 論叢現代語・現代文化　2015 Vol.14　pp. 1-92. (in French) * Nüffer, Laura. “Humans and Non-Humans: Animal Bridegrooms and Brides in Japanese Otogizōshi.” In: ''A Cultural History of Fairy Tales in the Age of the Marvelous''. Edited by Suzanne Magnanini. London: Bloomsbury Academic Press, 2021. pp. 95-118. * ITO, Yuko. "[https://tsuru.repo.nii.ac.jp/?action=pages_view_main&active_action=repository_view_main_item_detail&item_id=201&item_no=1&page_id=4&block_id=34 Origins and development of the two versions of "Ame no Wakahiko Soshi": a comparative study]". In: 都留文科大学研究紀要 [The Tsuru University Review], Mar/2007, volume 65, pp. 258–241. https://ci.nii.ac.jp/naid/110007055993/en/; {{ISSN|0286-3774}}. DOI: info:doi/10.34356/00000195 (in Japanese) * Yasufuku, Junko. "[http://ir.lib.osaka-kyoiku.ac.jp/dspace/handle/123456789/6149 The Tale of Ame no Wakahiko and the Psychic Development of the Feminine]". In: ''Memoirs of Osaka Kyoiku University. IV, Education, pshychology, special education and physical culture'', Osaka Kyoiku University, Feb/1995, volume 43, no. 2, pp. 251–258. {{ISSN|0389-3472}}. Following the advice of a wise woman, Ame no Wakahiko used his bow to shoot the bird.{{Cite book|title=Handbook of Japanese mythology|last=Ashkenazi|first=Michael|date=2008|publisher=Oxford University Press|isbn=978-0-19-533262-9|series=Handbooks of world mythology|location=Oxford|pages=114}} The bird was killed but the arrow flew all the way to heaven. {{ill|Takamimusubi|en}} saw the arrow and threw it back at the earth where it hit Ame no Wakahiko while he was laying in bed, killing him.{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=uAj_PQ8o40sC&q=Takamimusubi|title=The East|date=1992|publisher=East Publications, Incorporated|language=en}} Other versions state that {{ill|Amaterasu|en}} was the one who shot the arrow back at him.{{cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=FlZxh5OaZxoC&pg=PA38|title=Impurity and Death: A Japanese Perspective|last=Abe|first=C.|publisher=Universal Publishers|year=2003|isbn=978-1-58112-195-7|page=38|access-date=2020-09-29}} This myth is the origin of a Japanese saying about the returning arrow. It is likely also be a mythicisation of attempts made by the {{ill|Yamato Kingship|en}} to impose its authority over neighbouring states. === Funeral === After Ame no Wakahiko's death, his parents built a hut (喪屋 moya) for their son. {{ill|Ajisukitakahikone|en}} went down to pay his respect. However, due to Ajisukitakahikone looking similar to Ame no Wakahiko he was mistaken to be Ame no Wakahiko brought back to life. Ajisukitakahikone was offended by this and destroyed the hut and kicked it. The hut landed in the land of Mino and became a mountain called Moyama.{{Cite book|title=Nihongi: Chronicles of Japan from the Earliest Times to A.D. 697, Volume 1|chapter=Book II|chapter-url=https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/Nihongi:_Chronicles_of_Japan_from_the_Earliest_Times_to_A.D._697/Book_II}} When {{ill|Ame no Wakahiko|ja|10=en:draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ame-No-Wakahiko}} passed away, Shitateruhime's sorrowful voice was heard in the Plain of High Heaven. During his funeral, Amewakahiko's father, Amatsukunitama, and other family members confused Shitateruhime's step-brother, [[Ajisukitakahikone]], for the deceased Amewakahiko. [[Ajisukitakahikone]] left in rage. In response, Shitateruhime sang a song of a type called hinaburi, or "rustic song" to honor her deceased husband.{{Cite web|title=Encyclopedia of Shinto詳細|url=https://d-museum.kokugakuin.ac.jp/eos/detail/?id=9155|access-date=2024-03-24|website=國學院大學デジタルミュージアム|language=ja}} == See Also == * {{ill|Munakata clan|ja|宗像氏|simple|User:Immanuelle/Munakata_clan|ja|宗像氏|fr|Clan Munakata}} ==References== {{reflist|draft}} == Further reading == * Jugon, Jean-Claude. She established her residence on the mountain behind this shrine, and after her death, she was buried in a ''[[kofun|kofun]]'' constructed in the shrine's precincts.{{cite book |last1=Yoshiki |first1=Emi |title=Zenkoku 'Ichinomiya' tettei gaido |date=2007 |publisher=PHP Institute |isbn=978-4569669304 |language=Japanese}} ==overview== [[Category:Pages with redlinks to fill]] [[Category:kkk]]{{DEFAULTSORT:Shitateruhime}}[[category:kk]] {{Infobox Japanese deity | Name = Shitateruhime (下光比売命) | Generation = | Predecessor = | Successor = | DeityType = {{ill|Kunitsukami|ja|国津神}} | FullName = Shitateruhime-no-Mikoto (下光比売命) | OtherNames = Shitateruhime, Shitateruhime-no-Mikoto, Takahime, Takahime-no-Mikoto, Waka-kunitama, and others | AlternateNames = | DivineRank = | DivineRole = {{ill|God of Thunder|ja|雷神}} | BurialPlace = | Father = {{ill|Ōkuninushi|ja|大国主神}} | Mother = {{ill|Takirihime-no-Mikoto|ja|多紀理毘売命}} | Relatives = * {{ill|Ajisukitakahikone|ja|阿遅鉏高日子根神}} * {{ill|Kotoshironushi|ja|事代主神}} * {{ill|Takeminakata|ja|建御名方神}} * {{ill|Kimata-no-Kami|ja|木俣神}} * {{ill|Torinonami-no-Kami|ja|鳥鳴海神}} | Spouse = {{ill|Ame-wakahiko|ja|天若日子}} | Children = | Shrine = {{Plainlist| * {{ill|Mefu Shrine|ja|売布神社}} * {{ill|Himekoso Shrine|ja|比売許曽神社}} }} | Texts = {{ill|Kojiki|ja|古事記}}, {{ill|Nihon Shoki|ja|日本書紀}} }} '''Shitateruhime''' (下光比売命) is a female deity in {{ill|Japanese mythology|ja|日本神話}} associated with {{ill|Shinto|ja|神道}}. She is also known by the names '''Takahime''' (高比売) and '''Waka-kunitama''' (稚国玉). == Overview == In the ''{{ill|Kojiki|ja|古事記}}'', she is referred to as '''Takahime-no-Mikoto''' (高比売命) and also as '''Shitateruhime-no-Mikoto''' (下光比売命). In the ''{{ill|Nihon Shoki|ja|日本書紀}}'', she appears as '''Shitateruhime''' (下照姫) or '''Shitateruhime-no-Mikoto''', and in the ''{{ill|Sendai Kuji Hongi|ja|先代旧事本紀}}'', she is called '''Shitateruhime-no-Mikoto'''. According to the ''Kojiki'' and the ''Nihon Shoki,'' she married {{ill|Ame-wakahiko|ja|天若日子}}, who had been dispatched from {{ill|Takamagahara|ja|高天原}} to subjugate the {{ill|Ashihara no Nakatsukuni|ja|葦原中国}} (the Central Land of Reed Plains). However, Ame-wakahiko secretly plotted to claim the land for himself. When Ame-wakahiko was killed by a divine arrow sent from Takamagahara, Shitateruhime’s grief-stricken cries reached the heavens. Her mourning led to the descent of Ame-wakahiko's family, including his father {{ill|Amatsukunitama-no-Mikoto|ja|天津国玉神}}, to perform his funeral rites. During this event, her brother {{ill|Ajisukitakahikone|ja|阿遅鉏高日子根神}} was mistaken for the deceased Ame-wakahiko due to their resemblance, leading to a conflict. Shitateruhime composed a lament known as the ''Hina-buri'' (夷振), expressing her sorrow. == Genealogy == [[File:Ohokuninushi family tree.png|thumb|250px|right|Genealogy of Ōkuninushi (''Kojiki''). Blue indicates male deities, red indicates female deities, and yellow indicates unspecified gender.]] According to the ''Kojiki,'' Shitateruhime is the daughter of {{ill|Ōkuninushi|ja|大国主神}} and {{ill|Takirihime-no-Mikoto|ja|多紀理毘売命}}, making her the sister of {{ill|Ajisukitakahikone|ja|阿遅鉏高日子根神}}. She established her residence on the mountain behind this shrine, and after her death, she was buried in a ''[[kofun|kofun]]'' constructed in the shrine's precincts.{{cite book |last1=Yoshiki |first1=Emi |title=Zenkoku 'Ichinomiya' tettei gaido |date=2007 |publisher=PHP Institute |isbn=978-4569669304 |language=Japanese}} ==overview== [[Category:Pages with redlinks to fill]] [[Category:original pages]] [[Category:kkk]]{{DEFAULTSORT:Shitateruhime}}[[category:kk]] {{Infobox Japanese deity | Name = Shitateruhime (下光比売命) | Generation = | Predecessor = | Successor = | DeityType = {{ill|Kunitsukami|ja|国津神}} | FullName = Shitateruhime-no-Mikoto (下光比売命) | OtherNames = Shitateruhime, Shitateruhime-no-Mikoto, Takahime, Takahime-no-Mikoto, Waka-kunitama, and others | AlternateNames = | DivineRank = | DivineRole = {{ill|God of Thunder|ja|雷神}} | BurialPlace = | Father = {{ill|Ōkuninushi|ja|大国主神}} | Mother = {{ill|Takirihime-no-Mikoto|ja|多紀理毘売命}} | Relatives = * {{ill|Ajisukitakahikone|ja|阿遅鉏高日子根神}} * {{ill|Kotoshironushi|ja|事代主神}} * {{ill|Takeminakata|ja|建御名方神}} * {{ill|Kimata-no-Kami|ja|木俣神}} * {{ill|Torinonami-no-Kami|ja|鳥鳴海神}} | Spouse = {{ill|Ame-wakahiko|ja|天若日子}} | Children = | Shrine = {{Plainlist| * {{ill|Mefu Shrine|ja|売布神社}} * {{ill|Himekoso Shrine|ja|比売許曽神社}} }} | Texts = {{ill|Kojiki|ja|古事記}}, {{ill|Nihon Shoki|ja|日本書紀}} }} '''Shitateruhime''' (下光比売命) is a female deity in {{ill|Japanese mythology|ja|日本神話}} associated with {{ill|Shinto|ja|神道}}. She is also known by the names '''Takahime''' (高比売) and '''Waka-kunitama''' (稚国玉). == Overview == In the ''{{ill|Kojiki|ja|古事記}}'', she is referred to as '''Takahime-no-Mikoto''' (高比売命) and also as '''Shitateruhime-no-Mikoto''' (下光比売命). In the ''{{ill|Nihon Shoki|ja|日本書紀}}'', she appears as '''Shitateruhime''' (下照姫) or '''Shitateruhime-no-Mikoto''', and in the ''{{ill|Sendai Kuji Hongi|ja|先代旧事本紀}}'', she is called '''Shitateruhime-no-Mikoto'''. According to the ''Kojiki'' and the ''Nihon Shoki,'' she married {{ill|Ame-wakahiko|ja|天若日子}}, who had been dispatched from {{ill|Takamagahara|ja|高天原}} to subjugate the {{ill|Ashihara no Nakatsukuni|ja|葦原中国}} (the Central Land of Reed Plains). However, Ame-wakahiko secretly plotted to claim the land for himself. When Ame-wakahiko was killed by a divine arrow sent from Takamagahara, Shitateruhime’s grief-stricken cries reached the heavens. Her mourning led to the descent of Ame-wakahiko's family, including his father {{ill|Amatsukunitama-no-Mikoto|ja|天津国玉神}}, to perform his funeral rites. During this event, her brother {{ill|Ajisukitakahikone|ja|阿遅鉏高日子根神}} was mistaken for the deceased Ame-wakahiko due to their resemblance, leading to a conflict. Shitateruhime composed a lament known as the ''Hina-buri'' (夷振), expressing her sorrow. == Genealogy == [[File:Ohokuninushi family tree.png|thumb|250px|right|Genealogy of Ōkuninushi (''Kojiki''). Blue indicates male deities, red indicates female deities, and yellow indicates unspecified gender.]] According to the ''Kojiki,'' Shitateruhime is the daughter of {{ill|Ōkuninushi|ja|大国主神}} and {{ill|Takirihime-no-Mikoto|ja|多紀理毘売命}}, making her the sister of {{ill|Ajisukitakahikone|ja|阿遅鉏高日子根神}}. This genealogy is also supported by the ''Sendai Kuji Hongi.'' == Shrines == Shitateruhime is enshrined at several locations, including: * {{ill|Hime Shrine (Toyama)|ja|比賣神社}} in {{ill|Toyama Prefecture|ja|富山県}}, where she is the main deity. * {{ill|Tamatsuoka Shrine|ja|玉津岡神社}} in {{ill|Kyoto Prefecture|ja|京都府}}, dedicated to her worship. * {{ill|Himekoso Shrine|ja|比売許曽神社}} in {{ill|Osaka Prefecture|ja|大阪府}}. * {{ill|Izumo Taisha|ja|出雲大社}}’s external shrine, known as ''Ōanamochi-no-Miko Tamae Shrine'' (大穴持御子玉江神社). == References == {{Reflist}} == Related Articles == * {{ill|List of Japanese deities|ja|日本の神の一覧}} {{Japanese mythology}} {{Shinto Horizontal}} {{shinto-stub}} [[Category:Japanese deities]] [[Category:Kunitsukami]] [[Category:Goddesses]] [[ja:下光比売命]] == Marriage == In many versions of the myth {{ill|Ame no Hohi|en}} did not send a word for three years after going down to earth, all the gods gathered up, and {{ill|Ame no Wakahiko|ja|10=en:draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ame-No-Wakahiko}} was one who was chosen to rule the earth. In many versions {{ill|Ame no Wakahiko|ja|10=en:draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ame-No-Wakahiko}} was given a bow.{{Cite web|title=Encyclopedia of Shinto - Home: Kami in Classic Texts: Ame no Wakahiko|url=http://eos.kokugakuin.ac.jp/modules/xwords/entry.php?entryID=46|access-date=2020-09-29|website=eos.kokugakuin.ac.jp}}{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=xdfgjV2kw6oC&q=Ame+no+Wakahiko&pg=PA6|title=Japanese Mythology A to Z|last=Roberts|first=Jeremy|date=2009|publisher=Infobase Publishing|isbn=978-1-4381-2802-3|language=en}} In some versions, however, Ame no Wakahiko is the son of Ame no Hohi and Ame no Wakahiko was sent to earth to look for him.{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=xdfgjV2kw6oC&dq=Ame+no+Wakahiko&pg=PA6|title=Japanese Mythology a to Z|publisher=Infobase|year=2009|isbn=9781438128023}} She married {{ill|Ame no Wakahiko|ja|10=en:draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ame-No-Wakahiko}}, when he came from heaven to discuss the "{{ill|Kuni-yuzuri|en}}". === Death === Eight years later, the gods had not yet heard a response so they sent a bird named Nakime down to earth to check in on him. Following the advice of a wise woman, Ame no Wakahiko used his bow to shoot the bird.{{Cite book|title=Handbook of Japanese mythology|last=Ashkenazi|first=Michael|date=2008|publisher=Oxford University Press|isbn=978-0-19-533262-9|series=Handbooks of world mythology|location=Oxford|pages=114}} The bird was killed but the arrow flew all the way to heaven. {{ill|Takamimusubi|en}} saw the arrow and threw it back at the earth where it hit Ame no Wakahiko while he was laying in bed, killing him.{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=uAj_PQ8o40sC&q=Takamimusubi|title=The East|date=1992|publisher=East Publications, Incorporated|language=en}} Other versions state that {{ill|Amaterasu|en}} was the one who shot the arrow back at him.{{cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=FlZxh5OaZxoC&pg=PA38|title=Impurity and Death: A Japanese Perspective|last=Abe|first=C.|publisher=Universal Publishers|year=2003|isbn=978-1-58112-195-7|page=38|access-date=2020-09-29}} This myth is the origin of a Japanese saying about the returning arrow. It is likely also be a mythicisation of attempts made by the {{ill|Yamato Kingship|en}} to impose its authority over neighbouring states. === Funeral === After Ame no Wakahiko's death, his parents built a hut (喪屋 moya) for their son. {{ill|Ajisukitakahikone|en}} went down to pay his respect. However, due to Ajisukitakahikone looking similar to Ame no Wakahiko he was mistaken to be Ame no Wakahiko brought back to life. Ajisukitakahikone was offended by this and destroyed the hut and kicked it. The hut landed in the land of Mino and became a mountain called Moyama.{{Cite book|title=Nihongi: Chronicles of Japan from the Earliest Times to A.D. 697, Volume 1|chapter=Book II|chapter-url=https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/Nihongi:_Chronicles_of_Japan_from_the_Earliest_Times_to_A.D._697/Book_II}} When {{ill|Ame no Wakahiko|ja|10=en:draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ame-No-Wakahiko}} passed away, Shitateruhime's sorrowful voice was heard in the Plain of High Heaven. During his funeral, Amewakahiko's father, Amatsukunitama, and other family members confused Shitateruhime's step-brother, [[Ajisukitakahikone]], for the deceased Amewakahiko. [[Ajisukitakahikone]] left in rage. In response, Shitateruhime sang a song of a type called hinaburi, or "rustic song" to honor her deceased husband.{{Cite web|title=Encyclopedia of Shinto詳細|url=https://d-museum.kokugakuin.ac.jp/eos/detail/?id=9155|access-date=2024-03-24|website=國學院大學デジタルミュージアム|language=ja}} == See Also == * {{ill|Munakata clan|ja|宗像氏|simple|User:Immanuelle/Munakata_clan|ja|宗像氏|fr|Clan Munakata}} ==References== {{reflist|draft}} == Further reading == * Jugon, Jean-Claude. {{draft}} {{Expand Japanese|シタテルヒメ}}{{Infobox deity | type = [[Shinto]] | father = [[Ōkuninushi]] | mother = {{ill|Tagorihime|ja|タキリビメ|simple|User:Immanuelle/Takiribime|en:draft}} |cult_centre={{ill|Shitori Shrine (Tottori)|lt=Shitori Shrine|en}},
{{ill|Kifune Shrine|simple|User:Immanuelle/Kifune Shrine|en}}|name=Shitateruhime|siblings=[[Ajisukitakahikone]]|spouse={{ill|Ame no Wakahiko|ja|10=en:draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ame-No-Wakahiko}}|image=File:Shitori-jinja, haiden.jpg|caption={{ill|Shitori Shrine (Tottori)|lt=Shitori Shrine|en}} where she is worshipped}}{{complex}} {{User:Immanuelle/Promising Draft}} {{ill|Shitateruhime|lt=Shitateruhime-no-Mikoto|ja|シタテルヒメ|simple|User:Immanuelle/Shitateruhime|en:draft|8=fr}} is a daughter of {{ill|Tagorihime|ja|タキリビメ|simple|User:Immanuelle/Takiribime|en:draft|8=fr}}, one of the three sisters worshipped at [[Munakata Taisha|Munakata Taisha]] The origins of {{ill|Shitori Shrine (Tottori)|lt=Shitori Shrine|ja|4=fr|5=Shitori-jinja|6=ja|7=倭文神社_(湯梨浜町)|8=simple|9=User:Immanuelle/Shitori Shrine (Tottori)}} are unknown. Although there is no documentary evidence, it is believed that it began as the family shrine for the {{Nihongo|Shitori clan|倭文氏}} of [[Kofun period|Kofun period]] craftsmen who weavers, who regarded {{ill|Takehazuchi|lt=Takehazuchi-no-Mikoto|ja|天羽槌雄神|simple|User:Immanuelle/Takehazuchi|en:draft|8=fr}} as their ancestor. However, the shrine's legends are all centered around {{ill|Shitateruhime|lt=Shitateruhime-no-Mikoto|ja|シタテルヒメ|simple|User:Immanuelle/Shitateruhime|en:draft|8=fr}}, whom the shrine legend claims arrived in this location from [[Izumo Taisha|Izumo]] by boat. She established her residence on the mountain behind this shrine, and after her death, she was buried in a ''[[kofun|kofun]]'' constructed in the shrine's precincts.{{cite book |last1=Yoshiki |first1=Emi |title=Zenkoku 'Ichinomiya' tettei gaido |date=2007 |publisher=PHP Institute |isbn=978-4569669304 |language=Japanese}} ==overview== [[Category:Pages with redlinks to fill]] [[Category:original pages]] [[Category:kkk]]{{DEFAULTSORT:Shitateruhime}}[[category:kk]] {{Infobox Japanese deity | Name = Shitateruhime (下光比売命) | Generation = | Predecessor = | Successor = | DeityType = {{ill|Kunitsukami|ja|国津神}} | FullName = Shitateruhime-no-Mikoto (下光比売命) | OtherNames = Shitateruhime, Shitateruhime-no-Mikoto, Takahime, Takahime-no-Mikoto, Waka-kunitama, and others | AlternateNames = | DivineRank = | DivineRole = {{ill|God of Thunder|ja|雷神}} | BurialPlace = | Father = {{ill|Ōkuninushi|ja|大国主神}} | Mother = {{ill|Takirihime-no-Mikoto|ja|多紀理毘売命}} | Relatives = * {{ill|Ajisukitakahikone|ja|阿遅鉏高日子根神}} * {{ill|Kotoshironushi|ja|事代主神}} * {{ill|Takeminakata|ja|建御名方神}} * {{ill|Kimata-no-Kami|ja|木俣神}} * {{ill|Torinonami-no-Kami|ja|鳥鳴海神}} | Spouse = {{ill|Ame-wakahiko|ja|天若日子}} | Children = | Shrine = {{Plainlist| * {{ill|Mefu Shrine|ja|売布神社}} * {{ill|Himekoso Shrine|ja|比売許曽神社}} }} | Texts = {{ill|Kojiki|ja|古事記}}, {{ill|Nihon Shoki|ja|日本書紀}} }} '''Shitateruhime''' (下光比売命) is a female deity in {{ill|Japanese mythology|ja|日本神話}} associated with {{ill|Shinto|ja|神道}}. She is also known by the names '''Takahime''' (高比売) and '''Waka-kunitama''' (稚国玉). == Overview == In the ''{{ill|Kojiki|ja|古事記}}'', she is referred to as '''Takahime-no-Mikoto''' (高比売命) and also as '''Shitateruhime-no-Mikoto''' (下光比売命). In the ''{{ill|Nihon Shoki|ja|日本書紀}}'', she appears as '''Shitateruhime''' (下照姫) or '''Shitateruhime-no-Mikoto''', and in the ''{{ill|Sendai Kuji Hongi|ja|先代旧事本紀}}'', she is called '''Shitateruhime-no-Mikoto'''. According to the ''Kojiki'' and the ''Nihon Shoki,'' she married {{ill|Ame-wakahiko|ja|天若日子}}, who had been dispatched from {{ill|Takamagahara|ja|高天原}} to subjugate the {{ill|Ashihara no Nakatsukuni|ja|葦原中国}} (the Central Land of Reed Plains). However, Ame-wakahiko secretly plotted to claim the land for himself. When Ame-wakahiko was killed by a divine arrow sent from Takamagahara, Shitateruhime’s grief-stricken cries reached the heavens. Her mourning led to the descent of Ame-wakahiko's family, including his father {{ill|Amatsukunitama-no-Mikoto|ja|天津国玉神}}, to perform his funeral rites. During this event, her brother {{ill|Ajisukitakahikone|ja|阿遅鉏高日子根神}} was mistaken for the deceased Ame-wakahiko due to their resemblance, leading to a conflict. Shitateruhime composed a lament known as the ''Hina-buri'' (夷振), expressing her sorrow. == Genealogy == [[File:Ohokuninushi family tree.png|thumb|250px|right|Genealogy of Ōkuninushi (''Kojiki''). Blue indicates male deities, red indicates female deities, and yellow indicates unspecified gender.]] According to the ''Kojiki,'' Shitateruhime is the daughter of {{ill|Ōkuninushi|ja|大国主神}} and {{ill|Takirihime-no-Mikoto|ja|多紀理毘売命}}, making her the sister of {{ill|Ajisukitakahikone|ja|阿遅鉏高日子根神}}. This genealogy is also supported by the ''Sendai Kuji Hongi.'' == Shrines == Shitateruhime is enshrined at several locations, including: * {{ill|Hime Shrine (Toyama)|ja|比賣神社}} in {{ill|Toyama Prefecture|ja|富山県}}, where she is the main deity. * {{ill|Tamatsuoka Shrine|ja|玉津岡神社}} in {{ill|Kyoto Prefecture|ja|京都府}}, dedicated to her worship. * {{ill|Himekoso Shrine|ja|比売許曽神社}} in {{ill|Osaka Prefecture|ja|大阪府}}. * {{ill|Izumo Taisha|ja|出雲大社}}’s external shrine, known as ''Ōanamochi-no-Miko Tamae Shrine'' (大穴持御子玉江神社). == References == {{Reflist}} == Related Articles == * {{ill|List of Japanese deities|ja|日本の神の一覧}} {{Japanese mythology}} {{Shinto Horizontal}} {{shinto-stub}} [[Category:Japanese deities]] [[Category:Kunitsukami]] [[Category:Goddesses]] [[ja:下光比売命]] == Marriage == In many versions of the myth {{ill|Ame no Hohi|en}} did not send a word for three years after going down to earth, all the gods gathered up, and {{ill|Ame no Wakahiko|ja|10=en:draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ame-No-Wakahiko}} was one who was chosen to rule the earth. In many versions {{ill|Ame no Wakahiko|ja|10=en:draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ame-No-Wakahiko}} was given a bow.{{Cite web|title=Encyclopedia of Shinto - Home: Kami in Classic Texts: Ame no Wakahiko|url=http://eos.kokugakuin.ac.jp/modules/xwords/entry.php?entryID=46|access-date=2020-09-29|website=eos.kokugakuin.ac.jp}}{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=xdfgjV2kw6oC&q=Ame+no+Wakahiko&pg=PA6|title=Japanese Mythology A to Z|last=Roberts|first=Jeremy|date=2009|publisher=Infobase Publishing|isbn=978-1-4381-2802-3|language=en}} In some versions, however, Ame no Wakahiko is the son of Ame no Hohi and Ame no Wakahiko was sent to earth to look for him.{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=xdfgjV2kw6oC&dq=Ame+no+Wakahiko&pg=PA6|title=Japanese Mythology a to Z|publisher=Infobase|year=2009|isbn=9781438128023}} She married {{ill|Ame no Wakahiko|ja|10=en:draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ame-No-Wakahiko}}, when he came from heaven to discuss the "{{ill|Kuni-yuzuri|en}}". === Death === Eight years later, the gods had not yet heard a response so they sent a bird named Nakime down to earth to check in on him. Following the advice of a wise woman, Ame no Wakahiko used his bow to shoot the bird.{{Cite book|title=Handbook of Japanese mythology|last=Ashkenazi|first=Michael|date=2008|publisher=Oxford University Press|isbn=978-0-19-533262-9|series=Handbooks of world mythology|location=Oxford|pages=114}} The bird was killed but the arrow flew all the way to heaven. {{ill|Takamimusubi|en}} saw the arrow and threw it back at the earth where it hit Ame no Wakahiko while he was laying in bed, killing him.{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=uAj_PQ8o40sC&q=Takamimusubi|title=The East|date=1992|publisher=East Publications, Incorporated|language=en}} Other versions state that {{ill|Amaterasu|en}} was the one who shot the arrow back at him.{{cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=FlZxh5OaZxoC&pg=PA38|title=Impurity and Death: A Japanese Perspective|last=Abe|first=C.|publisher=Universal Publishers|year=2003|isbn=978-1-58112-195-7|page=38|access-date=2020-09-29}} This myth is the origin of a Japanese saying about the returning arrow. It is likely also be a mythicisation of attempts made by the {{ill|Yamato Kingship|en}} to impose its authority over neighbouring states. === Funeral === After Ame no Wakahiko's death, his parents built a hut (喪屋 moya) for their son. {{ill|Ajisukitakahikone|en}} went down to pay his respect. However, due to Ajisukitakahikone looking similar to Ame no Wakahiko he was mistaken to be Ame no Wakahiko brought back to life. Ajisukitakahikone was offended by this and destroyed the hut and kicked it. The hut landed in the land of Mino and became a mountain called Moyama.{{Cite book|title=Nihongi: Chronicles of Japan from the Earliest Times to A.D. 697, Volume 1|chapter=Book II|chapter-url=https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/Nihongi:_Chronicles_of_Japan_from_the_Earliest_Times_to_A.D._697/Book_II}} When {{ill|Ame no Wakahiko|ja|10=en:draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ame-No-Wakahiko}} passed away, Shitateruhime's sorrowful voice was heard in the Plain of High Heaven. During his funeral, Amewakahiko's father, Amatsukunitama, and other family members confused Shitateruhime's step-brother, [[Ajisukitakahikone]], for the deceased Amewakahiko. [[Ajisukitakahikone]] left in rage. In response, Shitateruhime sang a song of a type called hinaburi, or "rustic song" to honor her deceased husband.{{Cite web|title=Encyclopedia of Shinto詳細|url=https://d-museum.kokugakuin.ac.jp/eos/detail/?id=9155|access-date=2024-03-24|website=國學院大學デジタルミュージアム|language=ja}} == See Also == * {{ill|Munakata clan|ja|宗像氏|simple|User:Immanuelle/Munakata_clan|ja|宗像氏|fr|Clan Munakata}} ==References== {{reflist|draft}} == Further reading == * Jugon, Jean-Claude. "[https://www.france-japon.net/documents/La%20romance%20du%20sentiment%20et%20de%20la%20pensee.pdf?x36399 La romance du sentiment et de la pensée dans les légendes de Tanabata (Japon) et d’Éros-Psyché (Grèce), une interprétation transculturelle: «Oni» soit qui mal y pense!]". In: 論叢現代語・現代文化　2015 Vol.14　pp. 1-92. (in French) * Nüffer, Laura. “Humans and Non-Humans: Animal Bridegrooms and Brides in Japanese Otogizōshi.” In: ''A Cultural History of Fairy Tales in the Age of the Marvelous''. Edited by Suzanne Magnanini. London: Bloomsbury Academic Press, 2021. pp. 95-118. * ITO, Yuko. "[https://tsuru.repo.nii.ac.jp/?action=pages_view_main&active_action=repository_view_main_item_detail&item_id=201&item_no=1&page_id=4&block_id=34 Origins and development of the two versions of "Ame no Wakahiko Soshi": a comparative study]". In: 都留文科大学研究紀要 [The Tsuru University Review], Mar/2007, volume 65, pp. 258–241. https://ci.nii.ac.jp/naid/110007055993/en/; {{ISSN|0286-3774}}. DOI: info:doi/10.34356/00000195 (in Japanese) * Yasufuku, Junko. "[http://ir.lib.osaka-kyoiku.ac.jp/dspace/handle/123456789/6149 The Tale of Ame no Wakahiko and the Psychic Development of the Feminine]". In: ''Memoirs of Osaka Kyoiku University. IV, Education, pshychology, special education and physical culture'', Osaka Kyoiku University, Feb/1995, volume 43, no. 2, pp. 251–258. {{ISSN|0389-3472}}. URL: https://ci.nii.ac.jp/naid/110000119291/en/ (in Japanese) {{draft categories| [[Category:Japanese goddesses]] [[Category:Munakata Taisha]] [[Category:Shinto kami]] [[Category:Japanese deities]] [[Category:Munakata Shrines]] [[Category:Kunitsukami]] [[simple:User:Immanuelle/{{PAGENAME}} [[Category:Goddesses]] [[Category:Completed articles]] [[Category:Pages from Simple English Wikipedia]] [[simple:user:immanuelle/Shitateruhime]][[Category:Pages from Simple English Wikipedia]] [[Category:kk]][[category:kk]] [[Category:attempting to force efresh]] [[simple:user:immanuelle/Shitateruhime]][[fr:User:Immanuelle/Shitateruhime]] |draft}} [[ja:下照比売]] [[en:Shitateruhime]] [[simple:User:{{PAGENAME}} [[fr:User:{{PAGENAME}}

Following the advice of a wise woman, Ame no Wakahiko used his bow to shoot the bird.{{Cite book|title=Handbook of Japanese mythology|last=Ashkenazi|first=Michael|date=2008|publisher=Oxford University Press|isbn=978-0-19-533262-9|series=Handbooks of world mythology|location=Oxford|pages=114}} The bird was killed but the arrow flew all the way to heaven. {{ill|Takamimusubi|en}} saw the arrow and threw it back at the earth where it hit Ame no Wakahiko while he was laying in bed, killing him.{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=uAj_PQ8o40sC&q=Takamimusubi|title=The East|date=1992|publisher=East Publications, Incorporated|language=en}} Other versions state that {{ill|Amaterasu|en}} was the one who shot the arrow back at him.{{cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=FlZxh5OaZxoC&pg=PA38|title=Impurity and Death: A Japanese Perspective|last=Abe|first=C.|publisher=Universal Publishers|year=2003|isbn=978-1-58112-195-7|page=38|access-date=2020-09-29}} This myth is the origin of a Japanese saying about the returning arrow. It is likely also be a mythicisation of attempts made by the {{ill|Yamato Kingship|en}} to impose its authority over neighbouring states. === Funeral === After Ame no Wakahiko's death, his parents built a hut (喪屋 moya) for their son. {{ill|Ajisukitakahikone|en}} went down to pay his respect. However, due to Ajisukitakahikone looking similar to Ame no Wakahiko he was mistaken to be Ame no Wakahiko brought back to life. Ajisukitakahikone was offended by this and destroyed the hut and kicked it. The hut landed in the land of Mino and became a mountain called Moyama.{{Cite book|title=Nihongi: Chronicles of Japan from the Earliest Times to A.D. 697, Volume 1|chapter=Book II|chapter-url=https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/Nihongi:_Chronicles_of_Japan_from_the_Earliest_Times_to_A.D._697/Book_II}} When {{ill|Ame no Wakahiko|ja|10=en:draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ame-No-Wakahiko}} passed away, Shitateruhime's sorrowful voice was heard in the Plain of High Heaven. During his funeral, Amewakahiko's father, Amatsukunitama, and other family members confused Shitateruhime's step-brother, [[Ajisukitakahikone]], for the deceased Amewakahiko. [[Ajisukitakahikone]] left in rage. In response, Shitateruhime sang a song of a type called hinaburi, or "rustic song" to honor her deceased husband.{{Cite web|title=Encyclopedia of Shinto詳細|url=https://d-museum.kokugakuin.ac.jp/eos/detail/?id=9155|access-date=2024-03-24|website=國學院大學デジタルミュージアム|language=ja}} == See Also == * {{ill|Munakata clan|ja|宗像氏|simple|User:Immanuelle/Munakata_clan|ja|宗像氏|fr|Clan Munakata}} ==References== {{reflist|draft}} == Further reading == * Jugon, Jean-Claude. She established her residence on the mountain behind this shrine, and after her death, she was buried in a ''[[kofun|kofun]]'' constructed in the shrine's precincts.{{cite book |last1=Yoshiki |first1=Emi |title=Zenkoku 'Ichinomiya' tettei gaido |date=2007 |publisher=PHP Institute |isbn=978-4569669304 |language=Japanese}} ==overview== [[Category:Pages with redlinks to fill]][[Category:original pages]] [[Category:original pages]] [[Category:kkk]]{{DEFAULTSORT:Shitateruhime}}[[category:kk]] {{Infobox Japanese deity | Name = Shitateruhime (下光比売命) | Generation = | Predecessor = | Successor = | DeityType = {{ill|Kunitsukami|ja|国津神}} | FullName = Shitateruhime-no-Mikoto (下光比売命) | OtherNames = Shitateruhime, Shitateruhime-no-Mikoto, Takahime, Takahime-no-Mikoto, Waka-kunitama, and others | AlternateNames = | DivineRank = | DivineRole = {{ill|God of Thunder|ja|雷神}} | BurialPlace = | Father = {{ill|Ōkuninushi|ja|大国主神}} | Mother = {{ill|Takirihime-no-Mikoto|ja|多紀理毘売命}} | Relatives = * {{ill|Ajisukitakahikone|ja|阿遅鉏高日子根神}} * {{ill|Kotoshironushi|ja|事代主神}} * {{ill|Takeminakata|ja|建御名方神}} * {{ill|Kimata-no-Kami|ja|木俣神}} * {{ill|Torinonami-no-Kami|ja|鳥鳴海神}} | Spouse = {{ill|Ame-wakahiko|ja|天若日子}} | Children = | Shrine = {{Plainlist| * {{ill|Mefu Shrine|ja|売布神社}} * {{ill|Himekoso Shrine|ja|比売許曽神社}} }} | Texts = {{ill|Kojiki|ja|古事記}}, {{ill|Nihon Shoki|ja|日本書紀}} }} '''Shitateruhime''' (下光比売命) is a female deity in {{ill|Japanese mythology|ja|日本神話}} associated with {{ill|Shinto|ja|神道}}. She is also known by the names '''Takahime''' (高比売) and '''Waka-kunitama''' (稚国玉). == Overview == In the ''{{ill|Kojiki|ja|古事記}}'', she is referred to as '''Takahime-no-Mikoto''' (高比売命) and also as '''Shitateruhime-no-Mikoto''' (下光比売命). In the ''{{ill|Nihon Shoki|ja|日本書紀}}'', she appears as '''Shitateruhime''' (下照姫) or '''Shitateruhime-no-Mikoto''', and in the ''{{ill|Sendai Kuji Hongi|ja|先代旧事本紀}}'', she is called '''Shitateruhime-no-Mikoto'''. According to the ''Kojiki'' and the ''Nihon Shoki,'' she married {{ill|Ame-No-Wakahiko|ja|天若日子}}, who had been dispatched from {{ill|Takamagahara|ja|高天原}} to subjugate the {{ill|Ashihara no Nakatsukuni|ja|葦原中国}} (the Central Land of Reed Plains). However, Ame-wakahiko secretly plotted to claim the land for himself. When Ame-wakahiko was killed by a divine arrow sent from Takamagahara, Shitateruhime’s grief-stricken cries reached the heavens. Her mourning led to the descent of Ame-wakahiko's family, including his father {{ill|Amatsukunitama-no-Mikoto|ja|天津国玉神}}, to perform his funeral rites. During this event, her brother {{ill|Ajisukitakahikone|ja|阿遅鉏高日子根神}} was mistaken for the deceased Ame-wakahiko due to their resemblance, leading to a conflict. Shitateruhime composed a lament known as the ''Hina-buri'' (夷振), expressing her sorrow. == Genealogy == [[File:Ohokuninushi family tree.png|thumb|250px|right|Genealogy of Ōkuninushi (''Kojiki''). Blue indicates male deities, red indicates female deities, and yellow indicates unspecified gender.]] According to the ''Kojiki,'' Shitateruhime is the daughter of {{ill|Ōkuninushi|ja|大国主神}} and {{ill|Takirihime-no-Mikoto|ja|多紀理毘売命}}, making her the sister of {{ill|Ajisukitakahikone|ja|阿遅鉏高日子根神}}. She established her residence on the mountain behind this shrine, and after her death, she was buried in a ''[[kofun|kofun]]'' constructed in the shrine's precincts.{{cite book |last1=Yoshiki |first1=Emi |title=Zenkoku 'Ichinomiya' tettei gaido |date=2007 |publisher=PHP Institute |isbn=978-4569669304 |language=Japanese}} ==overview== [[Category:original pages]] [[Category:original pages]] [[Category:kkk]]{{DEFAULTSORT:Shitateruhime}}[[category:kk]] {{Infobox Japanese deity | Name = Shitateruhime (下光比売命) | Generation = | Predecessor = | Successor = | DeityType = {{ill|Kunitsukami|ja|国津神}} | FullName = Shitateruhime-no-Mikoto (下光比売命) | OtherNames = Shitateruhime, Shitateruhime-no-Mikoto, Takahime, Takahime-no-Mikoto, Waka-kunitama, and others | AlternateNames = | DivineRank = | DivineRole = {{ill|God of Thunder|ja|雷神}} | BurialPlace = | Father = {{ill|Ōkuninushi|ja|大国主神}} | Mother = {{ill|Takirihime-no-Mikoto|ja|多紀理毘売命}} | Relatives = * {{ill|Ajisukitakahikone|ja|阿遅鉏高日子根神}} * {{ill|Kotoshironushi|ja|事代主神}} * {{ill|Takeminakata|ja|建御名方神}} * {{ill|Kimata-no-Kami|ja|木俣神}} * {{ill|Torinonami-no-Kami|ja|鳥鳴海神}} | Spouse = {{ill|Ame-wakahiko|ja|天若日子}} | Children = | Shrine = {{Plainlist| * {{ill|Mefu Shrine|ja|売布神社}} * {{ill|Himekoso Shrine|ja|比売許曽神社}} }} | Texts = {{ill|Kojiki|ja|古事記}}, {{ill|Nihon Shoki|ja|日本書紀}} }} '''Shitateruhime''' (下光比売命) is a female deity in {{ill|Japanese mythology|ja|日本神話}} associated with {{ill|Shinto|ja|神道}}. She is also known by the names '''Takahime''' (高比売) and '''Waka-kunitama''' (稚国玉). == Overview == In the ''{{ill|Kojiki|ja|古事記}}'', she is referred to as '''Takahime-no-Mikoto''' (高比売命) and also as '''Shitateruhime-no-Mikoto''' (下光比売命). In the ''{{ill|Nihon Shoki|ja|日本書紀}}'', she appears as '''Shitateruhime''' (下照姫) or '''Shitateruhime-no-Mikoto''', and in the ''{{ill|Sendai Kuji Hongi|ja|先代旧事本紀}}'', she is called '''Shitateruhime-no-Mikoto'''. According to the ''Kojiki'' and the ''Nihon Shoki,'' she married {{ill|Ame-No-Wakahiko|ja|天若日子}}, who had been dispatched from {{ill|Takamagahara|ja|高天原}} to subjugate the {{ill|Ashihara no Nakatsukuni|ja|葦原中国}} (the Central Land of Reed Plains). However, Ame-wakahiko secretly plotted to claim the land for himself. When Ame-wakahiko was killed by a divine arrow sent from Takamagahara, Shitateruhime’s grief-stricken cries reached the heavens. Her mourning led to the descent of Ame-wakahiko's family, including his father {{ill|Amatsukunitama-no-Mikoto|ja|天津国玉神}}, to perform his funeral rites. During this event, her brother {{ill|Ajisukitakahikone|ja|阿遅鉏高日子根神}} was mistaken for the deceased Ame-wakahiko due to their resemblance, leading to a conflict. Shitateruhime composed a lament known as the ''Hina-buri'' (夷振), expressing her sorrow. == Genealogy == [[File:Ohokuninushi family tree.png|thumb|250px|right|Genealogy of Ōkuninushi (''Kojiki''). Blue indicates male deities, red indicates female deities, and yellow indicates unspecified gender.]] According to the ''Kojiki,'' Shitateruhime is the daughter of {{ill|Ōkuninushi|ja|大国主神}} and {{ill|Takirihime-no-Mikoto|ja|多紀理毘売命}}, making her the sister of {{ill|Ajisukitakahikone|ja|阿遅鉏高日子根神}}. This genealogy is also supported by the ''Sendai Kuji Hongi.'' == Shrines == Shitateruhime is enshrined at several locations, including: * {{ill|Hime Shrine (Toyama)|ja|比賣神社}} in {{ill|Toyama Prefecture|ja|富山県}}, where she is the main deity. * {{ill|Tamatsuoka Shrine|ja|玉津岡神社}} in {{ill|Kyoto Prefecture|ja|京都府}}, dedicated to her worship. * {{ill|Himekoso Shrine|ja|比売許曽神社}} in {{ill|Osaka Prefecture|ja|大阪府}}. * {{ill|Izumo Taisha|ja|出雲大社}}’s external shrine, known as ''Ōanamochi-no-Miko Tamae Shrine'' (大穴持御子玉江神社). == References == {{Reflist}} == Related Articles == * {{ill|List of Japanese deities|ja|日本の神の一覧}} {{Japanese mythology}} {{Shinto Horizontal}} {{shinto-stub}} [[Category:Japanese deities]] [[Category:Kunitsukami]] [[Category:Goddesses]] [[ja:下光比売命]] == Marriage == In many versions of the myth {{ill|Ame no Hohi|en}} did not send a word for three years after going down to earth, all the gods gathered up, and {{ill|Ame no Wakahiko|ja|10=en:draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ame-No-Wakahiko}} was one who was chosen to rule the earth. In many versions {{ill|Ame no Wakahiko|ja|10=en:draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ame-No-Wakahiko}} was given a bow.{{Cite web|title=Encyclopedia of Shinto - Home: Kami in Classic Texts: Ame no Wakahiko|url=http://eos.kokugakuin.ac.jp/modules/xwords/entry.php?entryID=46|access-date=2020-09-29|website=eos.kokugakuin.ac.jp}}{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=xdfgjV2kw6oC&q=Ame+no+Wakahiko&pg=PA6|title=Japanese Mythology A to Z|last=Roberts|first=Jeremy|date=2009|publisher=Infobase Publishing|isbn=978-1-4381-2802-3|language=en}} In some versions, however, Ame no Wakahiko is the son of Ame no Hohi and Ame no Wakahiko was sent to earth to look for him.{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=xdfgjV2kw6oC&dq=Ame+no+Wakahiko&pg=PA6|title=Japanese Mythology a to Z|publisher=Infobase|year=2009|isbn=9781438128023}} She married {{ill|Ame no Wakahiko|ja|10=en:draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ame-No-Wakahiko}}, when he came from heaven to discuss the "{{ill|Kuni-yuzuri|en}}". === Death === Eight years later, the gods had not yet heard a response so they sent a bird named Nakime down to earth to check in on him. Following the advice of a wise woman, Ame no Wakahiko used his bow to shoot the bird.{{Cite book|title=Handbook of Japanese mythology|last=Ashkenazi|first=Michael|date=2008|publisher=Oxford University Press|isbn=978-0-19-533262-9|series=Handbooks of world mythology|location=Oxford|pages=114}} The bird was killed but the arrow flew all the way to heaven. {{ill|Takamimusubi|en}} saw the arrow and threw it back at the earth where it hit Ame no Wakahiko while he was laying in bed, killing him.{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=uAj_PQ8o40sC&q=Takamimusubi|title=The East|date=1992|publisher=East Publications, Incorporated|language=en}} Other versions state that {{ill|Amaterasu|en}} was the one who shot the arrow back at him.{{cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=FlZxh5OaZxoC&pg=PA38|title=Impurity and Death: A Japanese Perspective|last=Abe|first=C.|publisher=Universal Publishers|year=2003|isbn=978-1-58112-195-7|page=38|access-date=2020-09-29}} This myth is the origin of a Japanese saying about the returning arrow. It is likely also be a mythicisation of attempts made by the {{ill|Yamato Kingship|en}} to impose its authority over neighbouring states. === Funeral === After Ame no Wakahiko's death, his parents built a hut (喪屋 moya) for their son. {{ill|Ajisukitakahikone|en}} went down to pay his respect. However, due to Ajisukitakahikone looking similar to Ame no Wakahiko he was mistaken to be Ame no Wakahiko brought back to life. Ajisukitakahikone was offended by this and destroyed the hut and kicked it. The hut landed in the land of Mino and became a mountain called Moyama.{{Cite book|title=Nihongi: Chronicles of Japan from the Earliest Times to A.D. 697, Volume 1|chapter=Book II|chapter-url=https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/Nihongi:_Chronicles_of_Japan_from_the_Earliest_Times_to_A.D._697/Book_II}} When {{ill|Ame no Wakahiko|ja|10=en:draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ame-No-Wakahiko}} passed away, Shitateruhime's sorrowful voice was heard in the Plain of High Heaven. During his funeral, Amewakahiko's father, Amatsukunitama, and other family members confused Shitateruhime's step-brother, [[Ajisukitakahikone]], for the deceased Amewakahiko. [[Ajisukitakahikone]] left in rage. In response, Shitateruhime sang a song of a type called hinaburi, or "rustic song" to honor her deceased husband.{{Cite web|title=Encyclopedia of Shinto詳細|url=https://d-museum.kokugakuin.ac.jp/eos/detail/?id=9155|access-date=2024-03-24|website=國學院大學デジタルミュージアム|language=ja}} == See Also == * {{ill|Munakata clan|ja|宗像氏|simple|User:Immanuelle/Munakata_clan|ja|宗像氏|fr|Clan Munakata}} ==References== {{reflist|draft}} == Further reading == * Jugon, Jean-Claude. {{draft}} {{Expand Japanese|シタテルヒメ}}{{Infobox deity | type = [[Shinto]] | father = [[Ōkuninushi]] | mother = {{ill|Tagorihime|ja|タキリビメ|simple|User:Immanuelle/Takiribime|en:draft}} |cult_centre={{ill|Shitori Shrine (Tottori)|lt=Shitori Shrine|en}},
{{ill|Kifune Shrine|simple|User:Immanuelle/Kifune Shrine|en}}|name=Shitateruhime|siblings=[[Ajisukitakahikone]]|spouse={{ill|Ame no Wakahiko|ja|10=en:draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ame-No-Wakahiko}}|image=File:Shitori-jinja, haiden.jpg|caption={{ill|Shitori Shrine (Tottori)|lt=Shitori Shrine|en}} where she is worshipped}}{{complex}} {{User:Immanuelle/Promising Draft}} {{ill|Shitateruhime|lt=Shitateruhime-no-Mikoto|ja|シタテルヒメ|simple|User:Immanuelle/Shitateruhime|en:draft|8=fr}} is a daughter of {{ill|Tagorihime|ja|タキリビメ|simple|User:Immanuelle/Takiribime|en:draft|8=fr}}, one of the three sisters worshipped at [[Munakata Taisha|Munakata Taisha]] The origins of {{ill|Shitori Shrine (Tottori)|lt=Shitori Shrine|ja|4=fr|5=Shitori-jinja|6=ja|7=倭文神社_(湯梨浜町)|8=simple|9=User:Immanuelle/Shitori Shrine (Tottori)}} are unknown. Although there is no documentary evidence, it is believed that it began as the family shrine for the {{Nihongo|Shitori clan|倭文氏}} of [[Kofun period|Kofun period]] craftsmen who weavers, who regarded {{ill|Takehazuchi|lt=Takehazuchi-no-Mikoto|ja|天羽槌雄神|simple|User:Immanuelle/Takehazuchi|en:draft|8=fr}} as their ancestor. However, the shrine's legends are all centered around {{ill|Shitateruhime|lt=Shitateruhime-no-Mikoto|ja|シタテルヒメ|simple|User:Immanuelle/Shitateruhime|en:draft|8=fr}}, whom the shrine legend claims arrived in this location from [[Izumo Taisha|Izumo]] by boat. She established her residence on the mountain behind this shrine, and after her death, she was buried in a ''[[kofun|kofun]]'' constructed in the shrine's precincts.{{cite book |last1=Yoshiki |first1=Emi |title=Zenkoku 'Ichinomiya' tettei gaido |date=2007 |publisher=PHP Institute |isbn=978-4569669304 |language=Japanese}} ==overview== {{DEFAULTSORT:Shitateruhime}}[[category:kk]] {{Infobox Japanese deity | Name = Shitateruhime (下光比売命) | Generation = | Predecessor = | Successor = | DeityType = {{ill|Kunitsukami|ja|国津神}} | FullName = Shitateruhime-no-Mikoto (下光比売命) | OtherNames = Shitateruhime, Shitateruhime-no-Mikoto, Takahime, Takahime-no-Mikoto, Waka-kunitama, and others | AlternateNames = | DivineRank = | DivineRole = {{ill|God of Thunder|ja|雷神}} | BurialPlace = | Father = {{ill|Ōkuninushi|ja|大国主神}} | Mother = {{ill|Takirihime-no-Mikoto|ja|多紀理毘売命}} | Relatives = * {{ill|Ajisukitakahikone|ja|阿遅鉏高日子根神}} * {{ill|Kotoshironushi|ja|事代主神}} * {{ill|Takeminakata|ja|建御名方神}} * {{ill|Kimata-no-Kami|ja|木俣神}} * {{ill|Torinonami-no-Kami|ja|鳥鳴海神}} | Spouse = {{ill|Ame-wakahiko|ja|天若日子}} | Children = | Shrine = {{Plainlist| * {{ill|Mefu Shrine|ja|売布神社}} * {{ill|Himekoso Shrine|ja|比売許曽神社}} }} | Texts = {{ill|Kojiki|ja|古事記}}, {{ill|Nihon Shoki|ja|日本書紀}} }} '''Shitateruhime''' (下光比売命) is a female deity in {{ill|Japanese mythology|ja|日本神話}} associated with {{ill|Shinto|ja|神道}}. She is also known by the names '''Takahime''' (高比売) and '''Waka-kunitama''' (稚国玉). == Overview == In the ''{{ill|Kojiki|ja|古事記}}'', she is referred to as '''Takahime-no-Mikoto''' (高比売命) and also as '''Shitateruhime-no-Mikoto''' (下光比売命). In the ''{{ill|Nihon Shoki|ja|日本書紀}}'', she appears as '''Shitateruhime''' (下照姫) or '''Shitateruhime-no-Mikoto''', and in the ''{{ill|Sendai Kuji Hongi|ja|先代旧事本紀}}'', she is called '''Shitateruhime-no-Mikoto'''. According to the ''Kojiki'' and the ''Nihon Shoki,'' she married {{ill|Ame-No-Wakahiko|ja|天若日子}}, who had been dispatched from {{ill|Takamagahara|ja|高天原}} to subjugate the {{ill|Ashihara no Nakatsukuni|ja|葦原中国}} (the Central Land of Reed Plains). However, Ame-wakahiko secretly plotted to claim the land for himself. When Ame-wakahiko was killed by a divine arrow sent from Takamagahara, Shitateruhime’s grief-stricken cries reached the heavens. Her mourning led to the descent of Ame-wakahiko's family, including his father {{ill|Amatsukunitama-no-Mikoto|ja|天津国玉神}}, to perform his funeral rites. During this event, her brother {{ill|Ajisukitakahikone|ja|阿遅鉏高日子根神}} was mistaken for the deceased Ame-wakahiko due to their resemblance, leading to a conflict. Shitateruhime composed a lament known as the ''Hina-buri'' (夷振), expressing her sorrow. == Genealogy == [[File:Ohokuninushi family tree.png|thumb|250px|right|Genealogy of Ōkuninushi (''Kojiki''). Blue indicates male deities, red indicates female deities, and yellow indicates unspecified gender.]] According to the ''Kojiki,'' Shitateruhime is the daughter of {{ill|Ōkuninushi|ja|大国主神}} and {{ill|Takirihime-no-Mikoto|ja|多紀理毘売命}}, making her the sister of {{ill|Ajisukitakahikone|ja|阿遅鉏高日子根神}}. This genealogy is also supported by the ''Sendai Kuji Hongi.'' == Shrines == Shitateruhime is enshrined at several locations, including: * {{ill|Hime Shrine (Toyama)|ja|比賣神社}} in {{ill|Toyama Prefecture|ja|富山県}}, where she is the main deity. * {{ill|Tamatsuoka Shrine|ja|玉津岡神社}} in {{ill|Kyoto Prefecture|ja|京都府}}, dedicated to her worship. * {{ill|Himekoso Shrine|ja|比売許曽神社}} in {{ill|Osaka Prefecture|ja|大阪府}}. * {{ill|Izumo Taisha|ja|出雲大社}}’s external shrine, known as ''Ōanamochi-no-Miko Tamae Shrine'' (大穴持御子玉江神社). == References == {{Reflist}} == Related Articles == * {{ill|List of Japanese deities|ja|日本の神の一覧}} [[Category:Japanese deities]] [[Category:Kunitsukami]] [[Category:Goddesses]] [[ja:下光比売命]] == Marriage == In many versions of the myth {{ill|Ame no Hohi|en}} did not send a word for three years after going down to earth, all the gods gathered up, and {{ill|Ame no Wakahiko|ja|10=en:draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ame-No-Wakahiko}} was one who was chosen to rule the earth. In many versions {{ill|Ame no Wakahiko|ja|10=en:draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ame-No-Wakahiko}} was given a bow.{{Cite web|title=Encyclopedia of Shinto - Home: Kami in Classic Texts: Ame no Wakahiko|url=http://eos.kokugakuin.ac.jp/modules/xwords/entry.php?entryID=46|access-date=2020-09-29|website=eos.kokugakuin.ac.jp}}{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=xdfgjV2kw6oC&q=Ame+no+Wakahiko&pg=PA6|title=Japanese Mythology A to Z|last=Roberts|first=Jeremy|date=2009|publisher=Infobase Publishing|isbn=978-1-4381-2802-3|language=en}} In some versions, however, Ame no Wakahiko is the son of Ame no Hohi and Ame no Wakahiko was sent to earth to look for him.{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=xdfgjV2kw6oC&dq=Ame+no+Wakahiko&pg=PA6|title=Japanese Mythology a to Z|publisher=Infobase|year=2009|isbn=9781438128023}} She married {{ill|Ame no Wakahiko|ja|10=en:draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ame-No-Wakahiko}}, when he came from heaven to discuss the "{{ill|Kuni-yuzuri|en}}". === Death === Eight years later, the gods had not yet heard a response so they sent a bird named Nakime down to earth to check in on him. Following the advice of a wise woman, Ame no Wakahiko used his bow to shoot the bird.{{Cite book|title=Handbook of Japanese mythology|last=Ashkenazi|first=Michael|date=2008|publisher=Oxford University Press|isbn=978-0-19-533262-9|series=Handbooks of world mythology|location=Oxford|pages=114}} The bird was killed but the arrow flew all the way to heaven. {{ill|Takamimusubi|en}} saw the arrow and threw it back at the earth where it hit Ame no Wakahiko while he was laying in bed, killing him.{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=uAj_PQ8o40sC&q=Takamimusubi|title=The East|date=1992|publisher=East Publications, Incorporated|language=en}} Other versions state that {{ill|Amaterasu|en}} was the one who shot the arrow back at him.{{cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=FlZxh5OaZxoC&pg=PA38|title=Impurity and Death: A Japanese Perspective|last=Abe|first=C.|publisher=Universal Publishers|year=2003|isbn=978-1-58112-195-7|page=38|access-date=2020-09-29}} This myth is the origin of a Japanese saying about the returning arrow. It is likely also be a mythicisation of attempts made by the {{ill|Yamato Kingship|en}} to impose its authority over neighbouring states. === Funeral === After Ame no Wakahiko's death, his parents built a hut (喪屋 moya) for their son. {{ill|Ajisukitakahikone|en}} went down to pay his respect. However, due to Ajisukitakahikone looking similar to Ame no Wakahiko he was mistaken to be Ame no Wakahiko brought back to life. Ajisukitakahikone was offended by this and destroyed the hut and kicked it. The hut landed in the land of Mino and became a mountain called Moyama.{{Cite book|title=Nihongi: Chronicles of Japan from the Earliest Times to A.D. 697, Volume 1|chapter=Book II|chapter-url=https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/Nihongi:_Chronicles_of_Japan_from_the_Earliest_Times_to_A.D._697/Book_II}} When {{ill|Ame no Wakahiko|ja|10=en:draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ame-No-Wakahiko}} passed away, Shitateruhime's sorrowful voice was heard in the Plain of High Heaven. During his funeral, Amewakahiko's father, Amatsukunitama, and other family members confused Shitateruhime's step-brother, [[Ajisukitakahikone]], for the deceased Amewakahiko. [[Ajisukitakahikone]] left in rage. In response, Shitateruhime sang a song of a type called hinaburi, or "rustic song" to honor her deceased husband.{{Cite web|title=Encyclopedia of Shinto詳細|url=https://d-museum.kokugakuin.ac.jp/eos/detail/?id=9155|access-date=2024-03-24|website=國學院大學デジタルミュージアム|language=ja}} == See Also == * {{ill|Munakata clan|ja|宗像氏|simple|User:Immanuelle/Munakata_clan|ja|宗像氏|fr|Clan Munakata}} ==References== {{reflist|draft}} == Further reading == * Jugon, Jean-Claude. In: 論叢現代語・現代文化　2015 Vol.14　pp. 1-92. (in French) * Nüffer, Laura. “Humans and Non-Humans: Animal Bridegrooms and Brides in Japanese Otogizōshi.” In: ''A Cultural History of Fairy Tales in the Age of the Marvelous''. Edited by Suzanne Magnanini. London: Bloomsbury Academic Press, 2021. pp. 95-118. * ITO, Yuko. It is likely also be a mythicisation of attempts made by the {{ill|Yamato Kingship|en}} to impose its authority over neighbouring states. === Funeral === After Ame no Wakahiko's death, his parents built a hut (喪屋 moya) for their son. {{ill|Ajisukitakahikone|en}} went down to pay his respect. However, due to Ajisukitakahikone looking similar to Ame no Wakahiko he was mistaken to be Ame no Wakahiko brought back to life. Ajisukitakahikone was offended by this and destroyed the hut and kicked it. The hut landed in the land of Mino and became a mountain called Moyama.{{Cite book|title=Nihongi: Chronicles of Japan from the Earliest Times to A.D. 697, Volume 1|chapter=Book II|chapter-url=https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/Nihongi:_Chronicles_of_Japan_from_the_Earliest_Times_to_A.D._697/Book_II}} When {{ill|Ame no Wakahiko|ja|10=en:draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ame-No-Wakahiko}} passed away, Shitateruhime's sorrowful voice was heard in the Plain of High Heaven. During his funeral, Amewakahiko's father, Amatsukunitama, and other family members confused Shitateruhime's step-brother, [[Ajisukitakahikone]], for the deceased Amewakahiko. [[Ajisukitakahikone]] left in rage. In response, Shitateruhime sang a song of a type called hinaburi, or "rustic song" to honor her deceased husband.{{Cite web|title=Encyclopedia of Shinto詳細|url=https://d-museum.kokugakuin.ac.jp/eos/detail/?id=9155|access-date=2024-03-24|website=國學院大學デジタルミュージアム|language=ja}} == See Also == * {{ill|Munakata clan|ja|宗像氏|simple|User:Immanuelle/Munakata_clan|ja|宗像氏|fr|Clan Munakata}} ==References== {{reflist|draft}} == Further reading == * Jugon, Jean-Claude. {{ill|Kifune Shrine|simple|User:Immanuelle/Kifune Shrine|en}}|name=Shitateruhime|siblings=[[Ajisukitakahikone]]|spouse={{ill|Ame no Wakahiko|ja|10=en:draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ame-No-Wakahiko}}|image=File:Shitori-jinja, haiden.jpg|caption={{ill|Shitori Shrine (Tottori)|lt=Shitori Shrine|en}} where she is worshipped}}{{complex}} {{User:Immanuelle/Promising Draft}} {{ill|Shitateruhime|lt=Shitateruhime-no-Mikoto|ja|シタテルヒメ|simple|User:Immanuelle/Shitateruhime|en:draft|8=fr}} is a daughter of {{ill|Tagorihime|ja|タキリビメ|simple|User:Immanuelle/Takiribime|en:draft|8=fr}}, one of the three sisters worshipped at [[Munakata Taisha|Munakata Taisha]] The origins of {{ill|Shitori Shrine (Tottori)|lt=Shitori Shrine|ja|4=fr|5=Shitori-jinja|6=ja|7=倭文神社_(湯梨浜町)|8=simple|9=User:Immanuelle/Shitori Shrine (Tottori)}} are unknown. Although there is no documentary evidence, it is believed that it began as the family shrine for the {{Nihongo|Shitori clan|倭文氏}} of [[Kofun period|Kofun period]] craftsmen who weavers, who regarded {{ill|Takehazuchi|lt=Takehazuchi-no-Mikoto|ja|天羽槌雄神|simple|User:Immanuelle/Takehazuchi|en:draft|8=fr}} as their ancestor. However, the shrine's legends are all centered around {{ill|Shitateruhime|lt=Shitateruhime-no-Mikoto|ja|シタテルヒメ|simple|User:Immanuelle/Shitateruhime|en:draft|8=fr}}, whom the shrine legend claims arrived in this location from [[Izumo Taisha|Izumo]] by boat. She established her residence on the mountain behind this shrine, and after her death, she was buried in a ''[[kofun|kofun]]'' constructed in the shrine's precincts.{{cite book |last1=Yoshiki |first1=Emi |title=Zenkoku 'Ichinomiya' tettei gaido |date=2007 |publisher=PHP Institute |isbn=978-4569669304 |language=Japanese}} ==overview== {{DEFAULTSORT:Shitateruhime}}[[category:kk]] {{Infobox Japanese deity | Name = Shitateruhime (下光比売命) | Generation = | Predecessor = | Successor = | DeityType = {{ill|Kunitsukami|ja|国津神}} | FullName = Shitateruhime-no-Mikoto (下光比売命) | OtherNames = Shitateruhime, Shitateruhime-no-Mikoto, Takahime, Takahime-no-Mikoto, Waka-kunitama, and others | AlternateNames = | DivineRank = | DivineRole = {{ill|God of Thunder|ja|雷神}} | BurialPlace = | Father = {{ill|Ōkuninushi|ja|大国主神}} | Mother = {{ill|Takirihime-no-Mikoto|ja|多紀理毘売命}} | Relatives = * {{ill|Ajisukitakahikone|ja|阿遅鉏高日子根神}} * {{ill|Kotoshironushi|ja|事代主神}} * {{ill|Takeminakata|ja|建御名方神}} * {{ill|Kimata-no-Kami|ja|木俣神}} * {{ill|Torinonami-no-Kami|ja|鳥鳴海神}} | Spouse = {{ill|Ame-wakahiko|ja|天若日子}} | Children = | Shrine = {{Plainlist| * {{ill|Mefu Shrine|ja|売布神社}} * {{ill|Himekoso Shrine|ja|比売許曽神社}} }} | Texts = {{ill|Kojiki|ja|古事記}}, {{ill|Nihon Shoki|ja|日本書紀}} }} '''Shitateruhime''' (下光比売命) is a female deity in {{ill|Japanese mythology|ja|日本神話}} associated with {{ill|Shinto|ja|神道}}. She is also known by the names '''Takahime''' (高比売) and '''Waka-kunitama''' (稚国玉). == Overview == In the ''{{ill|Kojiki|ja|古事記}}'', she is referred to as '''Takahime-no-Mikoto''' (高比売命) and also as '''Shitateruhime-no-Mikoto''' (下光比売命). In the ''{{ill|Nihon Shoki|ja|日本書紀}}'', she appears as '''Shitateruhime''' (下照姫) or '''Shitateruhime-no-Mikoto''', and in the ''{{ill|Sendai Kuji Hongi|ja|先代旧事本紀}}'', she is called '''Shitateruhime-no-Mikoto'''. According to the ''Kojiki'' and the ''Nihon Shoki,'' she married {{ill|Ame-No-Wakahiko|ja|天若日子}}, who had been dispatched from {{ill|Takamagahara|ja|高天原}} to subjugate the {{ill|Ashihara no Nakatsukuni|ja|葦原中国}} (the Central Land of Reed Plains). However, Ame-wakahiko secretly plotted to claim the land for himself. When Ame-wakahiko was killed by a divine arrow sent from Takamagahara, Shitateruhime’s grief-stricken cries reached the heavens. Her mourning led to the descent of Ame-wakahiko's family, including his father {{ill|Amatsukunitama-no-Mikoto|ja|天津国玉神}}, to perform his funeral rites. During this event, her brother {{ill|Ajisukitakahikone|ja|阿遅鉏高日子根神}} was mistaken for the deceased Ame-wakahiko due to their resemblance, leading to a conflict. Shitateruhime composed a lament known as the ''Hina-buri'' (夷振), expressing her sorrow. == Genealogy == [[File:Ohokuninushi family tree.png|thumb|250px|right|Genealogy of Ōkuninushi (''Kojiki''). Blue indicates male deities, red indicates female deities, and yellow indicates unspecified gender.]] According to the ''Kojiki,'' Shitateruhime is the daughter of {{ill|Ōkuninushi|ja|大国主神}} and {{ill|Takirihime-no-Mikoto|ja|多紀理毘売命}}, making her the sister of {{ill|Ajisukitakahikone|ja|阿遅鉏高日子根神}}. This genealogy is also supported by the ''Sendai Kuji Hongi.'' == Shrines == Shitateruhime is enshrined at several locations, including: * {{ill|Hime Shrine (Toyama)|ja|比賣神社}} in {{ill|Toyama Prefecture|ja|富山県}}, where she is the main deity. * {{ill|Tamatsuoka Shrine|ja|玉津岡神社}} in {{ill|Kyoto Prefecture|ja|京都府}}, dedicated to her worship. * {{ill|Himekoso Shrine|ja|比売許曽神社}} in {{ill|Osaka Prefecture|ja|大阪府}}. * {{ill|Izumo Taisha|ja|出雲大社}}’s external shrine, known as ''Ōanamochi-no-Miko Tamae Shrine'' (大穴持御子玉江神社). == References == {{Reflist}} == Related Articles == * {{ill|List of Japanese deities|ja|日本の神の一覧}} [[Category:Japanese deities]] [[Category:Kunitsukami]] [[Category:Goddesses]] [[ja:下光比売命]] == Marriage == In many versions of the myth {{ill|Ame no Hohi|en}} did not send a word for three years after going down to earth, all the gods gathered up, and {{ill|Ame no Wakahiko|ja|10=en:draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ame-No-Wakahiko}} was one who was chosen to rule the earth. In many versions {{ill|Ame no Wakahiko|ja|10=en:draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ame-No-Wakahiko}} was given a bow.{{Cite web|title=Encyclopedia of Shinto - Home: Kami in Classic Texts: Ame no Wakahiko|url=http://eos.kokugakuin.ac.jp/modules/xwords/entry.php?entryID=46|access-date=2020-09-29|website=eos.kokugakuin.ac.jp}}{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=xdfgjV2kw6oC&q=Ame+no+Wakahiko&pg=PA6|title=Japanese Mythology A to Z|last=Roberts|first=Jeremy|date=2009|publisher=Infobase Publishing|isbn=978-1-4381-2802-3|language=en}} In some versions, however, Ame no Wakahiko is the son of Ame no Hohi and Ame no Wakahiko was sent to earth to look for him.{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=xdfgjV2kw6oC&dq=Ame+no+Wakahiko&pg=PA6|title=Japanese Mythology a to Z|publisher=Infobase|year=2009|isbn=9781438128023}} She married {{ill|Ame no Wakahiko|ja|10=en:draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ame-No-Wakahiko}}, when he came from heaven to discuss the "{{ill|Kuni-yuzuri|en}}". === Death === Eight years later, the gods had not yet heard a response so they sent a bird named Nakime down to earth to check in on him. Following the advice of a wise woman, Ame no Wakahiko used his bow to shoot the bird.{{Cite book|title=Handbook of Japanese mythology|last=Ashkenazi|first=Michael|date=2008|publisher=Oxford University Press|isbn=978-0-19-533262-9|series=Handbooks of world mythology|location=Oxford|pages=114}} The bird was killed but the arrow flew all the way to heaven. {{ill|Takamimusubi|en}} saw the arrow and threw it back at the earth where it hit Ame no Wakahiko while he was laying in bed, killing him.{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=uAj_PQ8o40sC&q=Takamimusubi|title=The East|date=1992|publisher=East Publications, Incorporated|language=en}} Other versions state that {{ill|Amaterasu|en}} was the one who shot the arrow back at him.{{cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=FlZxh5OaZxoC&pg=PA38|title=Impurity and Death: A Japanese Perspective|last=Abe|first=C.|publisher=Universal Publishers|year=2003|isbn=978-1-58112-195-7|page=38|access-date=2020-09-29}} This myth is the origin of a Japanese saying about the returning arrow. It is likely also be a mythicisation of attempts made by the {{ill|Yamato Kingship|en}} to impose its authority over neighbouring states. === Funeral === After Ame no Wakahiko's death, his parents built a hut (喪屋 moya) for their son. {{ill|Ajisukitakahikone|en}} went down to pay his respect. However, due to Ajisukitakahikone looking similar to Ame no Wakahiko he was mistaken to be Ame no Wakahiko brought back to life. Ajisukitakahikone was offended by this and destroyed the hut and kicked it. The hut landed in the land of Mino and became a mountain called Moyama.{{Cite book|title=Nihongi: Chronicles of Japan from the Earliest Times to A.D. 697, Volume 1|chapter=Book II|chapter-url=https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/Nihongi:_Chronicles_of_Japan_from_the_Earliest_Times_to_A.D._697/Book_II}} When {{ill|Ame no Wakahiko|ja|10=en:draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ame-No-Wakahiko}} passed away, Shitateruhime's sorrowful voice was heard in the Plain of High Heaven. During his funeral, Amewakahiko's father, Amatsukunitama, and other family members confused Shitateruhime's step-brother, [[Ajisukitakahikone]], for the deceased Amewakahiko. [[Ajisukitakahikone]] left in rage. In response, Shitateruhime sang a song of a type called hinaburi, or "rustic song" to honor her deceased husband.{{Cite web|title=Encyclopedia of Shinto詳細|url=https://d-museum.kokugakuin.ac.jp/eos/detail/?id=9155|access-date=2024-03-24|website=國學院大學デジタルミュージアム|language=ja}} == See Also == * {{ill|Munakata clan|ja|宗像氏|simple|User:Immanuelle/Munakata_clan|ja|宗像氏|fr|Clan Munakata}} ==References== {{reflist|draft}} == Further reading == * Jugon, Jean-Claude.
