{{ill|Kifune Shrine|simple|User:Immanuelle/Kifune Shrine|en}}|name=Shitateruhime|siblings=[[Ajisukitakahikone]]|spouse={{ill|Ame no Wakahiko|ja|10=en:draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ame-No-Wakahiko}}|image=File:Shitori-jinja, haiden.jpg|caption={{ill|Shitori Shrine (Tottori)|lt=Shitori Shrine|en}} where she is worshipped |image=File:Shitateruhime shinbutsu-zue.jpg |caption=A book depiction of her }}{{complex}} {{DEFAULTSORT:Shitateruhime}} [[category:kk]] {{ill|Shitateruhime|lt=Shitateruhime-no-Mikoto|ja|シタテルヒメ|simple|User:Immanuelle/Shitateruhime|en:draft|8=fr}} is a daughter of {{ill|Tagorihime|ja|タキリビメ|simple|User:Immanuelle/Takiribime|en:draft|8=fr}}, one of the three sisters worshipped at [[Munakata Taisha|Munakata Taisha]] The origins of {{ill|Shitori Shrine (Tottori)|lt=Shitori Shrine|ja|4=fr|5=Shitori-jinja|6=ja|7=倭文神社_(湯梨浜町)|8=simple|9=User:Immanuelle/Shitori Shrine (Tottori)}} are unknown. Although there is no documentary evidence, it is believed that it began as the family shrine for the {{Nihongo|Shitori clan|倭文氏}} of [[Kofun period|Kofun period]] craftsmen who weavers, who regarded {{ill|Takehazuchi|lt=Takehazuchi-no-Mikoto|ja|天羽槌雄神|simple|User:Immanuelle/Takehazuchi|en:draft|8=fr}} as their ancestor. However, the shrine's legends are all centered around {{ill|Shitateruhime|lt=Shitateruhime-no-Mikoto|ja|シタテルヒメ|simple|User:Immanuelle/Shitateruhime|en:draft|8=fr}}, whom the shrine legend claims arrived in this location from [[Izumo Taisha|Izumo]] by boat. She established her residence on the mountain behind this shrine, and after her death, she was buried in a ''[[kofun|kofun]]'' constructed in the shrine's precincts.{{cite book |last1=Yoshiki |first1=Emi |title=Zenkoku 'Ichinomiya' tettei gaido |date=2007 |publisher=PHP Institute |isbn=978-4569669304 |language=Japanese}} == Overview == In the ''{{ill|Kojiki|ja|古事記}}'', she is referred to as '''Takahime-no-Mikoto''' (高比売命) and also as '''Shitateruhime-no-Mikoto''' (下光比売命). In the ''{{ill|Nihon Shoki|ja|日本書紀}}'', she appears as '''Shitateruhime''' (下照姫) or '''Shitateruhime-no-Mikoto''', and in the ''{{ill|Sendai Kuji Hongi|ja|先代旧事本紀}}'', she is called '''Shitateruhime-no-Mikoto'''. According to the ''Kojiki'' and the ''Nihon Shoki,'' she married {{ill|Ame-No-Wakahiko|ja|天若日子}}, who had been dispatched from {{ill|Takamagahara|ja|高天原}} to subjugate the {{ill|Ashihara no Nakatsukuni|ja|葦原中国}} (the Central Land of Reed Plains). However, Ame-wakahiko secretly plotted to claim the land for himself. When Ame-wakahiko was killed by a divine arrow sent from Takamagahara, Shitateruhime’s grief-stricken cries reached the heavens. Her mourning led to the descent of Ame-wakahiko's family, including his father {{ill|Amatsukunitama-no-Mikoto|ja|天津国玉神}}, to perform his funeral rites. During this event, her brother {{ill|Ajisukitakahikone|ja|阿遅鉏高日子根神}} was mistaken for the deceased Ame-wakahiko due to their resemblance, leading to a conflict. Shitateruhime composed a lament known as the ''Hina-buri'' (夷振), expressing her sorrow. [[Category:Japanese deities]] [[Category:Kunitsukami]] [[Category:Goddesses]] [[ja:下光比売命]] == Marriage == In many versions of the myth {{ill|Ame no Hohi|en}} did not send a word for three years after going down to earth, all the gods gathered up, and {{ill|Ame no Wakahiko|ja|10=en:draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ame-No-Wakahiko}} was one who was chosen to rule the earth. In many versions {{ill|Ame no Wakahiko|ja|10=en:draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ame-No-Wakahiko}} was given a bow.{{Cite web|title=Encyclopedia of Shinto - Home: Kami in Classic Texts: Ame no Wakahiko|url=http://eos.kokugakuin.ac.jp/modules/xwords/entry.php?entryID=46|access-date=2020-09-29|website=eos.kokugakuin.ac.jp}}{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=xdfgjV2kw6oC&q=Ame+no+Wakahiko&pg=PA6|title=Japanese Mythology A to Z|last=Roberts|first=Jeremy|date=2009|publisher=Infobase Publishing|isbn=978-1-4381-2802-3|language=en}} In some versions, however, Ame no Wakahiko is the son of Ame no Hohi and Ame no Wakahiko was sent to earth to look for him.{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=xdfgjV2kw6oC&dq=Ame+no+Wakahiko&pg=PA6|title=Japanese Mythology a to Z|publisher=Infobase|year=2009|isbn=9781438128023}} She married {{ill|Ame no Wakahiko|ja|10=en:draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ame-No-Wakahiko}}, when he came from heaven to discuss the "{{ill|Kuni-yuzuri|en}}". === Death === Eight years later, the gods had not yet heard a response so they sent a bird named Nakime down to earth to check in on him. Following the advice of a wise woman, Ame no Wakahiko used his bow to shoot the bird.{{Cite book|title=Handbook of Japanese mythology|last=Ashkenazi|first=Michael|date=2008|publisher=Oxford University Press|isbn=978-0-19-533262-9|series=Handbooks of world mythology|location=Oxford|pages=114}} The bird was killed but the arrow flew all the way to heaven. {{ill|Takamimusubi|en}} saw the arrow and threw it back at the earth where it hit Ame no Wakahiko while he was laying in bed, killing him.{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=uAj_PQ8o40sC&q=Takamimusubi|title=The East|date=1992|publisher=East Publications, Incorporated|language=en}} Other versions state that {{ill|Amaterasu|en}} was the one who shot the arrow back at him.{{cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=FlZxh5OaZxoC&pg=PA38|title=Impurity and Death: A Japanese Perspective|last=Abe|first=C.|publisher=Universal Publishers|year=2003|isbn=978-1-58112-195-7|page=38|access-date=2020-09-29}} This myth is the origin of a Japanese saying about the returning arrow. It is likely also be a mythicisation of attempts made by the {{ill|Yamato Kingship|en}} to impose its authority over neighbouring states. === Funeral === After Ame no Wakahiko's death, his parents built a hut (喪屋 moya) for their son. {{ill|Ajisukitakahikone|en}} went down to pay his respect. However, due to Ajisukitakahikone looking similar to Ame no Wakahiko he was mistaken to be Ame no Wakahiko brought back to life. Ajisukitakahikone was offended by this and destroyed the hut and kicked it. The hut landed in the land of Mino and became a mountain called Moyama.{{Cite book|title=Nihongi: Chronicles of Japan from the Earliest Times to A.D. 697, Volume 1|chapter=Book II|chapter-url=https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/Nihongi:_Chronicles_of_Japan_from_the_Earliest_Times_to_A.D._697/Book_II}} When {{ill|Ame no Wakahiko|ja|10=en:draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ame-No-Wakahiko}} passed away, Shitateruhime's sorrowful voice was heard in the Plain of High Heaven. During his funeral, Amewakahiko's father, Amatsukunitama, and other family members confused Shitateruhime's step-brother, [[Ajisukitakahikone]], for the deceased Amewakahiko. [[Ajisukitakahikone]] left in rage. In response, Shitateruhime sang a song of a type called hinaburi, or "rustic song" to honor her deceased husband.{{Cite web|title=Encyclopedia of Shinto詳細|url=https://d-museum.kokugakuin.ac.jp/eos/detail/?id=9155|access-date=2024-03-24|website=國學院大學デジタルミュージアム|language=ja}} == Genealogy == [[File:Ohokuninushi family tree.png|thumb|250px|right|Genealogy of Ōkuninushi (''Kojiki''). Blue indicates male deities, red indicates female deities, and yellow indicates unspecified gender.]] According to the ''Kojiki,'' Shitateruhime is the daughter of {{ill|Ōkuninushi|ja|大国主神}} and {{ill|Takirihime-no-Mikoto|ja|多紀理毘売命}}, making her the sister of {{ill|Ajisukitakahikone|ja|阿遅鉏高日子根神}}. This genealogy is also supported by the ''Sendai Kuji Hongi.'' == Shrines == Shitateruhime is enshrined at several locations, including: * {{ill|Hime Shrine (Toyama)|ja|比賣神社}} in {{ill|Toyama Prefecture|ja|富山県}}, where she is the main deity. * {{ill|Tamatsuoka Shrine|ja|玉津岡神社}} in {{ill|Kyoto Prefecture|ja|京都府}}, dedicated to her worship. * {{ill|Himekoso Shrine|ja|比売許曽神社}} in {{ill|Osaka Prefecture|ja|大阪府}}. * {{ill|Izumo Taisha|ja|出雲大社}}’s external shrine, known as ''Ōanamochi-no-Miko Tamae Shrine'' (大穴持御子玉江神社). == Related Articles == * {{ill|List of Japanese deities|ja|日本の神の一覧}} * {{ill|Munakata clan|ja|宗像氏|simple|User:Immanuelle/Munakata_clan|ja|宗像氏|fr|Clan Munakata}} ==References== {{reflist|draft}} == Further reading == * Jugon, Jean-Claude. [[User:Immanuelle|Immanuelle]] ([[User talk:Immanuelle|talk]]) 09:35, 18 February 2025 (UTC)}} {{Expand Japanese|シタテルヒメ}} {{Infobox deity | type = [[Shinto]] | father = [[Ōkuninushi]] | mother = {{ill|Tagorihime|ja|タキリビメ|simple|User:Immanuelle/Takiribime|en:draft}} |cult_centre={{ill|Shitori Shrine (Tottori)|lt=Shitori Shrine|en}},
{{ill|Kifune Shrine|simple|User:Immanuelle/Kifune Shrine|en}}|name=Shitateruhime|siblings=[[Ajisukitakahikone]]|spouse={{ill|Ame no Wakahiko|ja|10=en:draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ame-No-Wakahiko}}|image=File:Shitori-jinja, haiden.jpg|caption={{ill|Shitori Shrine (Tottori)|lt=Shitori Shrine|en}} where she is worshipped |image=File:Shitateruhime shinbutsu-zue.jpg |caption=A book depiction of her }} {{complex}} {{DEFAULTSORT:Shitateruhime}} [[category:kk]] {{ill|Shitateruhime|lt=Shitateruhime-no-Mikoto|ja|シタテルヒメ|simple|User:Immanuelle/Shitateruhime|en:draft|8=fr}} is a daughter of {{ill|Tagorihime|ja|タキリビメ|simple|User:Immanuelle/Takiribime|en:draft|8=fr}}, one of the three sisters worshipped at [[Munakata Taisha|Munakata Taisha]] The origins of {{ill|Shitori Shrine (Tottori)|lt=Shitori Shrine|ja|4=fr|5=Shitori-jinja|6=ja|7=倭文神社_(湯梨浜町)|8=simple|9=User:Immanuelle/Shitori Shrine (Tottori)}} are unknown. Although there is no documentary evidence, it is believed that it began as the family shrine for the {{Nihongo|Shitori clan|倭文氏}} of [[Kofun period|Kofun period]] craftsmen who weavers, who regarded {{ill|Takehazuchi|lt=Takehazuchi-no-Mikoto|ja|天羽槌雄神|simple|User:Immanuelle/Takehazuchi|en:draft|8=fr}} as their ancestor. However, the shrine's legends are all centered around {{ill|Shitateruhime|lt=Shitateruhime-no-Mikoto|ja|シタテルヒメ|simple|User:Immanuelle/Shitateruhime|en:draft|8=fr}}, whom the shrine legend claims arrived in this location from [[Izumo Taisha|Izumo]] by boat. She established her residence on the mountain behind this shrine, and after her death, she was buried in a ''[[kofun|kofun]]'' constructed in the shrine's precincts.{{cite book |last1=Yoshiki |first1=Emi |title=Zenkoku 'Ichinomiya' tettei gaido |date=2007 |publisher=PHP Institute |isbn=978-4569669304 |language=Japanese}} == Overview == In the ''{{ill|Kojiki|ja|古事記}}'', she is referred to as '''Takahime-no-Mikoto''' (高比売命) and also as '''Shitateruhime-no-Mikoto''' (下光比売命). In the ''{{ill|Nihon Shoki|ja|日本書紀}}'', she appears as '''Shitateruhime''' (下照姫) or '''Shitateruhime-no-Mikoto''', and in the ''{{ill|Sendai Kuji Hongi|ja|先代旧事本紀}}'', she is called '''Shitateruhime-no-Mikoto'''. According to the ''Kojiki'' and the ''Nihon Shoki,'' she married {{ill|Ame-No-Wakahiko|ja|天若日子}}, who had been dispatched from {{ill|Takamagahara|ja|高天原}} to subjugate the {{ill|Ashihara no Nakatsukuni|ja|葦原中国}} (the Central Land of Reed Plains). However, Ame-wakahiko secretly plotted to claim the land for himself. When Ame-wakahiko was killed by a divine arrow sent from Takamagahara, Shitateruhime’s grief-stricken cries reached the heavens. Her mourning led to the descent of Ame-wakahiko's family, including his father {{ill|Amatsukunitama-no-Mikoto|ja|天津国玉神}}, to perform his funeral rites. During this event, her brother {{ill|Ajisukitakahikone|ja|阿遅鉏高日子根神}} was mistaken for the deceased Ame-wakahiko due to their resemblance, leading to a conflict. Shitateruhime composed a lament known as the ''Hina-buri'' (夷振), expressing her sorrow. [[Category:Japanese deities]] [[Category:Kunitsukami]] [[Category:Goddesses]] [[ja:下光比売命]] == Marriage == In many versions of the myth {{ill|Ame no Hohi|en}} did not send a word for three years after going down to earth, all the gods gathered up, and {{ill|Ame no Wakahiko|ja|10=en:draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ame-No-Wakahiko}} was one who was chosen to rule the earth. In many versions {{ill|Ame no Wakahiko|ja|10=en:draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ame-No-Wakahiko}} was given a bow.{{Cite web|title=Encyclopedia of Shinto - Home: Kami in Classic Texts: Ame no Wakahiko|url=http://eos.kokugakuin.ac.jp/modules/xwords/entry.php?entryID=46|access-date=2020-09-29|website=eos.kokugakuin.ac.jp}}{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=xdfgjV2kw6oC&q=Ame+no+Wakahiko&pg=PA6|title=Japanese Mythology A to Z|last=Roberts|first=Jeremy|date=2009|publisher=Infobase Publishing|isbn=978-1-4381-2802-3|language=en}} In some versions, however, Ame no Wakahiko is the son of Ame no Hohi and Ame no Wakahiko was sent to earth to look for him.{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=xdfgjV2kw6oC&dq=Ame+no+Wakahiko&pg=PA6|title=Japanese Mythology a to Z|publisher=Infobase|year=2009|isbn=9781438128023}} She married {{ill|Ame no Wakahiko|ja|10=en:draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ame-No-Wakahiko}}, when he came from heaven to discuss the "{{ill|Kuni-yuzuri|en}}". === Death === Eight years later, the gods had not yet heard a response so they sent a bird named Nakime down to earth to check in on him. Following the advice of a wise woman, Ame no Wakahiko used his bow to shoot the bird.{{Cite book|title=Handbook of Japanese mythology|last=Ashkenazi|first=Michael|date=2008|publisher=Oxford University Press|isbn=978-0-19-533262-9|series=Handbooks of world mythology|location=Oxford|pages=114}} The bird was killed but the arrow flew all the way to heaven. {{ill|Takamimusubi|en}} saw the arrow and threw it back at the earth where it hit Ame no Wakahiko while he was laying in bed, killing him.{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=uAj_PQ8o40sC&q=Takamimusubi|title=The East|date=1992|publisher=East Publications, Incorporated|language=en}} Other versions state that {{ill|Amaterasu|en}} was the one who shot the arrow back at him.{{cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=FlZxh5OaZxoC&pg=PA38|title=Impurity and Death: A Japanese Perspective|last=Abe|first=C.|publisher=Universal Publishers|year=2003|isbn=978-1-58112-195-7|page=38|access-date=2020-09-29}} This myth is the origin of a Japanese saying about the returning arrow. It is likely also be a mythicisation of attempts made by the {{ill|Yamato Kingship|en}} to impose its authority over neighbouring states. === Funeral === After Ame no Wakahiko's death, his parents built a hut (喪屋 moya) for their son. {{ill|Ajisukitakahikone|en}} went down to pay his respect. However, due to Ajisukitakahikone looking similar to Ame no Wakahiko he was mistaken to be Ame no Wakahiko brought back to life. Ajisukitakahikone was offended by this and destroyed the hut and kicked it. The hut landed in the land of Mino and became a mountain called Moyama.{{Cite book|title=Nihongi: Chronicles of Japan from the Earliest Times to A.D. 697, Volume 1|chapter=Book II|chapter-url=https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/Nihongi:_Chronicles_of_Japan_from_the_Earliest_Times_to_A.D._697/Book_II}} When {{ill|Ame no Wakahiko|ja|10=en:draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ame-No-Wakahiko}} passed away, Shitateruhime's sorrowful voice was heard in the Plain of High Heaven. During his funeral, Amewakahiko's father, Amatsukunitama, and other family members confused Shitateruhime's step-brother, [[Ajisukitakahikone]], for the deceased Amewakahiko. [[Ajisukitakahikone]] left in rage. In response, Shitateruhime sang a song of a type called hinaburi, or "rustic song" to honor her deceased husband.{{Cite web|title=Encyclopedia of Shinto詳細|url=https://d-museum.kokugakuin.ac.jp/eos/detail/?id=9155|access-date=2024-03-24|website=國學院大學デジタルミュージアム|language=ja}} == Genealogy == [[File:Ohokuninushi family tree.png|thumb|250px|right|Genealogy of Ōkuninushi (''Kojiki''). Blue indicates male deities, red indicates female deities, and yellow indicates unspecified gender.]] According to the ''Kojiki,'' Shitateruhime is the daughter of {{ill|Ōkuninushi|ja|大国主神}} and {{ill|Takirihime-no-Mikoto|ja|多紀理毘売命}}, making her the sister of {{ill|Ajisukitakahikone|ja|阿遅鉏高日子根神}}. This genealogy is also supported by the ''Sendai Kuji Hongi.'' == Shrines == Shitateruhime is enshrined at several locations, including: * {{ill|Hime Shrine (Toyama)|ja|比賣神社}} in {{ill|Toyama Prefecture|ja|富山県}}, where she is the main deity. * {{ill|Tamatsuoka Shrine|ja|玉津岡神社}} in {{ill|Kyoto Prefecture|ja|京都府}}, dedicated to her worship. * {{ill|Himekoso Shrine|ja|比売許曽神社}} in {{ill|Osaka Prefecture|ja|大阪府}}. * {{ill|Izumo Taisha|ja|出雲大社}}’s external shrine, known as ''Ōanamochi-no-Miko Tamae Shrine'' (大穴持御子玉江神社). == Related Articles == * {{ill|List of Japanese deities|ja|日本の神の一覧}} * {{ill|Munakata clan|ja|宗像氏|simple|User:Immanuelle/Munakata_clan|ja|宗像氏|fr|Clan Munakata}} ==References== {{reflist|draft}} == Further reading == * Jugon, Jean-Claude. It is likely also be a mythicisation of attempts made by the {{ill|Yamato Kingship|en}} to impose its authority over neighbouring states. === Funeral === After Ame no Wakahiko's death, his parents built a hut (喪屋 moya) for their son. {{ill|Ajisukitakahikone|en}} went down to pay his respect. However, due to Ajisukitakahikone looking similar to Ame no Wakahiko he was mistaken to be Ame no Wakahiko brought back to life. Ajisukitakahikone was offended by this and destroyed the hut and kicked it. The hut landed in the land of Mino and became a mountain called Moyama.{{Cite book|title=Nihongi: Chronicles of Japan from the Earliest Times to A.D. 697, Volume 1|chapter=Book II|chapter-url=https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/Nihongi:_Chronicles_of_Japan_from_the_Earliest_Times_to_A.D._697/Book_II}} When {{ill|Ame no Wakahiko|ja|10=en:draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ame-No-Wakahiko}} passed away, Shitateruhime's sorrowful voice was heard in the Plain of High Heaven. [[Ajisukitakahikone]] left in rage. In response, Shitateruhime sang a song of a type called hinaburi, or "rustic song" to honor her deceased husband.{{Cite web|title=Encyclopedia of Shinto詳細|url=https://d-museum.kokugakuin.ac.jp/eos/detail/?id=9155|access-date=2024-03-24|website=國學院大學デジタルミュージアム|language=ja}} == Genealogy == [[File:Ohokuninushi family tree.png|thumb|250px|right|Genealogy of Ōkuninushi (''Kojiki''). This genealogy is also supported by the ''Sendai Kuji Hongi.'' == Shrines == Shitateruhime is enshrined at several locations, including: * {{ill|Hime Shrine (Toyama)|ja|比賣神社}} in {{ill|Toyama Prefecture|ja|富山県}}, where she is the main deity. * {{ill|Tamatsuoka Shrine|ja|玉津岡神社}} in {{ill|Kyoto Prefecture|ja|京都府}}, dedicated to her worship. * {{ill|Himekoso Shrine|ja|比売許曽神社}} in {{ill|Osaka Prefecture|ja|大阪府}}. * {{ill|Izumo Taisha|ja|出雲大社}}’s external shrine, known as ''Ōanamochi-no-Miko Tamae Shrine'' (大穴持御子玉江神社). == Related Articles == * {{ill|List of Japanese deities|ja|日本の神の一覧}} * {{ill|Munakata clan|ja|宗像氏|simple|User:Immanuelle/Munakata_clan|ja|宗像氏|fr|Clan Munakata}} ==References== {{reflist|draft}} == Further reading == * Jugon, Jean-Claude. {{ill|Kifune Shrine|simple|User:Immanuelle/Kifune Shrine|en}}|name=Shitateruhime|siblings=[[Ajisukitakahikone]]|spouse={{ill|Ame no Wakahiko|ja|10=en:draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ame-No-Wakahiko}}|image=File:Shitori-jinja, haiden.jpg|caption={{ill|Shitori Shrine (Tottori)|lt=Shitori Shrine|en}} where she is worshipped |image=File:Shitateruhime shinbutsu-zue.jpg |caption=A book depiction of her }} {{complex}} {{citation needed|Shitateruhime}} [[category:kk]] {{ill|Shitateruhime|lt=Shitateruhime-no-Mikoto|ja|シタテルヒメ|simple|User:Immanuelle/Shitateruhime|en:draft|8=fr}} is a daughter of {{ill|Tagorihime|ja|タキリビメ|simple|User:Immanuelle/Takiribime|en:draft|8=fr}}, one of the three sisters worshipped at [[Munakata Taisha|Munakata Taisha]] The origins of {{ill|Shitori Shrine (Tottori)|lt=Shitori Shrine|ja|4=fr|5=Shitori-jinja|6=ja|7=倭文神社_(湯梨浜町)|8=simple|9=User:Immanuelle/Shitori Shrine (Tottori)}} are unknown. Although there is no documentary evidence, it is believed that it began as the family shrine for the {{Nihongo|Shitori clan|倭文氏}} of [[Kofun period|Kofun period]] craftsmen who weavers, who regarded {{ill|Takehazuchi|lt=Takehazuchi-no-Mikoto|ja|天羽槌雄神|simple|User:Immanuelle/Takehazuchi|en:draft|8=fr}} as their ancestor. However, the shrine's legends are all centered around {{ill|Shitateruhime|lt=Shitateruhime-no-Mikoto|ja|シタテルヒメ|simple|User:Immanuelle/Shitateruhime|en:draft|8=fr}}, whom the shrine legend claims arrived in this location from [[Izumo Taisha|Izumo]] by boat. She established her residence on the mountain behind this shrine, and after her death, she was buried in a ''[[kofun|kofun]]'' constructed in the shrine's precincts.{{cite book |last1=Yoshiki |first1=Emi |title=Zenkoku 'Ichinomiya' tettei gaido |date=2007 |publisher=PHP Institute |isbn=978-4569669304 |language=Japanese}} == Overview == In the ''{{ill|Kojiki|ja|古事記}}'', she is referred to as '''Takahime-no-Mikoto''' (高比売命) and also as '''Shitateruhime-no-Mikoto''' (下光比売命). In the ''{{ill|Nihon Shoki|ja|日本書紀}}'', she appears as '''Shitateruhime''' (下照姫) or '''Shitateruhime-no-Mikoto''', and in the ''{{ill|Sendai Kuji Hongi|ja|先代旧事本紀}}'', she is called '''Shitateruhime-no-Mikoto'''. According to the ''Kojiki'' and the ''Nihon Shoki,'' she married {{ill|Ame-No-Wakahiko|ja|天若日子}}, who had been dispatched from {{ill|Takamagahara|ja|高天原}} to subjugate the {{ill|Ashihara no Nakatsukuni|ja|葦原中国}} (the Central Land of Reed Plains). However, Ame-wakahiko secretly plotted to claim the land for himself. When Ame-wakahiko was killed by a divine arrow sent from Takamagahara, Shitateruhime’s grief-stricken cries reached the heavens. Her mourning led to the descent of Ame-wakahiko's family, including his father {{ill|Amatsukunitama-no-Mikoto|ja|天津国玉神}}, to perform his funeral rites. During this event, her brother {{ill|Ajisukitakahikone|ja|阿遅鉏高日子根神}} was mistaken for the deceased Ame-wakahiko due to their resemblance, leading to a conflict. Shitateruhime composed a lament known as the ''Hina-buri'' (夷振), expressing her sorrow. {{ill|Kifune Shrine|simple|User:Immanuelle/Kifune Shrine|en}}|name=Shitateruhime|siblings=[[Ajisukitakahikone]]|spouse={{ill|Ame no Wakahiko|ja|10=en:draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ame-No-Wakahiko}}|image=File:Shitori-jinja, haiden.jpg|caption={{ill|Shitori Shrine (Tottori)|lt=Shitori Shrine|en}} where she is worshipped |image=File:Shitateruhime shinbutsu-zue.jpg |caption=A book depiction of her }} {{complex}} {{citation needed|Shitateruhime}} [[category:kk]] {{ill|Shitateruhime|lt=Shitateruhime-no-Mikoto|ja|シタテルヒメ|simple|User:Immanuelle/Shitateruhime|en:draft|8=fr}} is a daughter of {{ill|Tagorihime|ja|タキリビメ|simple|User:Immanuelle/Takiribime|en:draft|8=fr}}, one of the three sisters worshipped at [[Munakata Taisha|Munakata Taisha]] The origins of {{ill|Shitori Shrine (Tottori)|lt=Shitori Shrine|ja|4=fr|5=Shitori-jinja|6=ja|7=倭文神社_(湯梨浜町)|8=simple|9=User:Immanuelle/Shitori Shrine (Tottori)}} are unknown. Although there is no documentary evidence, it is believed that it began as the family shrine for the {{Nihongo|Shitori clan|倭文氏}} of [[Kofun period|Kofun period]] craftsmen who weavers, who regarded {{ill|Takehazuchi|lt=Takehazuchi-no-Mikoto|ja|天羽槌雄神|simple|User:Immanuelle/Takehazuchi|en:draft|8=fr}} as their ancestor. However, the shrine's legends are all centered around {{ill|Shitateruhime|lt=Shitateruhime-no-Mikoto|ja|シタテルヒメ|simple|User:Immanuelle/Shitateruhime|en:draft|8=fr}}, whom the shrine legend claims arrived in this location from [[Izumo Taisha|Izumo]] by boat. She established her residence on the mountain behind this shrine, and after her death, she was buried in a ''[[kofun|kofun]]'' constructed in the shrine's precincts.{{cite book |last1=Yoshiki |first1=Emi |title=Zenkoku 'Ichinomiya' tettei gaido |date=2007 |publisher=PHP Institute |isbn=978-4569669304 |language=Japanese}} == Overview == In the ''{{ill|Kojiki|ja|古事記}}'', she is referred to as '''Takahime-no-Mikoto''' (高比売命) and also as '''Shitateruhime-no-Mikoto''' (下光比売命). In the ''{{ill|Nihon Shoki|ja|日本書紀}}'', she appears as '''Shitateruhime''' (下照姫) or '''Shitateruhime-no-Mikoto''', and in the ''{{ill|Sendai Kuji Hongi|ja|先代旧事本紀}}'', she is called '''Shitateruhime-no-Mikoto'''. According to the ''Kojiki'' and the ''Nihon Shoki,'' she married {{ill|Ame-No-Wakahiko|ja|天若日子}}, who had been dispatched from {{ill|Takamagahara|ja|高天原}} to subjugate the {{ill|Ashihara no Nakatsukuni|ja|葦原中国}} (the Central Land of Reed Plains). However, Ame-wakahiko secretly plotted to claim the land for himself. When Ame-wakahiko was killed by a divine arrow sent from Takamagahara, Shitateruhime’s grief-stricken cries reached the heavens. Her mourning led to the descent of Ame-wakahiko's family, including his father {{ill|Amatsukunitama-no-Mikoto|ja|天津国玉神}}, to perform his funeral rites. During this event, her brother {{ill|Ajisukitakahikone|ja|阿遅鉏高日子根神}} was mistaken for the deceased Ame-wakahiko due to their resemblance, leading to a conflict. Shitateruhime composed a lament known as the ''Hina-buri'' (夷振), expressing her sorrow. [[Category:Japanese deities]] [[Category:Kunitsukami]] [[Category:Goddesses]] [[ja:下光比売命]] == Marriage == In many versions of the myth {{ill|Ame no Hohi|en}} did not send a word for three years after going down to earth, all the gods gathered up, and {{ill|Ame no Wakahiko|ja|10=en:draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ame-No-Wakahiko}} was one who was chosen to rule the earth. In many versions {{ill|Ame no Wakahiko|ja|10=en:draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ame-No-Wakahiko}} was given a bow.{{Cite web|title=Encyclopedia of Shinto - Home: Kami in Classic Texts: Ame no Wakahiko|url=http://eos.kokugakuin.ac.jp/modules/xwords/entry.php?entryID=46|access-date=2020-09-29|website=eos.kokugakuin.ac.jp}}{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=xdfgjV2kw6oC&q=Ame+no+Wakahiko&pg=PA6|title=Japanese Mythology A to Z|last=Roberts|first=Jeremy|date=2009|publisher=Infobase Publishing|isbn=978-1-4381-2802-3|language=en}} In some versions, however, Ame no Wakahiko is the son of Ame no Hohi and Ame no Wakahiko was sent to earth to look for him.{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=xdfgjV2kw6oC&dq=Ame+no+Wakahiko&pg=PA6|title=Japanese Mythology a to Z|publisher=Infobase|year=2009|isbn=9781438128023}} She married {{ill|Ame no Wakahiko|ja|10=en:draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ame-No-Wakahiko}}, when he came from heaven to discuss the "{{ill|Kuni-yuzuri|en}}". === Death === Eight years later, the gods had not yet heard a response so they sent a bird named Nakime down to earth to check in on him. Following the advice of a wise woman, Ame no Wakahiko used his bow to shoot the bird.{{Cite book|title=Handbook of Japanese mythology|last=Ashkenazi|first=Michael|date=2008|publisher=Oxford University Press|isbn=978-0-19-533262-9|series=Handbooks of world mythology|location=Oxford|pages=114}} The bird was killed but the arrow flew all the way to heaven. {{ill|Takamimusubi|en}} saw the arrow and threw it back at the earth where it hit Ame no Wakahiko while he was laying in bed, killing him.{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=uAj_PQ8o40sC&q=Takamimusubi|title=The East|date=1992|publisher=East Publications, Incorporated|language=en}} Other versions state that {{ill|Amaterasu|en}} was the one who shot the arrow back at him.{{cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=FlZxh5OaZxoC&pg=PA38|title=Impurity and Death: A Japanese Perspective|last=Abe|first=C.|publisher=Universal Publishers|year=2003|isbn=978-1-58112-195-7|page=38|access-date=2020-09-29}} This myth is the origin of a Japanese saying about the returning arrow. It is likely also be a mythicisation of attempts made by the {{ill|Yamato Kingship|en}} to impose its authority over neighbouring states. === Funeral === After Ame no Wakahiko's death, his parents built a hut (喪屋 moya) for their son. {{ill|Ajisukitakahikone|en}} went down to pay his respect. However, due to Ajisukitakahikone looking similar to Ame no Wakahiko he was mistaken to be Ame no Wakahiko brought back to life. Ajisukitakahikone was offended by this and destroyed the hut and kicked it. The hut landed in the land of Mino and became a mountain called Moyama.{{Cite book|title=Nihongi: Chronicles of Japan from the Earliest Times to A.D. 697, Volume 1|chapter=Book II|chapter-url=https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/Nihongi:_Chronicles_of_Japan_from_the_Earliest_Times_to_A.D._697/Book_II}} When {{ill|Ame no Wakahiko|ja|10=en:draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ame-No-Wakahiko}} passed away, Shitateruhime's sorrowful voice was heard in the Plain of High Heaven. During his funeral, Amewakahiko's father, Amatsukunitama, and other family members confused Shitateruhime's step-brother, [[Ajisukitakahikone]], for the deceased Amewakahiko. [[Ajisukitakahikone]] left in rage. In response, Shitateruhime sang a song of a type called hinaburi, or "rustic song" to honor her deceased husband.{{Cite web|title=Encyclopedia of Shinto詳細|url=https://d-museum.kokugakuin.ac.jp/eos/detail/?id=9155|access-date=2024-03-24|website=國學院大學デジタルミュージアム|language=ja}} == Genealogy == [[File:Ohokuninushi family tree.png|thumb|250px|right|Genealogy of Ōkuninushi (''Kojiki''). Blue indicates male deities, red indicates female deities, and yellow indicates unspecified gender.]] According to the ''Kojiki,'' Shitateruhime is the daughter of {{ill|Ōkuninushi|ja|大国主神}} and {{ill|Takirihime-no-Mikoto|ja|多紀理毘売命}}, making her the sister of {{ill|Ajisukitakahikone|ja|阿遅鉏高日子根神}}. This genealogy is also supported by the ''Sendai Kuji Hongi.'' == Shrines == Shitateruhime is enshrined at several locations, including: * {{ill|Hime Shrine (Toyama)|ja|比賣神社}} in {{ill|Toyama Prefecture|ja|富山県}}, where she is the main deity. * {{ill|Tamatsuoka Shrine|ja|玉津岡神社}} in {{ill|Kyoto Prefecture|ja|京都府}}, dedicated to her worship. * {{ill|Himekoso Shrine|ja|比売許曽神社}} in {{ill|Osaka Prefecture|ja|大阪府}}. * {{ill|Izumo Taisha|ja|出雲大社}}’s external shrine, known as ''Ōanamochi-no-Miko Tamae Shrine'' (大穴持御子玉江神社). == Related Articles == * {{ill|List of Japanese deities|ja|日本の神の一覧}} * {{ill|Munakata clan|ja|宗像氏|simple|User:Immanuelle/Munakata_clan|ja|宗像氏|fr|Clan Munakata}} ==References== {{reflist|draft}} == Further reading == * Jugon, Jean-Claude. [[User:Immanuelle|Immanuelle]] ([[User talk:Immanuelle|talk]]) 09:35, 18 February 2025 (UTC)}} {{Expand Japanese|シタテルヒメ}} {{Infobox deity | type = [[Shinto]] | father = [[Ōkuninushi]] | mother = {{ill|Tagorihime|ja|タキリビメ|simple|User:Immanuelle/Takiribime|en:draft}} |cult_centre={{ill|Shitori Shrine (Tottori)|lt=Shitori Shrine|en}},
{{ill|Kifune Shrine|simple|User:Immanuelle/Kifune Shrine|en}}|name=Shitateruhime|siblings=[[Ajisukitakahikone]]|spouse={{ill|Ame no Wakahiko|ja|10=en:draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ame-No-Wakahiko}}|image=File:Shitori-jinja, haiden.jpg|caption={{ill|Shitori Shrine (Tottori)|lt=Shitori Shrine|en}} where she is worshipped |image=File:Shitateruhime shinbutsu-zue.jpg |caption=A book depiction of her }} {{complex}} {{citation needed|Shitateruhime}} [[category:kk]] {{ill|Shitateruhime|lt=Shitateruhime-no-Mikoto|ja|シタテルヒメ|simple|User:Immanuelle/Shitateruhime|en:draft|8=fr}} is a daughter of {{ill|Tagorihime|ja|タキリビメ|simple|User:Immanuelle/Takiribime|en:draft|8=fr}}, one of the three sisters worshipped at [[Munakata Taisha|Munakata Taisha]] The origins of {{ill|Shitori Shrine (Tottori)|lt=Shitori Shrine|ja|4=fr|5=Shitori-jinja|6=ja|7=倭文神社_(湯梨浜町)|8=simple|9=User:Immanuelle/Shitori Shrine (Tottori)}} are unknown. Although there is no documentary evidence, it is believed that it began as the family shrine for the {{Nihongo|Shitori clan|倭文氏}} of [[Kofun period|Kofun period]] craftsmen who weavers, who regarded {{ill|Takehazuchi|lt=Takehazuchi-no-Mikoto|ja|天羽槌雄神|simple|User:Immanuelle/Takehazuchi|en:draft|8=fr}} as their ancestor. However, the shrine's legends are all centered around {{ill|Shitateruhime|lt=Shitateruhime-no-Mikoto|ja|シタテルヒメ|simple|User:Immanuelle/Shitateruhime|en:draft|8=fr}}, whom the shrine legend claims arrived in this location from [[Izumo Taisha|Izumo]] by boat. She established her residence on the mountain behind this shrine, and after her death, she was buried in a ''[[kofun|kofun]]'' constructed in the shrine's precincts.{{cite book |last1=Yoshiki |first1=Emi |title=Zenkoku 'Ichinomiya' tettei gaido |date=2007 |publisher=PHP Institute |isbn=978-4569669304 |language=Japanese}} [[ja:シタテルヒメ]] == Overview == In the ''{{ill|Kojiki|ja|古事記}}'', she is referred to as '''Takahime-no-Mikoto''' (高比売命) and also as '''Shitateruhime-no-Mikoto''' (下光比売命). In the ''{{ill|Nihon Shoki|ja|日本書紀}}'', she appears as '''Shitateruhime''' (下照姫) or '''Shitateruhime-no-Mikoto''', and in the ''{{ill|Sendai Kuji Hongi|ja|先代旧事本紀}}'', she is called '''Shitateruhime-no-Mikoto'''. According to the ''Kojiki'' and the ''Nihon Shoki,'' she married {{ill|Ame-No-Wakahiko|ja|天若日子}}, who had been dispatched from {{ill|Takamagahara|ja|高天原}} to subjugate the {{ill|Ashihara no Nakatsukuni|ja|葦原中国}} (the Central Land of Reed Plains). However, Ame-wakahiko secretly plotted to claim the land for himself. When Ame-wakahiko was killed by a divine arrow sent from Takamagahara, Shitateruhime’s grief-stricken cries reached the heavens. Her mourning led to the descent of Ame-wakahiko's family, including his father {{ill|Amatsukunitama-no-Mikoto|ja|天津国玉神}}, to perform his funeral rites. During this event, her brother {{ill|Ajisukitakahikone|ja|阿遅鉏高日子根神}} was mistaken for the deceased Ame-wakahiko due to their resemblance, leading to a conflict. Shitateruhime composed a lament known as the ''Hina-buri'' (夷振), expressing her sorrow. [[Category:Japanese deities]] [[Category:Kunitsukami]] [[Category:Goddesses]] [[ja:下光比売命]] == Marriage == In many versions of the myth {{ill|Ame no Hohi|en}} did not send a word for three years after going down to earth, all the gods gathered up, and {{ill|Ame no Wakahiko|ja|10=en:draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ame-No-Wakahiko}} was one who was chosen to rule the earth. In many versions {{ill|Ame no Wakahiko|ja|10=en:draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ame-No-Wakahiko}} was given a bow.{{Cite web|title=Encyclopedia of Shinto - Home: Kami in Classic Texts: Ame no Wakahiko|url=http://eos.kokugakuin.ac.jp/modules/xwords/entry.php?entryID=46|access-date=2020-09-29|website=eos.kokugakuin.ac.jp}}{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=xdfgjV2kw6oC&q=Ame+no+Wakahiko&pg=PA6|title=Japanese Mythology A to Z|last=Roberts|first=Jeremy|date=2009|publisher=Infobase Publishing|isbn=978-1-4381-2802-3|language=en}} In some versions, however, Ame no Wakahiko is the son of Ame no Hohi and Ame no Wakahiko was sent to earth to look for him.{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=xdfgjV2kw6oC&dq=Ame+no+Wakahiko&pg=PA6|title=Japanese Mythology a to Z|publisher=Infobase|year=2009|isbn=9781438128023}} She married {{ill|Ame no Wakahiko|ja|10=en:draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ame-No-Wakahiko}}, when he came from heaven to discuss the "{{ill|Kuni-yuzuri|en}}". === Death === Eight years later, the gods had not yet heard a response so they sent a bird named Nakime down to earth to check in on him. Following the advice of a wise woman, Ame no Wakahiko used his bow to shoot the bird.{{Cite book|title=Handbook of Japanese mythology|last=Ashkenazi|first=Michael|date=2008|publisher=Oxford University Press|isbn=978-0-19-533262-9|series=Handbooks of world mythology|location=Oxford|pages=114}} The bird was killed but the arrow flew all the way to heaven. {{ill|Takamimusubi|en}} saw the arrow and threw it back at the earth where it hit Ame no Wakahiko while he was laying in bed, killing him.{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=uAj_PQ8o40sC&q=Takamimusubi|title=The East|date=1992|publisher=East Publications, Incorporated|language=en}} Other versions state that {{ill|Amaterasu|en}} was the one who shot the arrow back at him.{{cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=FlZxh5OaZxoC&pg=PA38|title=Impurity and Death: A Japanese Perspective|last=Abe|first=C.|publisher=Universal Publishers|year=2003|isbn=978-1-58112-195-7|page=38|access-date=2020-09-29}} This myth is the origin of a Japanese saying about the returning arrow. It is likely also be a mythicisation of attempts made by the {{ill|Yamato Kingship|en}} to impose its authority over neighbouring states. === Funeral === After Ame no Wakahiko's death, his parents built a hut (喪屋 moya) for their son. {{ill|Ajisukitakahikone|en}} went down to pay his respect. However, due to Ajisukitakahikone looking similar to Ame no Wakahiko he was mistaken to be Ame no Wakahiko brought back to life. Ajisukitakahikone was offended by this and destroyed the hut and kicked it. The hut landed in the land of Mino and became a mountain called Moyama.{{Cite book|title=Nihongi: Chronicles of Japan from the Earliest Times to A.D. 697, Volume 1|chapter=Book II|chapter-url=https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/Nihongi:_Chronicles_of_Japan_from_the_Earliest_Times_to_A.D._697/Book_II}} When {{ill|Ame no Wakahiko|ja|10=en:draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ame-No-Wakahiko}} passed away, Shitateruhime's sorrowful voice was heard in the Plain of High Heaven. During his funeral, Amewakahiko's father, Amatsukunitama, and other family members confused Shitateruhime's step-brother, [[Ajisukitakahikone]], for the deceased Amewakahiko. [[Ajisukitakahikone]] left in rage. In response, Shitateruhime sang a song of a type called hinaburi, or "rustic song" to honor her deceased husband.{{Cite web|title=Encyclopedia of Shinto詳細|url=https://d-museum.kokugakuin.ac.jp/eos/detail/?id=9155|access-date=2024-03-24|website=國學院大學デジタルミュージアム|language=ja}} == Genealogy == [[File:Ohokuninushi family tree.png|thumb|250px|right|Genealogy of Ōkuninushi (''Kojiki''). Blue indicates male deities, red indicates female deities, and yellow indicates unspecified gender.]] According to the ''Kojiki,'' Shitateruhime is the daughter of {{ill|Ōkuninushi|ja|大国主神}} and {{ill|Takirihime-no-Mikoto|ja|多紀理毘売命}}, making her the sister of {{ill|Ajisukitakahikone|ja|阿遅鉏高日子根神}}. This genealogy is also supported by the ''Sendai Kuji Hongi.'' == Shrines == Shitateruhime is enshrined at several locations, including: * {{ill|Hime Shrine (Toyama)|ja|比賣神社}} in {{ill|Toyama Prefecture|ja|富山県}}, where she is the main deity. * {{ill|Tamatsuoka Shrine|ja|玉津岡神社}} in {{ill|Kyoto Prefecture|ja|京都府}}, dedicated to her worship. * {{ill|Himekoso Shrine|ja|比売許曽神社}} in {{ill|Osaka Prefecture|ja|大阪府}}. * {{ill|Izumo Taisha|ja|出雲大社}}’s external shrine, known as ''Ōanamochi-no-Miko Tamae Shrine'' (大穴持御子玉江神社). == Related Articles == * {{ill|List of Japanese deities|ja|日本の神の一覧}} * {{ill|Munakata clan|ja|宗像氏|simple|User:Immanuelle/Munakata_clan|ja|宗像氏|fr|Clan Munakata}} ==References== {{reflist|draft}} == Further reading == * Jugon, Jean-Claude. Following the advice of a wise woman, Ame no Wakahiko used his bow to shoot the bird.{{Cite book|title=Handbook of Japanese mythology|last=Ashkenazi|first=Michael|date=2008|publisher=Oxford University Press|isbn=978-0-19-533262-9|series=Handbooks of world mythology|location=Oxford|pages=114}} The bird was killed but the arrow flew all the way to heaven. {{ill|Takamimusubi|en}} saw the arrow and threw it back at the earth where it hit Ame no Wakahiko while he was laying in bed, killing him.{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=uAj_PQ8o40sC&q=Takamimusubi|title=The East|date=1992|publisher=East Publications, Incorporated|language=en}} Other versions state that {{ill|Amaterasu|en}} was the one who shot the arrow back at him.{{cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=FlZxh5OaZxoC&pg=PA38|title=Impurity and Death: A Japanese Perspective|last=Abe|first=C.|publisher=Universal Publishers|year=2003|isbn=978-1-58112-195-7|page=38|access-date=2020-09-29}} This myth is the origin of a Japanese saying about the returning arrow. It is likely also be a mythicisation of attempts made by the {{ill|Yamato Kingship|en}} to impose its authority over neighbouring states. === Funeral === After Ame no Wakahiko's death, his parents built a hut (喪屋 moya) for their son. {{ill|Ajisukitakahikone|en}} went down to pay his respect. However, due to Ajisukitakahikone looking similar to Ame no Wakahiko he was mistaken to be Ame no Wakahiko brought back to life. Ajisukitakahikone was offended by this and destroyed the hut and kicked it. The hut landed in the land of Mino and became a mountain called Moyama.{{Cite book|title=Nihongi: Chronicles of Japan from the Earliest Times to A.D. 697, Volume 1|chapter=Book II|chapter-url=https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/Nihongi:_Chronicles_of_Japan_from_the_Earliest_Times_to_A.D._697/Book_II}} When {{ill|Ame no Wakahiko|ja|10=en:draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ame-No-Wakahiko}} passed away, Shitateruhime's sorrowful voice was heard in the Plain of High Heaven. During his funeral, Amewakahiko's father, Amatsukunitama, and other family members confused Shitateruhime's step-brother, [[Ajisukitakahikone]], for the deceased Amewakahiko. [[Ajisukitakahikone]] left in rage. In response, Shitateruhime sang a song of a type called hinaburi, or "rustic song" to honor her deceased husband.{{Cite web|title=Encyclopedia of Shinto詳細|url=https://d-museum.kokugakuin.ac.jp/eos/detail/?id=9155|access-date=2024-03-24|website=國學院大學デジタルミュージアム|language=ja}} == Genealogy == [[File:Ohokuninushi family tree.png|thumb|250px|right|Genealogy of Ōkuninushi (''Kojiki''). Blue indicates male deities, red indicates female deities, and yellow indicates unspecified gender.]] According to the ''Kojiki,'' Shitateruhime is the daughter of {{ill|Ōkuninushi|ja|大国主神}} and {{ill|Takirihime-no-Mikoto|ja|多紀理毘売命}}, making her the sister of {{ill|Ajisukitakahikone|ja|阿遅鉏高日子根神}}. Although there is no documentary evidence, it is believed that it began as the family shrine for the {{Nihongo|Shitori clan|倭文氏}} of [[Kofun period|Kofun period]] craftsmen who weavers, who regarded {{ill|Takehazuchi|lt=Takehazuchi-no-Mikoto|ja|天羽槌雄神|simple|User:Immanuelle/Takehazuchi|en:draft|8=fr}} as their ancestor. However, the shrine's legends are all centered around {{ill|Shitateruhime|lt=Shitateruhime-no-Mikoto|ja|シタテルヒメ|simple|User:Immanuelle/Shitateruhime|en:draft|8=fr}}, whom the shrine legend claims arrived in this location from [[Izumo Taisha|Izumo]] by boat. She established her residence on the mountain behind this shrine, and after her death, she was buried in a ''[[kofun|kofun]]'' constructed in the shrine's precincts.{{cite book |last1=Yoshiki |first1=Emi |title=Zenkoku 'Ichinomiya' tettei gaido |date=2007 |publisher=PHP Institute |isbn=978-4569669304 |language=Japanese}} [[ja:シタテルヒメ]] == Overview == In the ''{{ill|Kojiki|ja|古事記}}'', she is referred to as '''Takahime-no-Mikoto''' (高比売命) and also as '''Shitateruhime-no-Mikoto''' (下光比売命). In the ''{{ill|Nihon Shoki|ja|日本書紀}}'', she appears as '''Shitateruhime''' (下照姫) or '''Shitateruhime-no-Mikoto''', and in the ''{{ill|Sendai Kuji Hongi|ja|先代旧事本紀}}'', she is called '''Shitateruhime-no-Mikoto'''. According to the ''Kojiki'' and the ''Nihon Shoki,'' she married {{ill|Ame-No-Wakahiko|ja|天若日子}}, who had been dispatched from {{ill|Takamagahara|ja|高天原}} to subjugate the {{ill|Ashihara no Nakatsukuni|ja|葦原中国}} (the Central Land of Reed Plains). However, Ame-wakahiko secretly plotted to claim the land for himself. When Ame-wakahiko was killed by a divine arrow sent from Takamagahara, Shitateruhime’s grief-stricken cries reached the heavens. Her mourning led to the descent of Ame-wakahiko's family, including his father {{ill|Amatsukunitama-no-Mikoto|ja|天津国玉神}}, to perform his funeral rites. During this event, her brother {{ill|Ajisukitakahikone|ja|阿遅鉏高日子根神}} was mistaken for the deceased Ame-wakahiko due to their resemblance, leading to a conflict. Shitateruhime composed a lament known as the ''Hina-buri'' (夷振), expressing her sorrow. {{ill|Kifune Shrine|simple|User:Immanuelle/Kifune Shrine|en}}|name=Shitateruhime|siblings=[[Ajisukitakahikone]]|spouse={{ill|Ame no Wakahiko|ja|10=en:draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ame-No-Wakahiko}}|image=File:Shitori-jinja, haiden.jpg|caption={{ill|Shitori Shrine (Tottori)|lt=Shitori Shrine|en}} where she is worshipped |image=File:Shitateruhime shinbutsu-zue.jpg |caption=A book depiction of her }} {{complex}} {{citation needed|Shitateruhime}} [[category:kk]] {{ill|Shitateruhime|lt=Shitateruhime-no-Mikoto|ja|シタテルヒメ|simple|User:Immanuelle/Shitateruhime|en:draft|8=fr}} is a daughter of {{ill|Tagorihime|ja|タキリビメ|simple|User:Immanuelle/Takiribime|en:draft|8=fr}}, one of the three sisters worshipped at [[Munakata Taisha|Munakata Taisha]] The origins of {{ill|Shitori Shrine (Tottori)|lt=Shitori Shrine|ja|4=fr|5=Shitori-jinja|6=ja|7=倭文神社_(湯梨浜町)|8=simple|9=User:Immanuelle/Shitori Shrine (Tottori)}} are unknown. Although there is no documentary evidence, it is believed that it began as the family shrine for the {{Nihongo|Shitori clan|倭文氏}} of [[Kofun period|Kofun period]] craftsmen who weavers, who regarded {{ill|Takehazuchi|lt=Takehazuchi-no-Mikoto|ja|天羽槌雄神|simple|User:Immanuelle/Takehazuchi|en:draft|8=fr}} as their ancestor. However, the shrine's legends are all centered around {{ill|Shitateruhime|lt=Shitateruhime-no-Mikoto|ja|シタテルヒメ|simple|User:Immanuelle/Shitateruhime|en:draft|8=fr}}, whom the shrine legend claims arrived in this location from [[Izumo Taisha|Izumo]] by boat. She established her residence on the mountain behind this shrine, and after her death, she was buried in a ''[[kofun|kofun]]'' constructed in the shrine's precincts.{{cite book |last1=Yoshiki |first1=Emi |title=Zenkoku 'Ichinomiya' tettei gaido |date=2007 |publisher=PHP Institute |isbn=978-4569669304 |language=Japanese}} [[ja:シタテルヒメ]] == Overview == In the ''{{ill|Kojiki|ja|古事記}}'', she is referred to as '''Takahime-no-Mikoto''' (高比売命) and also as '''Shitateruhime-no-Mikoto''' (下光比売命). In the ''{{ill|Nihon Shoki|ja|日本書紀}}'', she appears as '''Shitateruhime''' (下照姫) or '''Shitateruhime-no-Mikoto''', and in the ''{{ill|Sendai Kuji Hongi|ja|先代旧事本紀}}'', she is called '''Shitateruhime-no-Mikoto'''. According to the ''Kojiki'' and the ''Nihon Shoki,'' she married {{ill|Ame-No-Wakahiko|ja|天若日子}}, who had been dispatched from {{ill|Takamagahara|ja|高天原}} to subjugate the {{ill|Ashihara no Nakatsukuni|ja|葦原中国}} (the Central Land of Reed Plains). However, Ame-wakahiko secretly plotted to claim the land for himself. When Ame-wakahiko was killed by a divine arrow sent from Takamagahara, Shitateruhime’s grief-stricken cries reached the heavens. Her mourning led to the descent of Ame-wakahiko's family, including his father {{ill|Amatsukunitama-no-Mikoto|ja|天津国玉神}}, to perform his funeral rites. During this event, her brother {{ill|Ajisukitakahikone|ja|阿遅鉏高日子根神}} was mistaken for the deceased Ame-wakahiko due to their resemblance, leading to a conflict. Shitateruhime composed a lament known as the ''Hina-buri'' (夷振), expressing her sorrow. [[Category:Japanese deities]] [[Category:Kunitsukami]] [[Category:Goddesses]] [[ja:下光比売命]] == Marriage == In many versions of the myth {{ill|Ame no Hohi|en}} did not send a word for three years after going down to earth, all the gods gathered up, and {{ill|Ame no Wakahiko|ja|10=en:draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ame-No-Wakahiko}} was one who was chosen to rule the earth. In many versions {{ill|Ame no Wakahiko|ja|10=en:draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ame-No-Wakahiko}} was given a bow.{{Cite web|title=Encyclopedia of Shinto - Home: Kami in Classic Texts: Ame no Wakahiko|url=http://eos.kokugakuin.ac.jp/modules/xwords/entry.php?entryID=46|access-date=2020-09-29|website=eos.kokugakuin.ac.jp}}{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=xdfgjV2kw6oC&q=Ame+no+Wakahiko&pg=PA6|title=Japanese Mythology A to Z|last=Roberts|first=Jeremy|date=2009|publisher=Infobase Publishing|isbn=978-1-4381-2802-3|language=en}} In some versions, however, Ame no Wakahiko is the son of Ame no Hohi and Ame no Wakahiko was sent to earth to look for him.{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=xdfgjV2kw6oC&dq=Ame+no+Wakahiko&pg=PA6|title=Japanese Mythology a to Z|publisher=Infobase|year=2009|isbn=9781438128023}} She married {{ill|Ame no Wakahiko|ja|10=en:draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ame-No-Wakahiko}}, when he came from heaven to discuss the "{{ill|Kuni-yuzuri|en}}". === Death === Eight years later, the gods had not yet heard a response so they sent a bird named Nakime down to earth to check in on him. Following the advice of a wise woman, Ame no Wakahiko used his bow to shoot the bird.{{Cite book|title=Handbook of Japanese mythology|last=Ashkenazi|first=Michael|date=2008|publisher=Oxford University Press|isbn=978-0-19-533262-9|series=Handbooks of world mythology|location=Oxford|pages=114}} The bird was killed but the arrow flew all the way to heaven. {{ill|Takamimusubi|en}} saw the arrow and threw it back at the earth where it hit Ame no Wakahiko while he was laying in bed, killing him.{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=uAj_PQ8o40sC&q=Takamimusubi|title=The East|date=1992|publisher=East Publications, Incorporated|language=en}} Other versions state that {{ill|Amaterasu|en}} was the one who shot the arrow back at him.{{cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=FlZxh5OaZxoC&pg=PA38|title=Impurity and Death: A Japanese Perspective|last=Abe|first=C.|publisher=Universal Publishers|year=2003|isbn=978-1-58112-195-7|page=38|access-date=2020-09-29}} This myth is the origin of a Japanese saying about the returning arrow. It is likely also be a mythicisation of attempts made by the {{ill|Yamato Kingship|en}} to impose its authority over neighbouring states. === Funeral === After Ame no Wakahiko's death, his parents built a hut (喪屋 moya) for their son. {{ill|Ajisukitakahikone|en}} went down to pay his respect. However, due to Ajisukitakahikone looking similar to Ame no Wakahiko he was mistaken to be Ame no Wakahiko brought back to life. Ajisukitakahikone was offended by this and destroyed the hut and kicked it. The hut landed in the land of Mino and became a mountain called Moyama.{{Cite book|title=Nihongi: Chronicles of Japan from the Earliest Times to A.D. 697, Volume 1|chapter=Book II|chapter-url=https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/Nihongi:_Chronicles_of_Japan_from_the_Earliest_Times_to_A.D._697/Book_II}} When {{ill|Ame no Wakahiko|ja|10=en:draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ame-No-Wakahiko}} passed away, Shitateruhime's sorrowful voice was heard in the Plain of High Heaven. During his funeral, Amewakahiko's father, Amatsukunitama, and other family members confused Shitateruhime's step-brother, [[Ajisukitakahikone]], for the deceased Amewakahiko. [[Ajisukitakahikone]] left in rage. In response, Shitateruhime sang a song of a type called hinaburi, or "rustic song" to honor her deceased husband.{{Cite web|title=Encyclopedia of Shinto詳細|url=https://d-museum.kokugakuin.ac.jp/eos/detail/?id=9155|access-date=2024-03-24|website=國學院大學デジタルミュージアム|language=ja}} == Genealogy == [[File:Ohokuninushi family tree.png|thumb|250px|right|Genealogy of Ōkuninushi (''Kojiki''). Blue indicates male deities, red indicates female deities, and yellow indicates unspecified gender.]] According to the ''Kojiki,'' Shitateruhime is the daughter of {{ill|Ōkuninushi|ja|大国主神}} and {{ill|Takirihime-no-Mikoto|ja|多紀理毘売命|1=Tagorihime}}, making her the sister of {{ill|Ajisukitakahikone|ja|阿遅鉏高日子根神}}. This genealogy is also supported by the ''Sendai Kuji Hongi.'' == Shrines == Shitateruhime is enshrined at several locations, including: * {{ill|Hime Shrine (Toyama)|ja|比賣神社}} in {{ill|Toyama Prefecture|ja|富山県}}, where she is the main deity. * {{ill|Tamatsuoka Shrine|ja|玉津岡神社}} in {{ill|Kyoto Prefecture|ja|京都府}}, dedicated to her worship. * {{ill|Himekoso Shrine|ja|比売許曽神社}} in {{ill|Osaka Prefecture|ja|大阪府}}. * {{ill|Izumo Taisha|ja|出雲大社}}’s external shrine, known as ''Ōanamochi-no-Miko Tamae Shrine'' (大穴持御子玉江神社). == Related Articles == * {{ill|List of Japanese deities|ja|日本の神の一覧}} * {{ill|Munakata clan|ja|宗像氏|simple|User:Immanuelle/Munakata_clan|ja|宗像氏|fr|Clan Munakata}} ==References== {{reflist|draft}} == Further reading == * Jugon, Jean-Claude. [[User:Immanuelle|Immanuelle]] ([[User talk:Immanuelle|talk]]) 09:35, 18 February 2025 (UTC)}} {{Expand Japanese|シタテルヒメ}} {{Infobox deity | type = [[Shinto]] | father = [[Ōkuninushi]] | mother = {{ill|Tagorihime|ja|タキリビメ|simple|User:Immanuelle/Takiribime|en:draft}} |cult_centre={{ill|Shitori Shrine (Tottori)|lt=Shitori Shrine|en}},
{{ill|Kifune Shrine|simple|User:Immanuelle/Kifune Shrine|en}}|name=Shitateruhime|siblings=[[Ajisukitakahikone]]|spouse={{ill|Ame no Wakahiko|ja|10=en:draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ame-No-Wakahiko}}|image=File:Shitori-jinja, haiden.jpg|caption={{ill|Shitori Shrine (Tottori)|lt=Shitori Shrine|en}} where she is worshipped |image=File:Shitateruhime shinbutsu-zue.jpg |caption=A book depiction of her }} {{complex}} {{citation needed|Shitateruhime}} [[category:kk]] {{ill|Shitateruhime|lt=Shitateruhime-no-Mikoto|ja|シタテルヒメ|simple|User:Immanuelle/Shitateruhime|en:draft|8=fr}} is a daughter of {{ill|Tagorihime|ja|タキリビメ|simple|User:Immanuelle/Takiribime|en:draft|8=fr}}, one of the three sisters worshipped at [[Munakata Taisha|Munakata Taisha]] The origins of {{ill|Shitori Shrine (Tottori)|lt=Shitori Shrine|ja|4=fr|5=Shitori-jinja|6=ja|7=倭文神社_(湯梨浜町)|8=simple|9=User:Immanuelle/Shitori Shrine (Tottori)}} are unknown. Although there is no documentary evidence, it is believed that it began as the family shrine for the {{Nihongo|Shitori clan|倭文氏}} of [[Kofun period|Kofun period]] craftsmen who weavers, who regarded {{ill|Takehazuchi|lt=Takehazuchi-no-Mikoto|ja|天羽槌雄神|simple|User:Immanuelle/Takehazuchi|en:draft|8=fr}} as their ancestor. However, the shrine's legends are all centered around {{ill|Shitateruhime|lt=Shitateruhime-no-Mikoto|ja|シタテルヒメ|simple|User:Immanuelle/Shitateruhime|en:draft|8=fr}}, whom the shrine legend claims arrived in this location from [[Izumo Taisha|Izumo]] by boat. She established her residence on the mountain behind this shrine, and after her death, she was buried in a ''[[kofun|kofun]]'' constructed in the shrine's precincts.{{cite book |last1=Yoshiki |first1=Emi |title=Zenkoku 'Ichinomiya' tettei gaido |date=2007 |publisher=PHP Institute |isbn=978-4569669304 |language=Japanese}} [[ja:シタテルヒメ]] == Overview == In the ''{{ill|Kojiki|ja|古事記}}'', she is referred to as '''Takahime-no-Mikoto''' (高比売命) and also as '''Shitateruhime-no-Mikoto''' (下光比売命). In the ''{{ill|Nihon Shoki|ja|日本書紀}}'', she appears as '''Shitateruhime''' (下照姫) or '''Shitateruhime-no-Mikoto''', and in the ''{{ill|Sendai Kuji Hongi|ja|先代旧事本紀}}'', she is called '''Shitateruhime-no-Mikoto'''. According to the ''Kojiki'' and the ''Nihon Shoki,'' she married {{ill|Ame-No-Wakahiko|ja|天若日子}}, who had been dispatched from {{ill|Takamagahara|ja|高天原}} to subjugate the {{ill|Ashihara no Nakatsukuni|ja|葦原中国}} (the Central Land of Reed Plains). However, Ame-wakahiko secretly plotted to claim the land for himself. When Ame-wakahiko was killed by a divine arrow sent from Takamagahara, Shitateruhime’s grief-stricken cries reached the heavens. Her mourning led to the descent of Ame-wakahiko's family, including his father {{ill|Amatsukunitama-no-Mikoto|ja|天津国玉神}}, to perform his funeral rites. During this event, her brother {{ill|Ajisukitakahikone|ja|阿遅鉏高日子根神}} was mistaken for the deceased Ame-wakahiko due to their resemblance, leading to a conflict. Shitateruhime composed a lament known as the ''Hina-buri'' (夷振), expressing her sorrow. [[Category:Japanese deities]] [[Category:Kunitsukami]] [[Category:Goddesses]] [[ja:下光比売命]] == Marriage == In many versions of the myth {{ill|Ame no Hohi|en}} did not send a word for three years after going down to earth, all the gods gathered up, and {{ill|Ame no Wakahiko|ja|10=en:draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ame-No-Wakahiko}} was one who was chosen to rule the earth. In many versions {{ill|Ame no Wakahiko|ja|10=en:draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ame-No-Wakahiko}} was given a bow.{{Cite web|title=Encyclopedia of Shinto - Home: Kami in Classic Texts: Ame no Wakahiko|url=http://eos.kokugakuin.ac.jp/modules/xwords/entry.php?entryID=46|access-date=2020-09-29|website=eos.kokugakuin.ac.jp}}{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=xdfgjV2kw6oC&q=Ame+no+Wakahiko&pg=PA6|title=Japanese Mythology A to Z|last=Roberts|first=Jeremy|date=2009|publisher=Infobase Publishing|isbn=978-1-4381-2802-3|language=en}} In some versions, however, Ame no Wakahiko is the son of Ame no Hohi and Ame no Wakahiko was sent to earth to look for him.{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=xdfgjV2kw6oC&dq=Ame+no+Wakahiko&pg=PA6|title=Japanese Mythology a to Z|publisher=Infobase|year=2009|isbn=9781438128023}} She married {{ill|Ame no Wakahiko|ja|10=en:draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ame-No-Wakahiko}}, when he came from heaven to discuss the "{{ill|Kuni-yuzuri|en}}". === Death === Eight years later, the gods had not yet heard a response so they sent a bird named Nakime down to earth to check in on him. Following the advice of a wise woman, Ame no Wakahiko used his bow to shoot the bird.{{Cite book|title=Handbook of Japanese mythology|last=Ashkenazi|first=Michael|date=2008|publisher=Oxford University Press|isbn=978-0-19-533262-9|series=Handbooks of world mythology|location=Oxford|pages=114}} The bird was killed but the arrow flew all the way to heaven. {{ill|Takamimusubi|en}} saw the arrow and threw it back at the earth where it hit Ame no Wakahiko while he was laying in bed, killing him.{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=uAj_PQ8o40sC&q=Takamimusubi|title=The East|date=1992|publisher=East Publications, Incorporated|language=en}} Other versions state that {{ill|Amaterasu|en}} was the one who shot the arrow back at him.{{cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=FlZxh5OaZxoC&pg=PA38|title=Impurity and Death: A Japanese Perspective|last=Abe|first=C.|publisher=Universal Publishers|year=2003|isbn=978-1-58112-195-7|page=38|access-date=2020-09-29}} This myth is the origin of a Japanese saying about the returning arrow. It is likely also be a mythicisation of attempts made by the {{ill|Yamato Kingship|en}} to impose its authority over neighbouring states. === Funeral === After Ame no Wakahiko's death, his parents built a hut (喪屋 moya) for their son. {{ill|Ajisukitakahikone|en}} went down to pay his respect. However, due to Ajisukitakahikone looking similar to Ame no Wakahiko he was mistaken to be Ame no Wakahiko brought back to life. Ajisukitakahikone was offended by this and destroyed the hut and kicked it. The hut landed in the land of Mino and became a mountain called Moyama.{{Cite book|title=Nihongi: Chronicles of Japan from the Earliest Times to A.D. 697, Volume 1|chapter=Book II|chapter-url=https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/Nihongi:_Chronicles_of_Japan_from_the_Earliest_Times_to_A.D._697/Book_II}} When {{ill|Ame no Wakahiko|ja|10=en:draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ame-No-Wakahiko}} passed away, Shitateruhime's sorrowful voice was heard in the Plain of High Heaven. During his funeral, Amewakahiko's father, Amatsukunitama, and other family members confused Shitateruhime's step-brother, [[Ajisukitakahikone]], for the deceased Amewakahiko. [[Ajisukitakahikone]] left in rage. In response, Shitateruhime sang a song of a type called hinaburi, or "rustic song" to honor her deceased husband.{{Cite web|title=Encyclopedia of Shinto詳細|url=https://d-museum.kokugakuin.ac.jp/eos/detail/?id=9155|access-date=2024-03-24|website=國學院大學デジタルミュージアム|language=ja}} == Genealogy == [[File:Ohokuninushi family tree.png|thumb|250px|right|Genealogy of Ōkuninushi (''Kojiki''). Blue indicates male deities, red indicates female deities, and yellow indicates unspecified gender.]] According to the ''Kojiki,'' Shitateruhime is the daughter of {{ill|Ōkuninushi|ja|大国主神}} and {{ill|Takirihime-no-Mikoto|ja|多紀理毘売命|1=Tagorihime}}, making her the sister of {{ill|Ajisukitakahikone|ja|阿遅鉏高日子根神}}. Although there is no documentary evidence, it is believed that it began as the family shrine for the {{Nihongo|Shitori clan|倭文氏}} of [[Kofun period|Kofun period]] craftsmen who weavers, who regarded {{ill|Takehazuchi|lt=Takehazuchi-no-Mikoto|ja|天羽槌雄神|simple|User:Immanuelle/Takehazuchi|en:draft|8=fr}} as their ancestor. However, the shrine's legends are all centered around {{ill|Shitateruhime|lt=Shitateruhime-no-Mikoto|ja|シタテルヒメ|simple|User:Immanuelle/Shitateruhime|en:draft|8=fr}}, whom the shrine legend claims arrived in this location from [[Izumo Taisha|Izumo]] by boat. She established her residence on the mountain behind this shrine, and after her death, she was buried in a ''[[kofun|kofun]]'' constructed in the shrine's precincts.{{cite book |last1=Yoshiki |first1=Emi |title=Zenkoku 'Ichinomiya' tettei gaido |date=2007 |publisher=PHP Institute |isbn=978-4569669304 |language=Japanese}} [[ja:シタテルヒメ]] == Overview == In the ''{{ill|Kojiki|ja|古事記}}'', she is referred to as '''Takahime-no-Mikoto''' (高比売命) and also as '''Shitateruhime-no-Mikoto''' (下光比売命). In the ''{{ill|Nihon Shoki|ja|日本書紀}}'', she appears as '''Shitateruhime''' (下照姫) or '''Shitateruhime-no-Mikoto''', and in the ''{{ill|Sendai Kuji Hongi|ja|先代旧事本紀}}'', she is called '''Shitateruhime-no-Mikoto'''. According to the ''Kojiki'' and the ''Nihon Shoki,'' she married {{ill|Ame-No-Wakahiko|ja|天若日子}}, who had been dispatched from {{ill|Takamagahara|ja|高天原}} to subjugate the {{ill|Ashihara no Nakatsukuni|ja|葦原中国}} (the Central Land of Reed Plains). However, Ame-wakahiko secretly plotted to claim the land for himself. When Ame-wakahiko was killed by a divine arrow sent from Takamagahara, Shitateruhime’s grief-stricken cries reached the heavens. Her mourning led to the descent of Ame-wakahiko's family, including his father {{ill|Amatsukunitama-no-Mikoto|ja|天津国玉神}}, to perform his funeral rites. During this event, her brother {{ill|Ajisukitakahikone|ja|阿遅鉏高日子根神}} was mistaken for the deceased Ame-wakahiko due to their resemblance, leading to a conflict. Shitateruhime composed a lament known as the ''Hina-buri'' (夷振), expressing her sorrow. {{ill|Kifune Shrine|simple|User:Immanuelle/Kifune Shrine|en}}|name=Shitateruhime|siblings=[[Ajisukitakahikone]]|spouse={{ill|Ame no Wakahiko|ja|10=en:draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ame-No-Wakahiko}}|image=File:Shitori-jinja, haiden.jpg|caption={{ill|Shitori Shrine (Tottori)|lt=Shitori Shrine|en}} where she is worshipped |image=File:Shitateruhime shinbutsu-zue.jpg |caption=A book depiction of her }} {{complex}} {{citation needed|Shitateruhime}} [[category:kk]] {{ill|Shitateruhime|lt=Shitateruhime-no-Mikoto|ja|シタテルヒメ|simple|User:Immanuelle/Shitateruhime|en:draft|8=fr}} is a daughter of {{ill|Tagorihime|ja|タキリビメ|simple|User:Immanuelle/Takiribime|en:draft|8=fr}}, one of the three sisters worshipped at [[Munakata Taisha|Munakata Taisha]] The origins of {{ill|Shitori Shrine (Tottori)|lt=Shitori Shrine|ja|4=fr|5=Shitori-jinja|6=ja|7=倭文神社_(湯梨浜町)|8=simple|9=User:Immanuelle/Shitori Shrine (Tottori)}} are unknown. Although there is no documentary evidence, it is believed that it began as the family shrine for the {{Nihongo|Shitori clan|倭文氏}} of [[Kofun period|Kofun period]] craftsmen who weavers, who regarded {{ill|Takehazuchi|lt=Takehazuchi-no-Mikoto|ja|天羽槌雄神|simple|User:Immanuelle/Takehazuchi|en:draft|8=fr}} as their ancestor. However, the shrine's legends are all centered around {{ill|Shitateruhime|lt=Shitateruhime-no-Mikoto|ja|シタテルヒメ|simple|User:Immanuelle/Shitateruhime|en:draft|8=fr}}, whom the shrine legend claims arrived in this location from [[Izumo Taisha|Izumo]] by boat. She established her residence on the mountain behind this shrine, and after her death, she was buried in a ''[[kofun|kofun]]'' constructed in the shrine's precincts.{{cite book |last1=Yoshiki |first1=Emi |title=Zenkoku 'Ichinomiya' tettei gaido |date=2007 |publisher=PHP Institute |isbn=978-4569669304 |language=Japanese}} [[ja:シタテルヒメ]] == Overview == In the ''{{ill|Kojiki|ja|古事記}}'', she is referred to as '''Takahime-no-Mikoto''' (高比売命) and also as '''Shitateruhime-no-Mikoto''' (下光比売命). In the ''{{ill|Nihon Shoki|ja|日本書紀}}'', she appears as '''Shitateruhime''' (下照姫) or '''Shitateruhime-no-Mikoto''', and in the ''{{ill|Sendai Kuji Hongi|ja|先代旧事本紀}}'', she is called '''Shitateruhime-no-Mikoto'''. According to the ''Kojiki'' and the ''Nihon Shoki,'' she married {{ill|Ame-No-Wakahiko|ja|天若日子}}, who had been dispatched from {{ill|Takamagahara|ja|高天原}} to subjugate the {{ill|Ashihara no Nakatsukuni|ja|葦原中国}} (the Central Land of Reed Plains). However, Ame-wakahiko secretly plotted to claim the land for himself. When Ame-wakahiko was killed by a divine arrow sent from Takamagahara, Shitateruhime’s grief-stricken cries reached the heavens. Her mourning led to the descent of Ame-wakahiko's family, including his father {{ill|Amatsukunitama-no-Mikoto|ja|天津国玉神}}, to perform his funeral rites. During this event, her brother {{ill|Ajisukitakahikone|ja|阿遅鉏高日子根神}} was mistaken for the deceased Ame-wakahiko due to their resemblance, leading to a conflict. Shitateruhime composed a lament known as the ''Hina-buri'' (夷振), expressing her sorrow. [[Category:Japanese deities]] [[Category:Kunitsukami]] [[Category:Goddesses]] [[ja:下光比売命]] == Marriage == In many versions of the myth {{ill|Ame no Hohi|en}} did not send a word for three years after going down to earth, all the gods gathered up, and {{ill|Ame no Wakahiko|ja|10=en:draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ame-No-Wakahiko}} was one who was chosen to rule the earth. In many versions {{ill|Ame no Wakahiko|ja|10=en:draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ame-No-Wakahiko}} was given a bow.{{Cite web|title=Encyclopedia of Shinto - Home: Kami in Classic Texts: Ame no Wakahiko|url=http://eos.kokugakuin.ac.jp/modules/xwords/entry.php?entryID=46|access-date=2020-09-29|website=eos.kokugakuin.ac.jp}}{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=xdfgjV2kw6oC&q=Ame+no+Wakahiko&pg=PA6|title=Japanese Mythology A to Z|last=Roberts|first=Jeremy|date=2009|publisher=Infobase Publishing|isbn=978-1-4381-2802-3|language=en}} In some versions, however, Ame no Wakahiko is the son of Ame no Hohi and Ame no Wakahiko was sent to earth to look for him.{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=xdfgjV2kw6oC&dq=Ame+no+Wakahiko&pg=PA6|title=Japanese Mythology a to Z|publisher=Infobase|year=2009|isbn=9781438128023}} She married {{ill|Ame no Wakahiko|ja|10=en:draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ame-No-Wakahiko}}, when he came from heaven to discuss the "{{ill|Kuni-yuzuri|en}}". === Death === Eight years later, the gods had not yet heard a response so they sent a bird named Nakime down to earth to check in on him. Following the advice of a wise woman, Ame no Wakahiko used his bow to shoot the bird.{{Cite book|title=Handbook of Japanese mythology|last=Ashkenazi|first=Michael|date=2008|publisher=Oxford University Press|isbn=978-0-19-533262-9|series=Handbooks of world mythology|location=Oxford|pages=114}} The bird was killed but the arrow flew all the way to heaven. {{ill|Takamimusubi|en}} saw the arrow and threw it back at the earth where it hit Ame no Wakahiko while he was laying in bed, killing him.{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=uAj_PQ8o40sC&q=Takamimusubi|title=The East|date=1992|publisher=East Publications, Incorporated|language=en}} Other versions state that {{ill|Amaterasu|en}} was the one who shot the arrow back at him.{{cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=FlZxh5OaZxoC&pg=PA38|title=Impurity and Death: A Japanese Perspective|last=Abe|first=C.|publisher=Universal Publishers|year=2003|isbn=978-1-58112-195-7|page=38|access-date=2020-09-29}} This myth is the origin of a Japanese saying about the returning arrow. It is likely also be a mythicisation of attempts made by the {{ill|Yamato Kingship|en}} to impose its authority over neighbouring states. === Funeral === After Ame no Wakahiko's death, his parents built a hut (喪屋 moya) for their son. {{ill|Ajisukitakahikone|en}} went down to pay his respect. However, due to Ajisukitakahikone looking similar to Ame no Wakahiko he was mistaken to be Ame no Wakahiko brought back to life. Ajisukitakahikone was offended by this and destroyed the hut and kicked it. The hut landed in the land of Mino and became a mountain called Moyama.{{Cite book|title=Nihongi: Chronicles of Japan from the Earliest Times to A.D. 697, Volume 1|chapter=Book II|chapter-url=https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/Nihongi:_Chronicles_of_Japan_from_the_Earliest_Times_to_A.D._697/Book_II}} When {{ill|Ame no Wakahiko|ja|10=en:draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ame-No-Wakahiko}} passed away, Shitateruhime's sorrowful voice was heard in the Plain of High Heaven. During his funeral, Amewakahiko's father, Amatsukunitama, and other family members confused Shitateruhime's step-brother, [[Ajisukitakahikone]], for the deceased Amewakahiko. [[Ajisukitakahikone]] left in rage. In response, Shitateruhime sang a song of a type called hinaburi, or "rustic song" to honor her deceased husband.{{Cite web|title=Encyclopedia of Shinto詳細|url=https://d-museum.kokugakuin.ac.jp/eos/detail/?id=9155|access-date=2024-03-24|website=國學院大學デジタルミュージアム|language=ja}} == Genealogy == [[File:Ohokuninushi family tree.png|thumb|250px|right|Genealogy of Ōkuninushi (''Kojiki''). Blue indicates male deities, red indicates female deities, and yellow indicates unspecified gender.]] According to the ''Kojiki,'' Shitateruhime is the daughter of {{ill|Ōkuninushi|ja|大国主神}} and {{ill|Takirihime-no-Mikoto|ja|多紀理毘売命|1=Tagorihime}}, making her the sister of {{ill|Ajisukitakahikone|ja|阿遅鉏高日子根神}}. This genealogy is also supported by the ''Sendai Kuji Hongi.'' == Shrines == Shitateruhime is enshrined at several locations, including: * {{ill|Hime Shrine (Toyama)|ja|比賣神社}} in {{ill|Toyama Prefecture|ja|富山県}}, where she is the main deity. * {{ill|Tamatsuoka Shrine|ja|玉津岡神社}} in {{ill|Kyoto Prefecture|ja|京都府}}, dedicated to her worship. * {{ill|Himekoso Shrine|ja|比売許曽神社}} in {{ill|Osaka Prefecture|ja|大阪府}}. * {{ill|Izumo Taisha|ja|出雲大社}}’s external shrine, known as ''Ōanamochi-no-Miko Tamae Shrine'' (大穴持御子玉江神社). == Related Articles == * {{ill|List of Japanese deities|ja|日本の神の一覧}} * {{ill|Munakata clan|ja|宗像氏|simple|User:Immanuelle/Munakata_clan|ja|宗像氏|fr|Clan Munakata}} ==References== {{reflist|draft}} == Further reading == * Jugon, Jean-Claude. While most edits are by Immanuelle there might be a few from other users. [[User:Immanuelle|Immanuelle]] ([[User talk:Immanuelle|talk]]) 09:35, 18 February 2025 (UTC)}} {{Expand Japanese|シタテルヒメ}} {{Infobox deity | type = [[Shinto]] | father = [[Ōkuninushi]] | mother = {{ill|Tagorihime|ja|タキリビメ|simple|User:Immanuelle/Takiribime|en:draft}} |cult_centre={{ill|Shitori Shrine (Tottori)|lt=Shitori Shrine|en}},
{{ill|Kifune Shrine|simple|User:Immanuelle/Kifune Shrine|en}}|name=Shitateruhime|siblings=[[Ajisukitakahikone]]|spouse={{ill|Ame no Wakahiko|ja|10=en:draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ame-No-Wakahiko}}|image=File:Shitori-jinja, haiden.jpg|caption={{ill|Shitori Shrine (Tottori)|lt=Shitori Shrine|en}} where she is worshipped |image=File:Shitateruhime shinbutsu-zue.jpg |caption=A book depiction of her }} {{complex}} {{citation needed|Shitateruhime}} [[category:kk]] {{ill|Shitateruhime|lt=Shitateruhime-no-Mikoto|ja|シタテルヒメ|simple|User:Immanuelle/Shitateruhime|en:draft|8=fr}} is a daughter of {{ill|Tagorihime|ja|タキリビメ|simple|User:Immanuelle/Takiribime|en:draft|8=fr}}, one of the three sisters worshipped at [[Munakata Taisha|Munakata Taisha]] The origins of {{ill|Shitori Shrine (Tottori)|lt=Shitori Shrine|ja|4=fr|5=Shitori-jinja|6=ja|7=倭文神社_(湯梨浜町)|8=simple|9=User:Immanuelle/Shitori Shrine (Tottori)}} are unknown. Although there is no documentary evidence, it is believed that it began as the family shrine for the {{Nihongo|Shitori clan|倭文氏}} of [[Kofun period|Kofun period]] craftsmen who weavers, who regarded {{ill|Takehazuchi|lt=Takehazuchi-no-Mikoto|ja|天羽槌雄神|simple|User:Immanuelle/Takehazuchi|en:draft|8=fr}} as their ancestor. However, the shrine's legends are all centered around {{ill|Shitateruhime|lt=Shitateruhime-no-Mikoto|ja|シタテルヒメ|simple|User:Immanuelle/Shitateruhime|en:draft|8=fr}}, whom the shrine legend claims arrived in this location from [[Izumo Taisha|Izumo]] by boat. She established her residence on the mountain behind this shrine, and after her death, she was buried in a ''[[kofun|kofun]]'' constructed in the shrine's precincts.{{cite book |last1=Yoshiki |first1=Emi |title=Zenkoku 'Ichinomiya' tettei gaido |date=2007 |publisher=PHP Institute |isbn=978-4569669304 |language=Japanese}} [[ja:シタテルヒメ]] == Overview == In the ''{{ill|Kojiki|ja|古事記}}'', she is referred to as '''Takahime-no-Mikoto''' (高比売命) and also as '''Shitateruhime-no-Mikoto''' (下光比売命). In the ''{{ill|Nihon Shoki|ja|日本書紀}}'', she appears as '''Shitateruhime''' (下照姫) or '''Shitateruhime-no-Mikoto''', and in the ''{{ill|Sendai Kuji Hongi|ja|先代旧事本紀}}'', she is called '''Shitateruhime-no-Mikoto'''. According to the ''Kojiki'' and the ''Nihon Shoki,'' she married {{ill|Ame-No-Wakahiko|ja|天若日子}}, who had been dispatched from {{ill|Takamagahara|ja|高天原}} to subjugate the {{ill|Ashihara no Nakatsukuni|ja|葦原中国}} (the Central Land of Reed Plains). However, Ame-wakahiko secretly plotted to claim the land for himself. When Ame-wakahiko was killed by a divine arrow sent from Takamagahara, Shitateruhime’s grief-stricken cries reached the heavens. Her mourning led to the descent of Ame-wakahiko's family, including his father {{ill|Amatsukunitama-no-Mikoto|ja|天津国玉神}}, to perform his funeral rites. During this event, her brother {{ill|Ajisukitakahikone|ja|阿遅鉏高日子根神}} was mistaken for the deceased Ame-wakahiko due to their resemblance, leading to a conflict. Shitateruhime composed a lament known as the ''Hina-buri'' (夷振), expressing her sorrow. [[Category:Japanese deities]] [[Category:Kunitsukami]] [[Category:Goddesses]] [[ja:下光比売命]] == Marriage == In many versions of the myth {{ill|Ame no Hohi|en}} did not send a word for three years after going down to earth, all the gods gathered up, and {{ill|Ame no Wakahiko|ja|10=en:draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ame-No-Wakahiko}} was one who was chosen to rule the earth. In many versions {{ill|Ame no Wakahiko|ja|10=en:draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ame-No-Wakahiko}} was given a bow.{{Cite web|title=Encyclopedia of Shinto - Home: Kami in Classic Texts: Ame no Wakahiko|url=http://eos.kokugakuin.ac.jp/modules/xwords/entry.php?entryID=46|access-date=2020-09-29|website=eos.kokugakuin.ac.jp}}{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=xdfgjV2kw6oC&q=Ame+no+Wakahiko&pg=PA6|title=Japanese Mythology A to Z|last=Roberts|first=Jeremy|date=2009|publisher=Infobase Publishing|isbn=978-1-4381-2802-3|language=en}} In some versions, however, Ame no Wakahiko is the son of Ame no Hohi and Ame no Wakahiko was sent to earth to look for him.{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=xdfgjV2kw6oC&dq=Ame+no+Wakahiko&pg=PA6|title=Japanese Mythology a to Z|publisher=Infobase|year=2009|isbn=9781438128023}} She married {{ill|Ame no Wakahiko|ja|10=en:draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ame-No-Wakahiko}}, when he came from heaven to discuss the "{{ill|Kuni-yuzuri|en}}". === Death === Eight years later, the gods had not yet heard a response so they sent a bird named Nakime down to earth to check in on him. Following the advice of a wise woman, Ame no Wakahiko used his bow to shoot the bird.{{Cite book|title=Handbook of Japanese mythology|last=Ashkenazi|first=Michael|date=2008|publisher=Oxford University Press|isbn=978-0-19-533262-9|series=Handbooks of world mythology|location=Oxford|pages=114}} The bird was killed but the arrow flew all the way to heaven. {{ill|Takamimusubi|en}} saw the arrow and threw it back at the earth where it hit Ame no Wakahiko while he was laying in bed, killing him.{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=uAj_PQ8o40sC&q=Takamimusubi|title=The East|date=1992|publisher=East Publications, Incorporated|language=en}} Other versions state that {{ill|Amaterasu|en}} was the one who shot the arrow back at him.{{cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=FlZxh5OaZxoC&pg=PA38|title=Impurity and Death: A Japanese Perspective|last=Abe|first=C.|publisher=Universal Publishers|year=2003|isbn=978-1-58112-195-7|page=38|access-date=2020-09-29}} This myth is the origin of a Japanese saying about the returning arrow. It is likely also be a mythicisation of attempts made by the {{ill|Yamato Kingship|en}} to impose its authority over neighbouring states. === Funeral === After Ame no Wakahiko's death, his parents built a hut (喪屋 moya) for their son. {{ill|Ajisukitakahikone|en}} went down to pay his respect. However, due to Ajisukitakahikone looking similar to Ame no Wakahiko he was mistaken to be Ame no Wakahiko brought back to life. Ajisukitakahikone was offended by this and destroyed the hut and kicked it. The hut landed in the land of Mino and became a mountain called Moyama.{{Cite book|title=Nihongi: Chronicles of Japan from the Earliest Times to A.D. 697, Volume 1|chapter=Book II|chapter-url=https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/Nihongi:_Chronicles_of_Japan_from_the_Earliest_Times_to_A.D._697/Book_II}} When {{ill|Ame no Wakahiko|ja|10=en:draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ame-No-Wakahiko}} passed away, Shitateruhime's sorrowful voice was heard in the Plain of High Heaven. During his funeral, Amewakahiko's father, Amatsukunitama, and other family members confused Shitateruhime's step-brother, [[Ajisukitakahikone]], for the deceased Amewakahiko. [[Ajisukitakahikone]] left in rage. In response, Shitateruhime sang a song of a type called hinaburi, or "rustic song" to honor her deceased husband.{{Cite web|title=Encyclopedia of Shinto詳細|url=https://d-museum.kokugakuin.ac.jp/eos/detail/?id=9155|access-date=2024-03-24|website=國學院大學デジタルミュージアム|language=ja}} == Genealogy == [[File:Ohokuninushi family tree.png|thumb|250px|right|Genealogy of Ōkuninushi (''Kojiki''). Blue indicates male deities, red indicates female deities, and yellow indicates unspecified gender.]] According to the ''Kojiki,'' Shitateruhime is the daughter of {{ill|Ōkuninushi|ja|大国主神}} and {{ill|Takirihime-no-Mikoto|ja|多紀理毘売命|1=Tagorihime}}, making her the sister of {{ill|Ajisukitakahikone|ja|阿遅鉏高日子根神}}. This genealogy is also supported by the ''Sendai Kuji Hongi.'' == Shrines == Shitateruhime is enshrined at several locations, including: * {{ill|Hime Shrine (Toyama)|ja|比賣神社}} in {{ill|Toyama Prefecture|ja|富山県}}, where she is the main deity. * {{ill|Tamatsuoka Shrine|ja|玉津岡神社}} in {{ill|Kyoto Prefecture|ja|京都府}}, dedicated to her worship. * {{ill|Himekoso Shrine|ja|比売許曽神社}} in {{ill|Osaka Prefecture|ja|大阪府}}. * {{ill|Izumo Taisha|ja|出雲大社}}’s external shrine, known as ''Ōanamochi-no-Miko Tamae Shrine'' (大穴持御子玉江神社). == Related Articles == * {{ill|List of Japanese deities|ja|日本の神の一覧}} * {{ill|Munakata clan|ja|宗像氏|simple|User:Immanuelle/Munakata_clan|ja|宗像氏|fr|Clan Munakata}} ==References== {{reflist|draft}} == Further reading == * Jugon, Jean-Claude. Shitateruhime composed a lament known as the ''Hina-buri'' (夷振), expressing her sorrow.
